paragraphs.text: THE FIRST DAY

To think that men should have presumed so far! Some of them laid down three first principles of all things, God, the pattern and matter, as Plato and his disciples did. They asserted that these were incorruptible, uncreated and without beginning, and that God made the world not as the creator of matter but as a craftsman who looks to a pattern, that is, to an idea. He made it, they said, out of matter, which they call hyle and which is said to have given all things the causes of their coming into being. They also held that the world itself was incorruptible, neither created nor made. Others again, as Aristotle and his followers saw fit to argue, posited two principles, matter and form, and along with them a third, called the efficient principle, which had the power to carry out properly whatever it judged should be undertaken.

What could be more absurd, then, than to join the eternity of the work to the eternity of almighty God, or to call the work itself God, and to pay divine honours to the sky, the earth and the sea? This led them to believe that the parts of the world were gods, although they argue a good deal among themselves even about the world itself.

For Pythagoras asserts that there is one world; others say that there are countless worlds, as Democritus writes, to whom antiquity granted the greatest authority on matters of nature. Aristotle presumes to say that the world itself has always existed and always will. Plato, on the other hand, ventures to maintain that it has not always existed but will always exist. Very many, however, testify in their writings that it neither always existed nor will always exist.

Amid such disagreements among them, what judgement of the truth can there be, when some say that the world itself is God, because a divine mind seems, as they think, to dwell in it, others say its parts are gods, and others say both? On this view one cannot grasp what shape the gods have, how many there are, where they are, or what their life or concern is, since, if one judges by the world, one would have to think of God as revolving, round, burning, driven by certain motions, without sense, carried along by a motion not his own but another's.

Therefore holy Moses, foreseeing by the divine Spirit that these errors of men would arise, and had perhaps already begun, says at the opening of his account: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." In these words he embraces the beginning of things, the author of the world and the creation of matter, so that you might know that God was before the beginning of the world, or rather that he himself is the beginning of all things. So in the Gospel, when people said to the Son of God, "Who are you?", he answered, "The beginning, who also speak to you." He himself gave things the beginning of their coming into being, and he himself is the creator of the world, not an imitator of matter guided by some idea, shaping his works not as he willed but according to a model set before him. He also puts it beautifully: "In the beginning he made," to express the inconceivable speed of the work, since he set out the result of the completed operation before giving any sign that it had begun.

We ought to consider who says this. It is Moses, certainly, who was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; whom Pharaoh's daughter, having taken him from the river, loved as a son, and wished, supported by royal resources, to be trained and instructed in all the disciplines of worldly learning. Although he took his name from water, he did not think it right to say that all things consist of water, as Thales says. And although he was brought up in the royal court, he preferred for love of justice to go into voluntary exile rather than to acquire, at the summit of tyranny, the enjoyment of sin along with its delights. Indeed, before he was called to the task of freeing his people, moved by a natural zeal for fairness, he avenged one of his own people who was being wronged, thereby exposing himself to hatred and tearing himself away from pleasure. Shunning all the turmoil of the royal household, he withdrew into the seclusion of Ethiopia, and there, removed from all other business, he gave his whole mind to the knowledge of God, so that he might see the glory of God face to face. Scripture bears witness to him that no prophet has arisen again in Israel like Moses, who knew the Lord face to face, not in a vision nor in a dream, but who spoke with the most high God mouth to mouth, not in a likeness nor in riddles, but was granted the clear and plain favour of the divine presence.

So he opened his mouth and poured out what the Lord spoke within him, according to what he had said to him when he sent him to King Pharaoh: "Go, and I will open your mouth and teach you what you must say." For if he had received from God what he was to say about letting the people go, how much more what he was to say about heaven! And so, not in the persuasive words of human wisdom nor in the deceptive disputations of philosophy, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, as a witness of the divine work, he dared to say: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." He did not wait for the world to come together through the collision of atoms, a slow and idle business, nor did he think he should describe a kind of pupil of matter who by contemplating it could fashion the world; he thought he should describe God as its author. For this man, full of wisdom, saw that the divine mind alone holds the substance of things visible and invisible and the causes of things, and that it is not, as the philosophers argue, a stronger binding of atoms that accounts for their enduring permanence. He judged that those who gave heaven and earth such tiny and insubstantial first principles were weaving a spider's web; principles that came together by chance would fall apart by chance and at random, unless they held together by the divine power of their governor. And it is not surprising that those who do not know God, by whom all things are ruled and governed, do not know the governor. Let us therefore follow the one who knew both the author and the governor, and let us not be led astray by empty opinions.

"In the beginning," he says. What a fine order: first to assert what they usually deny, so that they might recognise that the world has a beginning, and men might not suppose that the world is without beginning. So David too, speaking of heaven and earth and sea, says: "In wisdom you have made all things." He gave the world a beginning, then, and he also gave the creature weakness, so that we should not believe it to be without beginning, uncreated, and a sharer in the divine substance. And he finely added "made," so that no one should think there was any delay in the making, and so that people might understand even from this how incomparable a worker he is, who completed so great a work in a brief and tiny moment of his activity, so that the effect of his will outran any sense of time. No one saw him at work, but they recognised that he had worked. Where, then, is any delay, when you read: "For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created"? He who completed the majesty of so great a work in a moment of his will needed neither the use of skill nor of strength, so that he caused what did not exist to exist so swiftly that neither did the will run ahead of the work nor the work ahead of the will.

You marvel at the work; you ask who the worker is, who gave a beginning to so great a work, who made it so quickly. He added at once, saying that God made heaven and earth. You have heard the author; you ought not to doubt. This is he in whom Melchizedek blessed Abraham, father of many nations, saying: "Blessed be Abraham by God most high, who made heaven and earth." And Abraham believed and said: "I stretch out my hand to God most high, who made heaven and earth." You see that no man discovered this, but God announced it. For Melchizedek is God, who is king of peace and of justice, having neither beginning of days nor end. It is no wonder, then, if God, who is without beginning, gave a beginning to all things, so that what did not exist might begin to exist. It is no wonder if God, who holds all things together by his power and embraces the universe in his incomprehensible majesty, made these things that are seen, since he also made those that are not seen. And who would deny that invisible things are greater than those that are seen, since the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal? Who would doubt that God made these things, who speaks through the prophet and says: "Who has measured the water in his hand, and the heaven with his palm, and the whole earth in his closed hand? Who has set the mountains on a scale, and the rocks in a balance, and the forests under a yoke? Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor, or who has instructed him?" Of him we also read elsewhere that he holds the circle of the earth and has made the earth as nothing. And Jeremiah says: "The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from under this heaven. The Lord, who made the earth by his power, and set it right and completed it by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretched out the heaven, and the multitude of water in the heaven." And he added: "Man has become foolish through his own knowledge." For whoever follows the corruptible things of the world, and thinks that from them he can grasp the truth of the divine nature, how can he fail to be made a fool by the cunning of crafty argument?

So when you hear so many oracles in which God testifies that he made the world, do not believe that it is without beginning just because the world is said to be like a sphere, so that it seems to have no beginning at all; and because, when it thunders, all things seem to be shaken as though in a circle, so that you cannot easily grasp where it begins and where it ends, since it is held to be impossible for the senses to determine the beginning of a circle. For you cannot find the beginning of a sphere, nor where the orb of the moon began or where it ends in the moon's monthly waning. Yet if you yourself cannot grasp it, that does not mean it did not begin or will never end. If you draw a circle yourself with ink or a stylus, or trace it with a compass, you will not easily make out with your eyes or recall with your mind, after some time has passed, where you began or where you stopped; and yet you yourself are your own witness that you both began and stopped. For even if it escapes the senses, that does not overturn the truth. Things that have a beginning also have an end, and it is clear that things to which an end is given were given a beginning. And the Saviour himself teaches in his Gospel that the world will have an end, saying: "For the form of this world is passing away," and "Heaven and earth will pass away," and below:

"Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world." How, then, do they assert that the world is coeternal with God, associate the creature with the creator of all things and argue that it is his equal, and think that the material body of the world should be joined to that invisible and inaccessible divine nature? This especially when, by their own reasoning, they cannot deny that if the parts of a thing are subject to corruption and change, then the whole must be subject to the same experiences to which its own portions are liable.

He who says, "In the beginning God made heaven and earth," teaches, then, that there is a beginning. "Beginning" refers either to time, or to number, or to a foundation, as in [?] a house the beginning is the foundation. We know from the authority of the Scriptures that one can also speak of the beginning of conversion and of corruption. The beginning of a craft, too, is the craft itself, from which the work of various craftsmen then began. The beginning of good works is also their highest end; thus the beginning of mercy is that what you do should please God, for it is chiefly this that moves us to bring help to others. The divine power, too, is expressed by this name. It refers to time if you mean to say at what time God made heaven and earth, that is, at the start of the world, when it began to be made, as Wisdom says: "When he was preparing the heavens, I was with him." If we refer it to number, it is fitting to understand it thus: first of all he made heaven and earth, and then hills, regions and uninhabitable borders; or thus: before the other visible creatures, the day, the night, the fruit-bearing trees and the various kinds of living things, he made heaven and earth. If you refer it to a foundation, you have read that the beginning of the earth is its foundation, as Wisdom says: "When he made the strong foundations of the earth, I was beside him, setting things in order." There is also a beginning of good instruction, as in the saying: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord," since whoever fears the Lord turns aside from error and directs his ways onto the path of virtue. For unless someone fears God, he cannot renounce sin.

We can take in the same way the saying: "This month shall be for you the beginning of months," although this may also be understood of time, since he was speaking of the Lord's Passover, which is celebrated at the beginning of spring. So it was in this beginning of months that he made heaven and earth, because it was from then that the world had to take its start, when the mild weather of spring was suited to all things. Hence the year, too, reflects the image of the world at its birth, so that after the ice of winter and the wintry gloom the brightness of springtime shines out more clearly than usual. The first rising of the world, then, gave a pattern to the future cycles of the years, so that by this law the turns of the years should arise, and at the beginning of each year the earth should bring forth new shoots from seeds, at the time when the Lord God first said: "Let the earth bring forth green grass, yielding seed according to its kind and likeness, and the fruit tree bearing fruit." And at once the earth brought forth green grass and the fruit tree. In this both the divine providence of perpetual moderation and the speed of the sprouting earth support the view that it was springtime. For although God could have commanded at any time, and earthly nature could have obeyed, so that the earth, quickened by the warmth of the heavenly command, would have sprouted and brought forth its offspring amid the ice of winter and the wintry frosts, it was not in keeping with the eternal plan that fields bound fast by hard frost should suddenly loosen into green fruits, or that flowers should be mingled with bristling frost. So, to show that the creation of the world took place in spring, Scripture says: "This month is for you the beginning of months; it is the first for you among the months of the year," calling springtime the first month. For it was fitting that the beginning of the year should be the beginning of generation, and that generation itself should be fostered by gentler breezes. For the tender beginnings of things could not have endured the hardship of harsher cold or borne the harm of scorching heat.

At the same time we may add [?] this, since it fits rightly: that entrance into this generation and into these uses seems to have been granted at the very time when the lawful passage from this generation into regeneration takes place. For it was in springtime that the children of Israel left Egypt and crossed through the sea, baptised in the cloud and in the sea, as the Apostle said; and at that time each year the Pasch of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, that is, the passage of souls from vices to virtue, from the passions of the flesh to grace and soberness of mind, from the leaven of malice and wickedness to truth and sincerity. So to the regenerated it is said: "This month is for you the beginning of months; it is the first for you among the months of the year." For the one who is washed abandons and forsakes that spiritual Pharaoh, the prince of this world, saying: "I renounce you, devil, and your works and your dominion." No longer will he serve him, either in the earthly passions of this body or in the errors of a depraved mind; with all malice sunk like lead, and armed on the right hand and on the left with good works, he strives to cross the straits of this world without stumbling. In the book called Numbers, too, Scripture says: "Amalek is the beginning of the nations, and his seed shall perish." Yet Amalek is certainly not the first of all the nations; but since by interpretation Amalek is taken [?] to mean "of the wicked," and the nations are wicked, consider whether we should not understand him as the prince of this world, who rules over the nations that do his will, and whose seed will perish. His seed are the ungodly and unbelieving, to whom the Lord says: [?] "You are of your father the devil."

There is also a mystical beginning, as in the saying: "I am the first and the last, the beginning and the end," and especially that passage in the Gospel where the Lord, asked who he was, answered: "The beginning, who also speak to you." He is truly, and according to [?], the beginning of all things, because there is no one before him, and the end, because there is no one beyond him. According to the Gospel he is the beginning of the ways of the Lord in his works, so that through him the human race might learn to follow the ways of the Lord and to do the works of God. In this beginning, then, that is, in Christ, God made heaven and earth, because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him, because in him all things hold together, and he is the firstborn of all creation, either because he is before every creature, or because he is holy, for the firstborn are holy, as Israel is firstborn, not because he was before all, but because he was holier than the rest. And the Lord is holy above every creature, even according to his taking on of a body, because he alone is without sin, he alone without vanity, while every creature is subject to vanity.

We can also understand "In the beginning God made heaven and earth" to mean before time, just as the beginning of a road is not yet the road and the beginning of a house is not yet the house. Indeed, others have said "en kephalaiō," as it were "in the head," by which it is meant that the sum of the work was completed briefly and in a tiny moment. There are, then, some who take "beginning" not as referring to time, but as before time, and as "kephalaion" or "head," so that we may call it [?] the sum of the work, because heaven and earth are the sum of visible things. These seem to concern not only [?] of this world, but also to serve as an indication of invisible things and a kind of proof of what is not seen, as in the prophetic saying: "The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands." Following this, the Apostle reached the same conclusion in other words, saying: "For his invisible things are understood through the things that have been made." For we easily understand that he is the author of angels and dominions and powers who, in a moment of his command, made out of nothing this great beauty of the world, which did not exist, and granted substance to things and causes that did not exist.

For this world is a model of the divine working, since when the work is seen, the worker is displayed. Among the arts, some are performative, consisting in the movement of the body or the sound of the voice: once the movement or sound has ceased, nothing is left over or remains for the spectators or listeners. Others are [?], exercising the vigour of the mind. Others are of such a kind that even when the work of the making has ceased, the product remains visible, such as building and weaving, which display the craftsman's skill even when he is silent, so that his work bears witness on behalf of its maker. In the same way this world is a sign of the divine majesty, so that through it the wisdom of God is made manifest. Seeing it, and at the same time lifting the eyes of his mind to the invisible things, the prophet says: "How magnificent are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made all things."

Nor is it without purpose that we read "made," since many of the pagans, who want the world to be coeternal with God as a kind of shadow of the divine power, also assert that it exists of its own accord. And although they admit that God is its cause, they want him to be its cause not by his will and design, but in the way that a body is the cause of a shadow; for a shadow clings to a body, and brightness to a light, by natural association rather than by the choice of the will. So Moses says beautifully that God made heaven and earth. He did not say that he caused it to subsist, nor that he provided the world with a cause of its existence, but that he made it: as one who is good, what would be useful; as one who is wise, what he judged best; as one who is almighty, what he foresaw would be greatest. And how could it be like a shadow when there was no body, since there cannot be a bodily shadow of the bodiless God?

How, too, could the radiance of a bodiless light be bodily? But if you seek the radiance of God, it is the Son, the image of the invisible God. As God is, so is the image: God is invisible, and the image too is invisible; for he is the radiance of the Father's glory and the image of his substance. "In the beginning," he says, "God made heaven and earth." So the world was made, and what did not exist began to exist; but the Word of God was in the beginning and always was. And the angels, dominions and powers, even if they began at some point, nevertheless already existed when this world was made. For all things were created and established, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers: "All things," he says, "were created through him and unto him." What does "created unto him" mean? That he is the heir of the Father, since the inheritance passed from the Father to him, as the Father says: "Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance." Yet this inheritance passed from the Father to the Son and returns from the Son to the Father. So the Apostle, both in this passage, excellently called the Son the author of all things who holds all things together by his majesty, and in Romans says of the Father: "For from him and through him and unto him are all things." "From him" is the beginning and origin of the substance of all things, that is, from his will and power, for all things began from his will, because there is one God the Father, from whom are all things; indeed he made them as if from his own, since he made them from whatever he willed. "Through him" is their continuance; "unto him," their end. From him, then, comes the matter; through him the working, which has bound and held the universe together; unto him, because all things abide and hold together by his power for as long as he wills, and their end returns to the will of God, and by his decision they are dissolved.

In the beginning of time, then, God made heaven and earth. Time begins with this world and not before it, and a day is a portion of time, not its beginning. From the order of the reading we could show that the Lord first made day and night, which are the alternations of time, and on the second day made the firmament, by which he divided the water under heaven from the water above heaven. Still, for the present argument it is enough that in the beginning he made heaven, which holds the first place in creation and is its cause, and made earth, in which the substance of creation would be. In these two the four elements were created, from which everything in the world is produced. The four elements are heaven (fire), air, water and earth, and they are mixed with one another in everything. You may find fire in earth, for it is often struck out of stones and iron; and in heaven, though the sky is fiery and sparkles with shining stars, water can be understood to exist, since there is water above heaven, and from that higher region it is often sent down to earth in heavy rain. We could gather much more on these matters if we saw that they did anything to build up the Church. But since busying ourselves with them is fruitless work, let us rather turn our minds to things that advance us toward eternal life.

On the quality and substance of heaven, then, it is enough to set out what we find in the writings of Isaiah, who described the nature of heaven in plain and ordinary words when he said that God made heaven firm like smoke, meaning to show that its nature is fine and not solid. As for its appearance, what he himself said of the firmament of heaven is more than enough, that God made heaven like a vault, because everything that happens on sea and land is enclosed within the circuit of heaven. The same is meant when we read that God stretched out the heaven. It is stretched out either like a skin for tents, the dwellings of the saints, or like a book, so that in it may be written the names of the many who by faith and devotion have earned the grace of Christ, to whom it is said: "Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven [?]."

Likewise, discussing the quality or position of the earth would do nothing for our hope of what is to come, since for knowledge it is enough that the course of the divine Scriptures contains this: that he hung the earth upon nothing. Why should we debate whether it hangs in the air or rests on water, and so start a dispute over how the thin and softer nature of air could bear the mass of the earth, or how, if it rests on the waters, the heavy bulk of the land does not sink and plunge into the water? Or how the waves of the sea do not give way before it and, driven from their place, pour out over its sides? Many have also said that the earth is in the middle of the air and stays unmoved by its own mass, because it stretches out evenly this way and that on every side. On this we think enough was said by the Lord to his servant Job, when he spoke through the cloud and said: "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have knowledge. Who set its measurements, if you know? Or who stretched the line upon it? Or on what were its circles fastened?" And further on: "I shut in the sea with gates and said: Thus far you shall come and no farther, but your waves shall be broken within you." Does God not plainly show that all things stand by his majesty, not by number, weight and measure? For a created thing does not give the law; it receives it, or keeps the law it has received. So the earth is not suspended as though on an even balance because it lies in the middle; rather, the majesty of God binds it by the law of his will, so that it remains stable above what is unstable and empty. The prophet David also bears witness to this when he says: "He founded the earth upon its firmness; it shall not be moved for ever and ever." Here God is proclaimed not merely as a craftsman but as almighty, one who has hung the earth not on some center but on the firm support of his command, and does not allow it to be moved. We ought therefore to take the measure spoken of as the measure not of a center but of divine judgment, for it is a measure not of skill but of power, a measure of justice, a measure of knowledge: nothing slips past his knowledge as though it were beyond measure, but all things lie under his knowledge as already measured. And when we read, "I have made firm its pillars," we cannot really suppose that the earth rests on pillars, but on the power that props up and sustains the substance of the earth. Further, you may gather how much the founding of the earth lies in God's power from this too, that it is written: "He looks on the earth and makes it tremble," and elsewhere: "Yet once more I shake the earth." So it does not stay unmoved by its own balance, but is often shaken at God's nod and will, as Job also says, that the Lord shakes it from its foundations and its pillars are made to totter; and elsewhere: "The underworld is naked before him, and death has no covering. He stretches out the north over nothing, he hangs the earth upon nothing, he binds up the water in his clouds. The pillars of heaven flew apart and trembled at his rebuke. By his power he calmed the sea, by his discipline he laid low the sea monster, and the bars of heaven fear him." By the will of God, then, the earth remains unmoved and stands for ever, according to the saying of Ecclesiastes, and by the will of God it is moved and shakes. It does not stand resting on its own foundations, nor does it stay stable on its own props; rather, the Lord established it and holds it by the firm support of his will, because in his hand are all the ends of the earth. And this simplicity of faith surpasses all arguments. Let others praise the fact that the earth never falls anywhere because by nature it holds its own region in the middle, since it must stay in that region and not lean to one side or the other, as it is not moved against nature but according to nature. Let them proclaim the excellence of the divine craftsman and eternal maker—for what craftsman has not received his skill from him, or who gave women wisdom in weaving or skill in varied work? I, however, who cannot grasp the depth of his majesty and the excellence of his art, do not entrust myself to calculations [?], balances and measures. I hold that all things rest on his will, because his will is the foundation of the universe, and it is because of him that this world still remains. This too we may support by the example of apostolic authority. For it is written that creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope. And creation itself will also be set free from slavery to corruption when the grace of divine reward [?].

As for the nature and quality of the substance of heaven, why should I list what the philosophers have [?] in their disputations? Some assert that heaven is composed of the four elements; others bring in some fifth nature, a new kind of body, to make it up, and imagine that there is an ethereal body in which neither fire nor air nor water nor earth is mixed. For, they say, the elements of this world each have their own course and use and natural motion: the heavier sink and are carried downward, while the empty and light rise upward, since each has its own proper motion. But in the circuit of a sphere these motions are confused and lose the force of their course, because a sphere revolves in its own orbit, and the upper parts change places with the lower and the lower with the upper. And where natural motions are changed, they say, the qualities of the substances must also usually change. Why then, they ask, do we not maintain that heaven is an ethereal body, so that it may not seem subject to corruption? For whatever is composed of corruptible elements must be dissolved. Indeed, precisely because these elements are of different natures, they cannot have a simple and undisturbed motion, since the differing motions of the elements fight against one another. For one motion [?] cannot suit all things and fit elements so far apart; what is suited to the light elements becomes unsuited to the heavier ones. So when heaven must move upward, it is weighed down by the earthy elements; when a downward course is required, that fiery vigor is dragged along by force, for it is compelled downward against the bent of its nature. But whatever is compelled toward its opposite, not by [?] nature but by necessity, is quickly dissolved and split into the parts it seems to be composed of, each returning to its own region. Considering this, then, and that such things cannot be stable, some have supposed that the body of heaven and the stars is ethereal, introducing some fifth nature of body, so that they might think the substance of heaven would last for ever.

But this opinion could not stand against the prophetic saying, which the divine majesty of our Lord Jesus Christ, our God, also confirmed in the Gospel. For David said: "In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail." The Lord confirmed this in the Gospel so fully as to say: "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away." So those who thought a fifth, ethereal body had to be brought in to defend the everlastingness of heaven achieve nothing, since they can equally see that a portion of a single member added unlike the rest usually brings decay to a body rather than otherwise. Notice at the same time that the prophet David, by naming earth first and heaven afterward, believed he was declaring the work of the Lord. For when he spoke and they were made, it makes no difference which you mention first, since both were made together; and at the same time he did so lest by this at least some precedence of divine substance seem to be awarded to heaven, so that it might be thought superior by the privilege of being created first. Let us therefore leave to their own quarrels those who refute one another in their disputations. For us, what is enough for salvation is not controversy in disputations but the truth of the commandments, not cleverness in argument but the faith of the mind, so that we may serve the Creator rather than the creature, who is God blessed for ever.

"Now the earth was invisible and unformed." A good builder first lays the foundation; then, once the foundation is laid, he marks out the parts of the building and adds its adornment. So when the foundation of the earth had been laid and the substance of heaven made firm—for these two are, as it were, the hinges of the universe—he went on: "Now the earth was invisible and unformed." Why "was"? Perhaps so that people would not [?] stretch their opinion out to infinity and without beginning, and say: "See, matter—that is, hylē, as the philosophers call it—had no beginning even according to divine Scripture." To those who say this you will answer that it is written: "Now Cain was a tiller of the earth"; and of the one called Jubal Scripture says: "He was the father who showed forth the psaltery and the harp"; and: "There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job." Let them stop raising a question about the word, especially since Moses said beforehand that God made the earth. It "was," then, from the time it was made. For if they say it exists without beginning, then, since they call not only the Lord but also hylē without beginning, let them define where it was. If it was in a place, then the place in which the matter of things, which had no beginning, existed is also claimed to have had no beginning. And if that seems absurd to believe of a place, see whether we must not perhaps suppose the earth to have been able to fly, held up by the oars of its wings, having no foundation. Where then shall we get wings for it—unless perhaps we turn to this purpose the meaning of the prophetic words, "From the wings of the earth we have heard wonders," and that other saying, "Woe to the land, the wings of ships"? But even if we take it so, in what air was the earth flying? Without air it could not fly, yet air could not yet exist, because no separation of the elements had been made out of the matter of things, since the elements themselves had not yet been made. Where then was this matter, held up by the oars of its wings? It was not in the air, for air is a body of the world; and that air is a body is taught by the reading, since when an arrow is shot at the spot the archer aims at, the air it cuts closes back up on itself at once. Where then was hylē—unless someone with a kind of mad persistence should say that it was in God? In that case God, whose nature is invisible and inviolable, who dwells in unapproachable light, the incomprehensible and most pure Spirit, would have been the place of the world's matter, and a portion of the world would have been in God—when not even his servants [?] are of this world, as we have it written: "They are not of this world, just as I am not of the world."

How then could invisible things be joined to visible things, and things unformed to him who gave order and beauty to all? Unless perhaps, because he said, "Now the earth was invisible," they believe it was invisible in its substance, and not because, being covered by the waters, it could not be visible to bodily eyes, just as many things lying in the depths of the waters escape the sight and keenness of the eyes. For nothing is invisible to God; the created world is judged, of course, by the estimate of a creature. The earth was invisible also because there was not yet light to illumine the world, not yet the sun; for the lights of heaven were made later. And if the ray of the sun often lights up even things covered [?] and by the splendor of its light reveals things sunk in the deep, who would doubt that what lies in the deep cannot be invisible to God? Unless perhaps we take the earth to be invisible in this sense: that it was not yet visited by the word and protection of God, since it had no human being for whose sake the Lord would look upon the earth, as it is written: "The Lord looked down on the children of men, to see if there were any who understood or sought God." And elsewhere it says: "From heaven he hurled judgment; the earth trembled and was still." And rightly was it invisible, because it was unformed, not yet having received fitting shape and appearance from its own Maker.

And perhaps they may say: "Why did God, as soon as he spoke and things were made, not at once give fitting adornment to the elements as they arose? As though heaven could not have shone out studded with stars the moment it was created, and earth have been clothed with flowers and fruits!" He certainly could have. But things are declared to have been first made and afterward set in order so that they would not be believed to be truly uncreated and without beginning, as they would be if the beauty of things seemed unbegotten from the start and not added later. The earth is read to have been unformed, and yet the same philosophers honor it with the privileges of eternity with which God is honored. What would they say if it had come forth complete [?] from its beginning? It is described as sunk beneath the waters, as though given over to a kind of shipwreck at its very start, and still some do not believe it was made: what if it could claim a beauty born with it? Add to this that God wished us to imitate him, so that we first make something and afterward make it beautiful, lest by attempting both at once we manage neither. Our faith, moreover, grows by a kind of steps. That is why God first made and afterward beautified: so that we might believe that the one who made is the one who adorned, and the one who adorned is the one who made; that we might not think one adorned and another created, but that the same one did both, first making and afterward setting in order, so that each might be believed by means of the other. You have clear testimony of this in the Gospel. [?] When he was about to raise Lazarus, the Lord ordered the Jews to roll the stone away from the tomb, so that having seen him dead they might afterward believe him raised. Then he called Lazarus, and he rose and came out with his hands and feet bound. Could not the one who could raise [?] the dead remove the stone? And could the one who was able to give life back to the dead not undo the knots of the bands? Could he who gave the power to walk to one whose feet were bound not have broken the bands and given him back free movement? But we surely see that he wished first to show that the man was dead, so that they might believe their own eyes; then to raise him; and third, to give the order that they themselves should loose the bands of burial, so that through these things faith might be poured into the unbelieving and belief might be born by certain steps.

So God first made heaven and earth, yet he willed that they be subject to an end, not as everlasting but as a corruptible creation. Hence he says in the book of Isaiah: "Lift up your eyes to heaven and look at the earth beneath, for heaven was made firm like smoke, but the earth will grow old like a garment." This is the earth that was formerly unformed. The seas had not yet been marked off by their bounds, and so the earth was flooded by wandering waves and deep whirlpools. Consider how even now the earth tends to bristle with marshy ooze and will not bear the plough where moisture poured over the land overflows. So it was unformed, being unploughed by the work of a skilful farmer, since there was as yet no one to till it. It was unformed because it was bare of growing things: not grassy along the banks of rivers, not shady with woods, not glad with crops, not shadowed by the brows of mountains, not fragrant with flowers, not pleasing with vineyards. Rightly was it unformed, since it lacked adornment, lacking the garlands of budding vines. For God wished to show that the world itself would have no charm unless its Maker clothed [?] it with varied adornment. Heaven itself, when overlaid with clouds, usually brings dread to the eyes and sadness to the mind; earth soaked with rain is distasteful; and the seas tossed by storms—what fears do they not strike? The beauty of the world is most lovely; but what would it be without light, what without mildness of climate, what without the gathering of the waters, beneath which the beginnings of this firmament were once held submerged? Take the sun from the earth, take the globes of the stars from heaven: all things bristle with darkness. So it was before the Lord poured light into this world. And so Scripture says that darkness was over the abyss. There was darkness because the brightness of light was lacking; there was darkness because the air itself is dark. Water itself is dark beneath a cloud, for "dark is the water in the clouds of the air." So darkness was over the abysses of the waters. For I do not think we should understand evil powers here, as though the Lord had created their wickedness, since wickedness is surely not substantial but accidental, a turning aside from the goodness of nature.

So in the founding of the world let the notion of wickedness be set aside for now, so that we may not seem to mix things that are tarnished into the divine work and the most beautiful creation, especially since there follows: "And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters." Though some take this to mean the air, and others the breath we breathe and draw in, the breath of this life-giving air, we nevertheless, in agreement with the judgment of the saints and the faithful, take it to mean the Holy Spirit, so that the working of the Trinity may shine out in the founding of the world. For after it was said first that in the beginning God made heaven and earth—that is, God made them in Christ, or God the Son of God made them, or God made them through the Son, since all things were made through him and without him nothing was made—there remained the fullness of the work in the Spirit, as it is written: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the breath of his mouth." So just as in the psalm we are taught the working of the Word, which is the Word of God, and the power that the Holy Spirit gave, so here the prophetic oracle rang out that God spoke and God made. The Spirit of God too was borne over the waters. For fittingly the Spirit was borne over them as the vault of heaven was to be adorned and the lands were to sprout, since through him the seeds of new births were to spring up, according to what the prophet said: "Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you will renew the face of the earth." Indeed, the Syriac, which is close to the Hebrew and agrees and corresponds with it in most of its language, reads: "And the Spirit of God was brooding over the waters," that is, giving them life, so as to bring them together into new creatures and by its warmth to quicken them to life. For we read also that the Holy Spirit is Creator, as [?] says: "The divine Spirit, who made me." So if the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, the darkness of hostile powers could not be over them where so great a grace claimed the place for itself. Or if, as some would have it, they take it to mean the air, let them answer why he said "the Spirit of God," when it would have been enough to say "spirit."

These people, then, hold that four elements were first produced by the Lord our God: heaven, earth, sea and air. They reason that fire and air, earth and water are the causes of things, and that the appearance and form of the world are made up of them. Where, then, could the darkness of spiritual wickedness have found a place, when the world was putting on the beauty of this majestic shape? Did God create wickedness at the same time? No: wickedness arises from us. It was not made by God the Creator; it is born of fickleness of character. It has no rank as a creature and no standing as a natural substance. It is a defect of changeability and an error of falling away. God wants it rooted out of each person's soul: how could he himself have produced it? The prophet cries out: “Cease from your wicked deeds.” Holy David says above all: “Turn away from evil and do good.” How then can we make the Lord its source? This deadly opinion belongs to those who thought fit to throw the Church into confusion. From this source the Marcionites, the Valentinians and that fatal plague of the Manichaeans tried to infect the minds of the saints. Why do we go looking for the darkness of death in the light of life? Divine Scripture offers salvation and breathes the fragrance of life, so that as you read you may take in its sweetness, not rush headlong into danger. Read simply, O man, and do not dig a pit for yourself as a perverse interpreter. The statement is simple: God made heaven and earth. He made what did not exist, not what already existed. “And the earth was invisible”: from the moment it was made, it existed, and it was invisible, because water overflowed it and covered it, and darkness was spread over it, since there was not yet the light of day, nor yet the ray of the sun, which usually reveals even what lies hidden under the waters. Why then do they say that God created evil, when opposites can never be produced from things contrary to them? Life does not produce death, and light does not produce darkness. The process of generation does not work like the changes of feeling. Feelings turn from one thing into its contrary when the will swerves. Things that are generated do not [?] from contraries into opposites. They are created from authors or causes of the same kind, and they reproduce the likeness of their author.

What then shall we say? If wickedness neither exists without a beginning, as though uncreated, nor was made by God, where does nature get it from? No wise man has denied that there are evils in this world, since falling into death is so common in this age. But from what we have already said we can gather that wickedness is not a living substance. It is a corruption of mind and soul, a straying from the path of virtue, which often creeps into the souls of the careless. So the greater danger to us comes not from outside but from ourselves. The enemy is within; the author of error is within, shut up, I say, inside us. Look closely at your intentions, examine the disposition of your mind, and set a guard against the thoughts of your mind and the desires of your soul. You yourself are the cause of your wickedness, you yourself the leader of your shameful deeds and the one who stirs up your crimes. Why do you summon some other nature to excuse your falls? If only you did not drive yourself on, did not hurl yourself headlong, did not entangle yourself in [?] pursuits, in anger or in desires, which hold us bound as though in nets! Certainly it is in our power to moderate our pursuits, restrain our anger and check our desires. It is also in our power to give way to luxury, kindle our lusts, inflame our anger or lend an ear to someone who inflames it, to be puffed up with pride and pour ourselves out in cruelty rather than restrain ourselves in humility and love gentleness. Why do you blame nature, O man? Nature does have certain hindrances, so to speak: old age and weakness. But old age itself makes us gentler in character, more useful in counsel, readier to face death with constancy and stronger in restraining our lusts. Weakness of body, too, is soberness of mind. That is why the apostle says: “When I am weak, then I am strong.” So he boasted not in his powers but in his weaknesses. The divine answer also shone out in a saving oracle: “Power is made perfect in weakness.” What we must guard against are the sins of youth and the irrational passions of the body, which come from our own will. So let us not look outside ourselves for the origins of the things we are masters of, nor shift them onto others, but let us acknowledge what is our own. If we can refrain from doing something when we do not want to do it, we ought to ascribe the choice of that evil to ourselves rather than to others. That is why even in the courts of this world guilt binds and punishment condemns those who are guilty by their own will, not those compelled by necessity. If someone kills an innocent person in a fit of madness, he is not liable to death. Indeed, by the oracle of the divine law itself, anyone who causes a death unintentionally receives hope of impunity and the chance of a refuge, so that he can escape. Let this be said, then, about what is properly considered evil. For the only evils are those that entangle the mind in crime and bind the conscience. But no wise man would call poverty, low birth, sickness or death evils, or count them among evils, since their opposites are not counted among the greatest goods either. Of these, some appear to come to us by nature and others by circumstance.

This digression has not been pointless. Its purpose was to prove that the darkness and the abyss are to be understood simply. There was darkness because heaven overshadowed the earth. Every body casts a shadow, with which it overshadows what lies next to it or beneath it, and above all what it seems to cover and enclose. The vault of heaven does enclose, because heaven is stretched out like a vault, as we showed above. So the darkness was not a primary substance; the gloom of darkness followed the body of the world like a shadow. As the world rose at the moment of the divine command, it enclosed a shadow within itself. Suppose someone in the middle of a field lit by the midday sun suddenly fences off a spot and covers it with thick leafy branches. Does not the hut inside grow darker beneath that shaggy canopy overhead, the more brightly the place shines outside? Or why else have people called such a place, closed on every side, a cave, unless because it is grim with black neglect and a shroud of darkness? This darkness, then, lay over the abysses of the waters. The Gospel reading teaches that “abyss” means a great mass and depth of waters, where the demons begged the Savior not to order them to go into the abyss. But he, who was teaching that the wishes of demons are not to be carried out, ordered them to go into the pigs. The pigs threw themselves into a lake of water, so that the demons did not escape what they were refusing but were plunged down in a fitting fall. Such, then, was the world's appearance and form, not yet set in order.

“And the Spirit of God,” it says, “was moving over the waters. And God said: Let there be light.” It is fitting, then, that the Spirit of God was mentioned first, where the divine work was about to begin. “Let there be light,” it says. Where should the voice of God in divine Scripture begin, if not with light? Where should the adornment of the world take its start, if not with light? It would be pointless if it could not be seen. God himself was indeed in light, for he “dwells in unapproachable light,” and he was “the true light that enlightens every man coming into this world.” But he willed that light to be made which could be perceived by bodily eyes. Someone who wants to build a house worthy to be the home of the head of a household looks for a way to let light into it before he lays the foundation. That is the first grace: if it is lacking, the whole house is grim and shabby and unsightly. It is light that sets off the other adornments of a house. “Let there be light,” it says. This word, full of light, does not signify the preparation of a plan; it shines forth in the effect of the work. The maker of nature spoke light and created it. God's speech is his will; God's work is nature. He created light; he lit up the darkness. “And God said: Let there be light. And there was light.” He did not speak so that the work might follow; by speaking he completed the task. That is why David's words put it so well: “He spoke, and they were made,” because the effect fulfilled the word. God, then, is the author of light, while the world is the place and cause of darkness. But the good author spoke light in such a way that he opened up the world itself by pouring light into it and made its appearance lovely. So the air suddenly shone, and the darkness shrank in terror at the brightness of the new light. The flash of light, poured suddenly through the whole world, drove the darkness back and plunged it, as it were, into the abysses. So Scripture said beautifully and fittingly: “There was light.” Light swiftly illuminates heaven, the earth and [?]. In a moment of time, with no perceptible interval, the regions are uncovered by the splendor of the rising day and light floods all around our sight. In the same way its origin had to be told swiftly. Why do we wonder that God spoke light and light flashed out on a world in gloom? If someone plunged under water lets out oil from his mouth, he makes clearer the things that lay hidden in the depths. God spoke, not so that a spoken sound came out through the organs of voice, nor so that a movement of the tongue formed a heavenly address and a clatter of words struck the air. He spoke so that he might reveal the knowledge of his will through the effect of his work.

“And he divided the light from the darkness. And God saw the light, that it was good.” He spoke, and no one heard the sound of a voice. He divided, and no one perceived the labor of the work. He saw, and no one saw his eyes looking. “And God saw the light,” it says, “that it was good.” He did not see something he was unaware of, nor approve something he did not know before or had not seen. It is the mark of good works that they need no outside [?], but bear witness to their own grace when they are seen. What is approved by sight counts for more than what is praised in words: it relies on its own testimony, not on another's vote. Among us, judgment is given by the eyes, which take in both the grace of beauty and the nature of things. How much more does God see all that he approves and approve all that he sees, as it is written: “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous.” The nature of light is such that its grace lies not in number, measure or weight, as with other things, but entirely in its appearance. So Scripture expressed the nature of light in fitting words. Light pleases by being seen, since it is what makes the work of seeing possible. And it deserved to find so great a herald. It is rightly the first to be praised by him, since it is light that makes the other parts of the world worthy of praise too. So God saw the light and lit it up with his face, and saw that it was good. This is not a partial judgment on God's part but a general one. So the grace of light is approved not only for its brightness but for all its usefulness. That is why a division is made between light and darkness, so that once the nature of light has been separated from the nature of darkness, nothing may seem confused within it.

“And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night,” so that he might distinguish day and night by their very names. We notice, then, that the rising of light seems to open the day before the rising of the sun does. The beginnings of day close the end of night, and a set boundary of time and a fixed limit seem to have been laid down for night and day. The sun brightens the day, but light makes it. The sky is often covered with clouds, so that the sun is hidden and none of its rays appears. Yet light shows the day and hides the darkness.

“And there was evening and there was morning, one day.” Some ask why Scripture mentioned evening first and then morning, in case it might seem to mean night before day. They fail to notice, first, that Scripture had already mentioned day when it said: “And God called the light day, and the darkness he called night”; and second, that evening is the end of day and morning the end of night. So to give day the privilege and first place in birth, it first indicated the end of day, after which night would follow, and then added the end of night. Scripture was so far from putting night before day that it included the times of both day and night under the name “day” and claimed them by the authority of that name as the principal one. We can prove with many examples that it is Scripture's custom to give the name to the more important: Jacob said, “The days of my life have been few and evil,” and again, “all the days of my life,” and David wrote, “the days of my years.” He did not add “and nights.” From this we notice that what is now handed down in the form of history has established the force of a law for the future. The beginning of day, then, is the voice of God: “Let there be light. And there was light.” The end of day is evening. The following day then succeeds from the end of night. God's meaning is clear: first he called the light day, and second he called the darkness night.

Scripture also did very well to say “one day,” not “the first day.” Since a second, a third and then the remaining days were to follow, it could have said “first,” and that seemed to suit the order. But it laid down a law that the twenty-four hours of day and night are to be defined by the name “day” alone, as if to say: the measure of twenty-four hours is the time of one day. When the generations of men are counted, women are understood as well, because the secondary is joined to the more important. In the same way the days are counted and the nights are reckoned as joined to them. So just as there is one cycle, there is one day. Many people even call one week one day, because it returns into itself as though into one day and recurs, as it were, seven times into itself. This is the shape of a cycle: to begin from itself and return into itself. That is why Scripture sometimes speaks of one age. In other places it does speak of “ages,” but there it seems to mean the various conditions of public life or of affairs rather than to define some succession of ages. It says: “for the day of the Lord is great and glorious,” and elsewhere: “Why do you seek the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light.” It is clear that that day will be dark for those with guilty consciences and the unworthy, a day when innocence will shine and the guilty mind will be tormented. But Scripture teaches us that the everlasting day of eternal reward will come without any interruption of nights or succession of darkness.

It is fine, too, that when Scripture meant to call both turns a single day, it ended that day with morning. It was teaching that the day begins from light and ends in light. The full span of day and night is not complete until it has been fulfilled. So let us always walk honestly, as in the day, and cast off the works of darkness. We know that night was given for the body's rest, not for [?] any activity or the performance of work. Night passes in sleep and forgetfulness. Let there be no reveling and drunkenness among us, no debauchery and indecency. Let us not say: “Darkness and walls cover us, and who knows whether the Most High will see?” Rather, let there be in us a love of light and a concern for what is honorable, so that, walking as in the day, we may long for our works to shine before God. To him be honor, praise, glory and power, with our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, from the ages, now and always and for all ages of ages. Amen.
THE SECOND DAY

We have finished, as best we could, our treatment of the first day, or rather of "one day", for the prophetic wording should keep its special privilege. In it we learned that the heaven was established, the earth created, the waters poured forth, the air spread around, and light and darkness divided, by the working of almighty God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and also of the Holy Spirit. Who, then, would not marvel that a world made of such different and unequal parts rises up into one body, and that things so far apart come together into fellowship and union by an unbreakable law of harmony and love, so that things separate by nature are bound in a bond of unity and peace, as if by an indivisible fellow-feeling? Or who, seeing these things, could probe with his weak mind how such an order is possible? All these things the divine power, which human minds cannot grasp and our words cannot express, has woven together by the authority of its own will.

So God made heaven and earth, and he commanded them to exist as their author: not as one who merely devised their shape, but as the maker of their nature. For how could the impassible power of God, which works, and the passible nature of matter fit together, as though each borrowed from the other what it lacked? If matter was uncreated, then it seems that God lacked the power to create matter, and borrowed from it something to be subject to his work. If, on the other hand, matter was merely unformed, it is very strange that matter, coeternal with God, could not give itself beauty, since it did not receive its substance from a creator but possessed it timelessly. In that case the maker of all things found more than he contributed: he found matter on which he could work, and he contributed only the form that gave beauty to what he found. That is why the first day must be set apart from the others as "one day," and not ranked alongside them as "the first day." On it the foundations of all things were laid and the causes came into being on which the substance of this world and of all visible creation rests. So let our discourse now go on to the wonderful works of the second day. Their greatness must be referred to the praise of the Creator, not according to what our treatment of them can manage, but according to Scripture. I therefore ask you to judge naturally

what we say, and to be good enough to weigh it with a simple mind and careful thought, not gathering plausibilities according to the traditions of philosophy and the empty seduction of persuasive argument, but according to the rule of truth, which is expressed in the oracles of the divine word and poured into the hearts of the faithful through the contemplation of so great a majesty. For it is written: "Strengthen me in your words. The unjust have told me their exercises, but not as your law is, O Lord. All your commandments are truth." So let us consider what was made, and question the possibilities of nature, not according to the natures of the elements but according to Christ, who made all that he willed, abounding in the fullness of his divinity. When in the Gospel he healed the leper and restored sight to the blind, the people who were present and watched did not recognize there the procedure of medicine; rather, marveling at the Lord's power, they gave praise to God, as it is written. Nor did Moses stretch out his hand to divide the Red Sea according to the numbers of the Egyptians, the conjunctions of the stars, or the measurements of the elements, but in obedience to the command of divine power. That is why he himself says: "Your right hand, O Lord, is glorified in strength; your right hand, O Lord, has shattered the enemies." Lift up your mind to him, then, holy people, and direct your whole soul there. God does not see as man sees: God looks on the heart, man on the face. Neither, then, does man see as God sees. You hear that God saw and praised. So do not judge what was made with your own eyes and gather it up from opinions; [?] what God has seen and approved, you must not think needs to be reconsidered.

And God said: "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water." And so it was done. Listen to the words of God: "Let there be," he says. This is the language of one who commands, not of one who calculates. He gives orders to nature; he does not defer to what is possible; he does not gather measurements or weigh out weights. His will is the measure of things; his word is the completion of the work. "Let there be a firmament [?] in the midst of the water," he says. Whatever God establishes is firm. And he did very well to put "firmament" first, before adding "in the midst of the water," so that you would first believe that the firmament was made by God's command before you could raise doubts about the flowing nature of water. If you consider the nature of the elements, how could a firmament be made solid among the waters? They flow; it is held fast. They run; it stays put. "And let it divide," he says, "between water." But water usually mingles, not divides. How can he command what he knows to be contrary to the principle of the elements? Yet since his word is the origin of nature, he who gave nature its beginning rightly claims the right to give it its law.

But first let us consider what the firmament is: whether it is the same thing that he called "heaven" above, or something else, and whether there are two heavens or more. For there are some who say that there is only one heaven, and that since [?] matter was one, as they themselves claim, there could not have been enough substance left over to make another heaven; for since all of it had been spent on the upper heaven, nothing remained that could serve to build a second or a third. Others, however, maintain that there are countless heavens and worlds, and they are laughed at by their own people — for they have a greater fight with their own than with us — who strive to prove by geometrical numbers and necessities that there cannot be another heaven, that nature does not permit a second or a third, and that the Maker's power is not capable of making many heavens. Who would not laugh at this artful eloquence of theirs? They do not deny that men can make many things of the same kind from one and the same cause, yet they doubt whether the Creator of all could make several heavens — he of whom it is written: "But the Lord made the heavens," and elsewhere: "Whatever he willed, he has done." What is difficult for one for whom to will is to have done? Their argument from impossibility therefore falters when they argue about God, to whom it is truly said: "Nothing is impossible for you."

So we cannot deny that there is not only a second but even a third heaven, since the Apostle confirms by the testimony of his writings that he was caught up to the third heaven. David too places "the heavens of heavens" in that choir which praises God. Imitating him, the philosophers introduced the harmonious motion of the spheres of the five planets and of the sun and the moon, to whose orbits, or rather spheres, they say all things are joined. They suppose that these are interlocked and, as it were, set into one another, that they revolve backward and are carried in a motion contrary to the rest, and that by the impulse and motion of these orbits a sweet sound is produced, full of charm and art and the most pleasing melody; for the air, cut by so artful a motion, which tempers high notes with low, produces such varied harmonies so evenly that it surpasses all the sweetness of musical song.

If you ask for proof of this and demand that it be demonstrated to us by sense and hearing, they hesitate. [?] If it were true, how is it that, with the orbits resounding in so great a motion — since that heavenly orbit to which they say the courses of the stars are fixed, which revolve without pause, has a swifter rotation and gives out a high sound, while the lunar one gives out the deepest — we do not hear it, when we commonly hear fainter sounds? So if we demand that the truth of this argument be proven by our own testimony and the gift of hearing, they reply that our ears have gone deaf and our sense of hearing has been dulled through our habituation to that sound, taken in from the very beginning of our birth. And they offer the example of the Nile, the greatest of rivers, at the place where it hurls itself from the highest mountains down those cataracts: the magnitude of its roar so blocks the ears of those who live nearby that they are said to lack the gift of hearing. But the truth itself readily answers them. We hear the thunder produced by clouds colliding; would we not hear the revolutions of such great orbits, which, just as they are thought to move with a far greater motion, would surely produce more violent sounds? They add, moreover, that this sound does not reach the earth so that men, captivated by the charm and sweetness produced by that most rapid motion of the heavens from east to west, would not abandon their own business and work, and everything here be left idle through a kind of rapture of the human mind toward heavenly sounds. But let us leave to those who are outside the things that are foreign to our pursuit and to the course of divine reading; let us hold fast to the teaching of the heavenly Scriptures.

What is set before us, then, is that God said: "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water, and let it divide between water and water." And here the question is raised whether he calls "firmament" what he had already made before, of which it is written: "In the beginning God made heaven and earth." I am well aware that some before us have taken it this way: that Scripture expressed above that heaven was created and founded by God as its author, and here spread out the explanation of the work and of the creation, so that there the sum of the work is briefly comprehended, and here the character of the working is set out through the very forms of the things that come together. But we are moved by the fact that a different name is used, a more solid form is indicated, a cause is distinguished, and the person of a fellow worker is added. For it is written thus: "And God divided between the midst of the water that was under the firmament and the midst of the water that was above the firmament."

And first they want to destroy what has been planted and impressed in our minds by frequent reading of the Scriptures: they say that there cannot be waters above the heavens, claiming that the orb of heaven is round, with the earth in its middle, and that water cannot stay on that circuit, since it must flow off and slip down when its course runs from higher to lower. For how, they say, can water stand on an orb when the orb itself revolves? This is that well-known trickery of dialectic: "Grant me something so that I can answer you" — and if it is not granted, not a word is offered in reply. They ask us to concede that the axis of heaven turns with a swift motion while the orb of the earth is immovable, so that they may establish that there cannot be waters above the heavens, since the revolving axis would pour them all off. As if — to grant them what they ask and answer them according to their own opinions — they could deny that in that height and depth there is also length and breadth, which no one can comprehend except one who is filled with all the fullness of God, as the Apostle says. For who can easily judge a divine work? So there is breadth in the very height of heaven. There are also — to speak of things we can know — many buildings that are round outside and square inside, or square outside and round inside, whose tops are flat, and water commonly stays on them. We say this, however, so that they may notice that their opinions can be refuted by opinions more plausible than theirs, and may stop measuring so great a work of God by reflecting on human workmanship and on what we ourselves are able to do.

We, however, follow the sequence and order of the Scriptures and judge the work by considering its author: what was said, who said it, and to whom [?]. "Let there be a firmament," he says, "in the midst of the water, and let it divide between the waters." I hear that the firmament was made by a command, so that the water might be divided and the upper separated from the lower. What could be clearer? He who ordered the water to be divided by a firmament placed between, in the middle, provided how it could remain divided and separated. The word of God is the power of nature and the permanence of substance, for as long as he who established it wishes it to remain, as it is written: "He established them for ever and for ever and ever; he laid down a command, and it shall not pass away." And so that you may know that he said this of those very waters which you deny can be in the upper regions of heaven, listen to what comes before: "Praise him, you heavens of heavens, and let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord." Did he not say, as if to you who oppose him: "For he spoke and they were made, he commanded and they were created; he established them for ever and for ever and ever; he laid down a command, and it shall not pass away"? Or does he not seem to you an author fit to give a law to his own work? It is God who speaks — venerable in nature, beyond estimate in greatness, immeasurable in his rewards, incomprehensible in his works, the height of whose wisdom who can easily search out? But he speaks to the Son, that is, to his arm; he speaks to his power, to his wisdom, to his righteousness. And the Son acts as one who is mighty; he acts as the power of God, as the wisdom of God, as the divine righteousness. When you hear this, why are you amazed that, by the working of so great a majesty, water could be suspended above the firmament of heaven?

Infer these things from other cases, from what is seen by human eyes: how, if you look for an explanation, the water parted for the crossing of the Jews. It is not usual in nature for water to separate itself from water, or for the flowing waters in the deep to be divided by land in the middle. "The waves froze," Scripture says, and in the form of a firmament they checked their course at an unaccustomed boundary. Could he not have freed the Hebrew people in some other way? But he wished to show you, so that by that spectacle you might judge that even what you have not seen must be believed. The Jordan, too, turned its stream back toward its source. It is unheard of for water to stand still while it is flowing, and it is held impossible for it to go back uphill without any barrier. But what is impossible for him who gave ability to the weak, so that a weak man can say: "I can do all things in him who strengthens me"? Let them tell us, at any rate, how air is condensed into cloud, and whether rain is generated by the clouds or gathered in their bosom. We often see clouds rising from mountains. I ask whether the water rises from the earth or whether the water that is above the heavens comes down in abundant rain. If it rises, it is certainly against nature that water, which is heavier, should go up to the heights and be carried by the air, since air is finer. Or if the water is snatched up by the motion of the whole orb as it turns, then just as it is snatched up from the lower part of the orb, so it is poured out from the upper part. If, as they would have it, it never stops being poured out, then it certainly never stops being snatched up, because if the axis of heaven is always moving, the water too is always being drawn up. If it comes down, then the water that has somewhere to come down from remains continually above the heavens. Besides, what prevents them from admitting that water is suspended above the heavens? For with what argument do they say that the earth is suspended in the middle and remains immovable, although it is surely heavier than water? By the same reasoning they can say that the water above the heavens is not flung off by the revolution of that heavenly orb. For just as the earth is suspended in the void, or remains immovable because its weight is balanced on every side, so the water too is weighed in balance with the earth, with weights either heavier or equal. And that is why the sea does not easily pour over the land, unless it is commanded to come forth.

Then again, since they themselves say that the orb of heaven revolves, shining with blazing stars, did divine providence not necessarily see to it that water should overflow within the orb of heaven and above it, to temper those fires of the burning axis? Because fire overflows and burns, water too has overflowed on the earth, so that the heat of the rising sun and the twinkling stars might not burn it up, and an unaccustomed heat might not harm the tender beginnings of things. How many springs, rivers and lakes water the earth, because a kind of inner fire heats it! For how would trees put forth shoots, or grain and crops spring up, or ripen once they had sprung up, unless an inner fire also gave them life? This fire is often struck out of stones, and often leaps out of the very wood while it is being cut. So just as the creation of fire is necessary, so that things may remain ordered and arranged and the mildness of heaven may temper the coldness of the waters, so too the abundance of the waters is not superfluous, so that the one may not be consumed by the other; for unless there is a fitting measure of both, just as fire dries up water, so water puts out fire. That is why he weighed out all things by weight and measure; for even the drops of rain are numbered by him, as we read in the book of Job. Knowing that things would readily fail, or the universe be dissolved, if one were overpowered by the other, he so tempered the losses of each that fire would not burn off more, nor water abound more, than allowed a moderate diminishing of both, which would take away the excess and preserve what is necessary.
