So, although such great streams of the mightiest rivers burst forth from the earth — the Nile, flooding Egypt as its river spreads out; the Danube, cutting between the barbarian and Roman peoples from the western regions until it is itself buried in the Black Sea; the Rhine, directing its course from the heights of the Alps to the depths of the ocean, a memorable wall of the Roman Empire against savage nations; the Po, faithful carrier of maritime supplies for Italy's needs; the Rhône, driven on by its swift course, cleaves the straits of the Tyrrhenian Sea, where sailors are said to face no small danger while the waves of the sea and the streams of the river contend with each other; and likewise, from the north, the Phasis, pouring from the Caucasus mountains, rushes with many others into the Euxine Sea — it would take too long to list the names of each of the rivers that are channeled into our sea or emptied into the ocean — although, then, there is such an abundance of waters, the land of the southern region is often scorched by heat and, loosened by the blazing sun, crumbles into dust, the labor of the wretched farmer wasted, so that often, when the wells have dried up and the pools are parched, the very means of life fail for want of drink. And indeed a time will come when he will say to the abyss, "You will be desolate, and I will dry up all the rivers," as he announced through Isaiah would happen. But even before that day comes, fixed by divine decision, the very nature of the elements engages in no small contest with itself. So the world is often shaken by harsh floods or tormented by excessive heat and drought.

So do not think the great quantity of the waters incredible, but look at the force of heat and you will not be incredulous. Fire absorbs a great deal, as ought to be plain to us at least from this: when physicians attach to the body certain vessels with narrow mouths, flatter on top and hollow inside, after kindling a slight lamp-flame in them, see how that heat draws all the moisture into itself! Who, then, would doubt that the fiery ether, burning with great heat, would inflame and burn up everything, unless it were held in check by a certain law of its author, so that neither rivers nor lakes nor the seas themselves could quench its force? And that is why water, coming down from above with a kind of rush, often bursts into such great rainstorms that rivers and lakes are suddenly filled and the seas themselves overflow. Hence we often see even the sun wet and dripping with dew.

In this it gives clear evidence that it has taken the element of water to itself to temper itself. But they have such a zeal for attacking the truth that they deny that the sun itself is hot by nature, because it is white and not red or glowing like fire. And so they say that it is not fiery by nature, and that whatever heat it has comes, they claim, from the excessive motion of its revolution. They think they must say this so that it may not appear to consume any moisture, since it does not have natural heat, by which moisture is diminished or often used up entirely. But they achieve nothing by putting this together, because it makes no difference whether something has heat by nature or as an effect or from some other cause, since all fire consumes moisture or any material of the kind that flame usually burns up. For whether fire struck from pieces of wood that are not at all half-burned, but [?] against one another, is caught on leaves, the flame still blazes up just as if you lit a torch from a fire; or whether you light a light from the light of a flame, the appearance and nature of the light are the same, as if not natural fire but some incidental cause had kindled it. Let them at least consider the sun's heat from this: that God appointed different places and seasons for its course, so that it would not burn up those places with daily heat if it always lingered in the same ones. They themselves say that the sea has salty and bitter water because the water that flows into it from the rivers is consumed by heat, and as much is used up by the heat of the day as is brought in daily by the various courses of the rivers. This is said to happen through a kind of sifting by the sun, which takes to itself what is pure and light and leaves what is heavy and earthy; from this there remains that salty and dry residue, which is useless and unpleasant to drink.

But let us return to our subject. "Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water." Let it not trouble anyone, as I have already said, that above he says "heaven" and here he says "firmament," since David also says: "The heavens tell the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands" — that is, the work of the world, when it is seen, praises its author; for his invisible majesty is recognized through the things that are seen. And it seems to me that "heaven" is a general name, since Scripture testifies to many heavens, while "firmament" is a specific name; for here too the text says: "And he called the firmament heaven." So it seems that above he said in general that heaven was made in the beginning, in order to include the whole fabric of heavenly creation, but here he means the specific solidity of this outer firmament, which is called "the firmament of heaven," as we read in the prophetic hymn: "Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven." For heaven, which is called οὐρανός in Greek, is called caelum in Latin because it has the lights of the stars stamped on it like engraved figures, as if "engraved" (caelatum); just as we call silver that gleams with raised figures "engraved." But οὐρανός is so called [?] from being seen (ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι). By way of contrast with the earth, then, which is darker, it is called οὐρανός, because it is bright and, as it were, visible. Hence, I think, the sayings "The birds of heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven" and "birds about the firmament of heaven": because the powers that are in that visible place watch over all these things and keep what lies beneath them in their sight.

Thus the heaven was said to be shut in the days of Elijah, when faithlessness reigned in Ahab and Jezebel and the people were enslaved to the king's sacrilege. No one lifted his eyes to heaven and no one worshipped its maker; instead they worshipped wood and stones. How do we infer this? Because among the curses on the people of Israel God also said: “The heaven over your head shall be bronze, and your earth iron.” This was when the Jewish people, paying the price of their faithlessness, were punished with harsh weather from the sky and barrenness in the land, for fertility comes from heaven. So Moses too, among his blessings, granted this to the tribe of Joseph: “from the bounds of heaven and the dew of the deep, of the springs below, and by the season from the course of the sun and from the meeting of the months, and from the top of the mountains and of the everlasting hills,” because the fruitfulness of the earth is nourished by heaven's tempering. So the heaven is iron when it pours out no moisture, when no rain bursts from the clouds. The heaven is also iron when the air is dim, heavy and misty, the colour of rust, and the earth is gripped by the stiffness of frost. Then the moisture seems to hang over our heads and to threaten to fall at any moment. Often, too, the waters, frozen by icy blasts of wind, harden into snow, and when the air is broken open the snow pours down. For this firmament cannot be broken without some crash. That is why it is called the firmament: because it is neither weak nor slack. So too Scripture speaks of thunder, which crashes with a great noise when the wind trapped in the hollow of the clouds strikes violently as it is about to burst out: “who makes firm the thunder.” The firmament, then, is named from its firmness, or because it was made firm by divine power, as Scripture also teaches us when it says: “Praise him in the firmament of his power.”

I should not pass over the fact that some have referred the heavens of heavens to the intelligible powers, and the firmament to the operative ones [?]. On this view the heavens praise God, or tell his glory, and the firmament proclaims it, not as spiritual beings, but in the sense that the works of the world declare it, as we said above. Others again have interpreted the waters above the heavens as purifying powers. We accept these views as adding grace to the discussion; yet it does not seem strange or absurd to us if we understand them as real waters, for the reason we have given. For according to the prophetic hymn, dew and frost, cold and heat bless the Lord; the earth blesses him, <and the stars bless him>. And we do not refer the stars to intelligible natures but take them literally. Even the dragons praise the Lord, because their nature and appearance, when seen, display no small beauty and show that there is a plan in them.

“And God saw that it was good.” The Son does what the Father wills; the Father praises what the Son does. Nothing of an inferior nature is found in him whose work does not fall short of the Father's will. “He saw”: certainly he did not look with bodily eyes, but he determined that it fitted the fullness of grace, so that I might come to know his judgment; for we are in the habit of disputing even about things that are divine. And what wonder if people can find fault with the work when they raise questions about the begetting of the Worker himself? They put him on trial; they try to claim that he is unequal and inferior. That is why you read both “God said” and “God made”: the Father and the Son are honoured with the same name of majesty. “And God saw that it was good.” He spoke as to one who knew all that the Father willed, and he saw as one who holds by knowledge all that the Son would do and brings it about by a shared working. “He saw that it was good.”

He certainly did not learn what he had not known; rather, he approved what pleased him. The work did not please him as something unknown, any more than the Father was pleased with the Son as one unknown, as it is written: “This is my most beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” The Son always knows the Father's will and the Father the Son's, and the Son always hears the Father and the Father the Son, through the unity of their nature, will and substance. The Son himself bears witness to this in his Gospel, saying to the Father: “I knew that you always hear me.” For the Son is the image of [?] God. As the image, he expresses everything of the Father; as the radiance of his glory, he illuminates and reveals everything of him to us. The Son too sees the Father's work, as the Father sees the Son's, as the Lord himself declared: “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he has seen the Father doing.” So he sees the Father doing it, and he sees through the hidden depth of their invisible nature, and likewise he hears. So he says: “As I hear, so I judge, and my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

That is the mystical sense; this is the moral one. He saw for my sake; he approved for my sake. What God has approved, do not call blameworthy, for you remember that it is written for you: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.” So let no one blaspheme what is good in God's eyes. And if the firmament is good, how much more good is its Creator, even if the Arians object and the Eunomians protest, the worse fruit of a degenerate root.

“God saw,” it says, “that it was good.” Craftsmen usually make each part first and afterwards join them together skilfully. Those who carve faces or bodies of men in marble, or cast them in bronze, or model them in [?], do not know in advance how the separate limbs can fit together, or what grace the eventual joining will bring. So they either do not dare to praise their work or praise it only in part. But God, as one who judges the whole and foresees what is to come, praises as already complete things that are still only at the first beginning of the work, anticipating the end of the work by his knowledge. Nor is this surprising in one for whom the perfection of things lies not in the completion of the work but in the predetermination of his will. He praises each part as fitting with what is to come; he praises the whole as composed of the beauty of the parts. For true beauty is this: that there should be what is fitting both in each part and in the whole, so that grace is praised in each part, and in all of them together the fullness of a harmonious form.

But now let us close the second day, so that while we build up the work of the firmament we do not make our hearers less firm with a flood [?] of words, by drawing out our discourse into the night. The night, still lacking the light of moon and stars, since the lights of heaven have not yet been created, might bring darkness on those going home. At the same time, let our bodies be refreshed with food and drink, so that while our souls are feasting, the frailty of the flesh does not complain of fasting through the night as well.
THE THIRD DAY

Today the third day is born for us in our sermon, as it rose in the reading: a glorious day, which set the earth free from shipwreck when God said, “Let the water that is under heaven be gathered into one gathering.” I would like to begin my introduction from this. “Let the water be gathered” was said, and it was gathered; yet people are often told, “Let the people gather,” and they do not gather. It is no small shame that elements without feeling obey God’s command while human beings, to whom the Creator himself gave feeling, do not obey. And perhaps this sense of shame is what brought more of you together today, so that on the day when the water was gathered into one gathering, the people would not be seen failing to gather into the Lord’s church.

Nor is this the only example we have of the water’s obedience, for it is written elsewhere: “The waters saw you, O God, the waters saw you and were afraid.” And it does not seem unlikely that this was said of the waters themselves, since elsewhere too the prophet likewise says: “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan was turned back.” For who does not know that this really happened, that the sea fled when the Hebrews crossed? When the waves parted, the people crossed over on dusty ground, believing that the sea had vanished and the billows had fled. Indeed the Egyptian believed it too and went in, but the water that had fled came back upon him. So water knows how to be gathered, how to fear, and how to flee when God commands. Let us imitate this water, and [?] one gathering of the Lord, one church.

Here once the water was gathered from every valley, from every marsh, from every lake. Heresy is a valley, paganism is a valley, for God is God of the mountains, not of the valleys. So in the church there is rejoicing, while in heresy and paganism there is weeping and grief. Hence it says, “He set weeping in the valley.” From every valley, then, the catholic people has been gathered. There are no longer many gatherings; there is one gathering, one church. Here too it was said, “Let the water be gathered from every valley,” and a spiritual gathering came into being, one people came into being. The church has been filled from heretics and pagans. The theater is a valley; the circus is a valley, where the horse that is a false hope of safety runs, where there is cheap and degraded rivalry, where quarreling is a foul disgrace. From those, then, who used to cling to the circus the faith of the church has grown, and [?] its assembly increases.

Luxury is a marsh, intemperance is a marsh, incontinence is a marsh: in it are the wallowing places of lust, the growling of beasts, the hiding places of the passions, where whoever falls in sinks and does not come up again, where the feet slip, where every step wavers, where coots dirty themselves while they bathe, where the mournful moaning of doves sounds overhead, where the sluggish tortoise sticks fast in the muddy pool. In short, the boar is in the marsh, the deer at the springs. So from every marsh, where people croaked their old complaint like frogs, faith has been gathered, purity of soul and simplicity of mind have been gathered.

The water was gathered from every lake and from every pit, so that no one should dig a pit for his brother into which he himself will fall, but all should love one another, all should cherish one another, and, like different members of one body, support one another. Let them take delight not in the deadly songs of stage performers, which soften the mind toward love affairs, but in the harmony of the church, in the people’s voice united in the praises of God, and in a devout life. Let their pleasure be to gaze not on purple hangings or costly curtains, but on this most beautiful fabric of the world, this union of elements that differ from one another: the heaven stretched out like a vault to cover those who dwell in this world, the earth given to be worked, the air spread abroad, the seas shut in; this people, the instrument of divine working, in which the melody of the divine oracle resounds and the Spirit of God works within; this temple, the sanctuary of the Trinity, the dwelling place of holiness, the holy church, in which heavenly curtains shine, of which it was said: “Enlarge the place of your tents and of your curtains; fix them, do not hold back; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes; spread out further to the right and to the left; and your offspring will possess the nations as an inheritance, and you will inhabit the deserted cities.” So the church has curtains with which she sets off a good life, covers sins, and casts a shade over guilt.

This is the church which is founded upon the seas and established upon the rivers. For she is made firm and established upon you, who flow down into her like rivers from the pure spring of the world, of whom it was said: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voices, from the voice of many waters.” And he added: “Wonderful are the surgings of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high.” Good rivers! For you have drawn from that everlasting and full spring [?] of him who says to you: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” Now he said this about the Spirit, which those who were to believe in him were beginning to receive. But now, like the streams of the good Jordan, turn back with me to the beginning.

“Let the water that is under heaven,” he says, “be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear. And so it was.” Perhaps someone did not quite believe what we said in our earlier sermons, where we argued that the earth was invisible because it was covered by the waters, so that it could not be seen by bodily eyes. For the prophet was speaking with reference to us, that is, to our condition, not to the majesty of the divine nature, which of course sees all things. But so that you may see that we have undertaken the labor of this discussion not to show off our own cleverness but for your instruction, we call as our witness the order of the reading, which supports us and plainly proves that the dry land appeared after the water that was over the earth was gathered and drawn off into the seas. So let them stop making trouble for us with their dialectical arguments, saying: “How was the earth invisible, when every body naturally has shape and color, and every color is subject to sight?” The voice of God cries out: “Let the water be gathered and let the dry land appear.” And again Scripture says: “The water was gathered into one gathering, and the dry land appeared.” Why did it need to repeat this, unless the prophet was taking care to meet such questions in advance? Does he not seem to say: “I did not call it invisible by nature, but because of the waters poured over it”? Indeed he added that once the covering was removed the dry land appeared, which had not been seen before.

Again they raise other questions, saying: “If the water was in various gatherings, then if those gatherings were in higher places, why did the water not flow down to the place into which it was drawn off after the Lord’s command? For it is the nature of water to slide downward of its own accord. But if those gatherings were in lower places, how did the water climb upward against its own nature? So either its natural course had no need of a command, or a command could achieve nothing against nature.” I will easily answer this question if they will first answer me whether, before the Lord’s command, it was the nature of water to slide and to flow. For water does not have this from the way the other elements behave; it is something special and its own, and comes not from some fixed order but rather from the will and working of the most high God. They hear what God commanded. Now the voice of God is what makes nature. The effect of his working fulfilled that voice. The water began to slide and to flow together into one gathering, though before it had been spread over the lands and lay in a great many basins. I have not read of its course before this, I have not learned of its movement before this; my eye has not seen it, nor my ear heard it. The water stood still in various places; at the voice of God it was set in motion. Does it not seem that the voice of God gave it such a nature? The creature followed the command and turned the law into habit; for the law of the first ordering left a pattern for the future. Thus God made day and night once, and ever since the daily succession and daily renewal of each remains. The water too was commanded to run into a gathering, and ever since it has run: springs slide into rivers, rivers run into straits, lakes are drawn off into seas; the water goes ahead of itself, presses on, and follows. It is one channel, one body. And though its depth varies, the level of its surface is still unbroken. That, I think, is why it is called aequor, “the level,” because its surface is level.

I have answered according to their own proposition; now let them answer me whether they have never seen springs gush up from low places, water rising from the ground. Who forces it? Where does it burst out from? How does it not run dry? How is it that the lowest openings of the soil spew out water? These things belong to the hidden secrets of nature. Besides, who does not know that water, often rushing down to the lowest places with swift force, rises up again and lifts itself to the brow of a mountain, and that often, when it is channeled by a craftsman’s hand, it climbs back up as far as it came down? So if it is carried by its own force, or led and raised against its own nature by a craftsman’s skill, are you surprised if by the working of a divine command something was added to its natural behavior that had not been part of it before? Let them now tell me how he gathered the waters of the sea as if into a wineskin, as it is written, and how he brought water out of the rock. Could he who was able to bring water out of a rock, where there was none, not move water that was there? “He struck the rock, and the waters flowed,” cries David, “and the torrents overflowed”; and elsewhere: “The waters will stand above the mountains.” You have in the Gospel that when there was a severe storm and a great upheaval on the sea, so that the apostles feared shipwreck, they woke the Lord Jesus who was sleeping in the stern, and he rose and commanded the wind and the sea, and the storm was stilled and calm returned. Could he who was able to still the whole sea by his command not move the waters by his command? Indeed, concerning the flood we have read that the springs of the deep burst forth, and that afterwards he sent a wind and dried up the water. If they will not accept that nature obeyed and that the behavior of the element was changed at God’s command, let them at least grant that the waters could have run when a wind was sent upon them, as we see every day at sea, where the waters run in the direction the wind blows. If in the time of Moses the sea was dried up when a strong south wind was roused, could the gathered waters not have been dried up in the same way, and the water that was afterwards separated from the deep have flowed into the sea? But let them learn that nature can be changed, since the rock poured out [?] waters and iron floated on water, which the prophet [?] was granted to do by praying, not by commanding. If, then, Elisha raised iron against nature, could Christ not [?] move the waters? But he moved them—he who could say, “Lazarus, come out,” and raised the dead man; for God does what he commands. So take what was said by the same pattern: “Let the water be gathered,” and it was gathered. And by saying “Let it be gathered” he not only moved it from its place but also fixed it in its place, so that it would not flow past but remain.

So this is the greater miracle: how all the gatherings flowed down into one gathering, and yet that one gathering was not filled to overflowing. For Scripture too counts this among the wonders, saying: “All the torrents run into the sea, and the sea is not filled.” Both things, then, come from God’s command: that the water flows and that it does not overflow. So the seas are hemmed in and shut up by a set boundary, lest they pour over the lands and flood everything, leave the fields uncultivated, and hinder the gift of the earth’s fruitfulness. Let them recognize, then, that this is the work of a divine command and of heavenly power. For among other things the Lord spoke to Job through the cloud about the barrier of the sea as well: “I set limits for it, putting bars and doors; and I said to it: Thus far you shall come and no further, but your waves shall break within you.” Do we not ourselves see that the sea is often so stormy that its waves rise up high like a sheer mountain of water, yet when it has hurled its force against the shore it dissolves into foam, driven back by the barrier, as it were, of the low-lying sand? As it is written: “Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea?” So by the weakest thing of all, the dust of worthless sand, the wild force of the sea is held in check, and, as though by the reins of heaven’s command, it is called back within its prescribed limit; the movement of the violent waters breaks upon itself and splits apart into its receding bays.

Otherwise, if the force of heaven’s decree did not restrain it, what would prevent the Red Sea from mingling with the Egyptian sea across the plains of Egypt, which is said to be flat country lying very low in valleys? This is shown by those who wanted to connect these two seas and let one flow into the other: Sesostris the Egyptian, who was earlier, and Darius the Mede, who, mindful of his greater power, wished to carry out what a native king had attempted before. This shows that the Indian Sea, of which the Red Sea is part, lies higher than the Egyptian sea, which washes the lower land. And perhaps both kings abandoned their undertakings for this reason: so that the sea would not pour down from the higher to the lower level and spread more widely.

Now I ask, since he said, “Let the water be collected into one gathering,” how one collection could receive the waters spread through lakes, marshes, and pools, poured over valleys and plains and all the flatter places, and running in springs and rivers; or how there can be one collection, when even today there are different seas. For we speak of the Ocean sea and the Tyrrhenian and the Adriatic and the Indian and the Egyptian and the Pontus and the Propontis and the Hellespont and the Euxine, the Aegean, the Ionian, the Atlantic; many also name a Cretan sea and the northern Caspian. So let us consider the words of Scripture, which have been weighed in a balanced scale.

“Let the water,” he says, “be collected into one collection.” There is one gathering of the waters, unbroken and continuous, but there are different gulfs of the sea, as one of the secular writers says. For the Pontus is the largest gulf of our sea, and it is right that there are different names in different places, because the waters have taken their names from the names of the regions. But there is one gathering of the waters, because an unbroken and continuous body of water, from the Indian Sea to the shore of Gades, and from there to the furthest Red Sea, encloses the world with the ocean that flows around it; and within, too, the Adriatic mingles with the Tyrrhenian and the other seas with the Adriatic, distinguished by names, not by waters. So you see how fittingly God called the gatherings of the waters “seas.” Thus there is both one general collection, which is called the sea, and many collections, which are named seas after their regions. For just as there are many lands, such as Africa, Spain, Thrace, Macedonia, [?] Egypt, Gaul, and Italy, called by the names of their regions, and yet the earth is one, so there are said to be many seas, named after their localities, and yet the sea is one, as the prophet says: “Yours are the heavens and yours is the earth; you founded the world and its fullness. You created the north and the sea.” And the Lord himself says to Job: “I shut in the sea with doors.”

Now since we have spoken of one collection, the question arises whether, when the waters had been spread over almost the whole earth and above it—through the valleys [?] of the fields, the hollows of the mountains, and the level of the plains—one gathering, poured out in the form of a sea, could receive all those waters and drain the lands that had previously been flooded by the waters spread over everything. [?] If everything was covered in this way—for it would not say “the earth appeared” unless it meant to show that it was uncovered in every place—and if in Noah’s time the flood hid even the mountains, when the separation of the waters above the heavens and below the firmament had already been made, how much less can it be doubted that the mountain peaks were hidden by that flood? Where, then, was all that overflow of waters drawn off? What basins could absorb it, so continuous and connected as it was? On this a great deal could be said.

First, the Creator of all was able to spread out the expanses of the lands themselves, as some before us have affirmed in their own opinions. I do not pass over what he was able to do; but what he did, since I have not plainly learned it from the authority of Scripture, I pass over as a secret, lest they look for further questions here as well. Still, I affirm according to the Scriptures that he was able to widen the low places and the open plains, as he himself says: “I will go before you and make the mountains level.” The very force of the waters, too, could have deepened the places it had settled in, by such great movement of the waves and such surging of a restless element, which daily churns the depths of the sea and turns over the sand from the bottom. Then who can know how far that great sea extends, which no sailor dares or attempts, which encloses Britain in its vast waters and stretches to further regions unreached even by legend? And who would not reckon how much the sea has added to the Lucrine and Avernian lakes in Italy, to Tiberias in Palestine, and to the lake between Palestine and Egypt that stretches along the deserts of Arabia, and to the various harbors of Augustus and Trajan and the others throughout the whole world into which it has flowed? But there are also lakes and

pools that are not mixed in and do not mingle with the sea’s waves, such as Larius and Benacus, the Alban lake too, and many others: how, then, is there one gathering of waters? But just as it is said that God made two lights, that is, the sun and the moon, though there are of course the lights of the stars as well, so too there is said to be one gathering, though there are a great many; for things that do not bear comparison are not counted.

But it seems that, since I was speaking about the sea, we have overflowed somewhat. Let us return to our subject and consider what it means that the Lord said, “Let the water be gathered into one gathering and let the dry land appear,” and did not say “the earth.” Who does not notice how admirably this was put? For earth can be mixed with mud and soaked with water, and its appearance does not show when water covers it. But “dry land” refers not only to the kind but also to the appearance of the earth, so that it is useful, dry, workable, and fit for cultivation. At the same time care was taken that it should not seem to have been dried by the sun rather than by God’s command, for it was made dry before the sun was created. So David too, distinguishing sea and land, says of the Lord God: “For the sea is his, and he made it, and his hands founded the dry land.” For “dry land” expresses its nature, whereas “earth” is a simple name for the thing, which contains its proper quality within itself. For just as “animal” signifies a genus that has something proper and distinctive within it, while “rational” is proper to man, so too “earth” can be said in common of land that is either teeming with water or deserted, pathless, and waterless. So even land that teems with water has dryness within it; for once the water is removed, it begins to be dry, as you have it written: “He turned rivers into a desert and springs of water into thirst”; that is, he made dry land out of watery land.

So the earth has its own proper quality, just as the individual elements do: air has the quality of moisture, water of cold, and fire of heat. This is the principal property of each element, which we infer by reason. But if we seek [?] to grasp them by the senses and in bodily form, we find them, as it were, joined and combined, so that earth is dry and cold, water cold and moist, air warm and moist, fire hot and dry. And in this way the individual elements are mingled with one another through these paired qualities. For since earth has the quality of dryness and cold, it is joined to water through their kinship in the quality of cold, and through water to air, because air is moist. So water seems to embrace earth with one of two arms, cold and moisture, and air with the other: earth with cold, air with moisture. Air too, standing between two things opposed by nature, that is, between water and fire, reconciles both of those elements to itself, for it is joined to water by moisture and to fire by heat. Fire too, being hot and dry by nature, is bound to air by heat, and by dryness is brought back into communion and partnership with earth. And so, through this circuit and a kind of chorus of concord and fellowship, they come together. That is why what we call elementa in Latin are called stoicheia in Greek, because they agree and harmonize with one another.

We have come this far because Scripture says that God called the earth “dry land”; that is, he named it by the property of its nature, which is its principal feature. For its natural property is dryness [?]; this privilege has been kept for it. Dryness, then, is principal. It also has the quality of being cold, but secondary things are not put before primary ones. Its being moist, however, it gets from its affinity with the waters. So the one is its own, the other belongs to something else: its own, that it is dry; another’s, that it is moist. The Author of nature therefore kept to what he gave it first, since the one comes from its nature, the other from a cause. So the property of the earth had to be defined from its principal qualities, not from its accidental ones, so that our understanding might be shaped according to the chief of its qualities.
And God saw that it was good.

We will not pass over the fact that some think these words are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the other translations: "And the water was gathered into its gatherings, and the dry land appeared. And God called the dry land earth, and the gatherings of the waters he called seas." Since God has already said, "And it was so," they think the voice of the Maker is enough to show that the work was done. But in the other creatures, too, Scripture gives both the terms of the command and a repeated statement of the work, whether as a sign or as its result. So we do not think the passage said to have been added is absurd, even if the other translators are shown to have the truth or the authority on their side. For we find that the seventy men added and attached many things to the Hebrew text, and not idly. And God saw that the sea was good.

The appearance of this element is beautiful. It whitens as the waves rise in heaps and crests, and sprinkles the rocks with snowy spray. Or, when its surface is rippled by gentler breezes and the soothing calm of fair weather, it shows a purple colour that often spreads before those who look on from afar, when it does not pound the nearby shores with violent waves but embraces and greets them as if with peaceful arms. How sweet the sound, how pleasant the roar, how welcome and harmonious the echo! Yet I do not think that the beauty of the creature was judged by the eyes. Rather, it was declared fitting and in keeping with the judgment of the Maker according to the purpose of his work.

The sea, then, is good, first because it supports the lands with needed moisture, supplying them secretly through certain veins with a sap that is far from useless. The sea is good as a lodging for rivers, a source of rains, a [?] of floods, and a conveyance of supplies. By it peoples far apart from one another are joined; by it the dangers of war are kept away; by it barbarian fury is shut out. It is a help in need, a refuge in danger, a delight in pleasure, a support of health, a bond between those who are separated, a shortcut for the journey, an escape for those in distress, a source of revenue, and nourishment in times of barrenness. From it rain is poured down upon the lands, since water is drawn up from the sea by the rays of the sun and its finer part is carried off. Then the higher it is lifted, the more it is cooled by the shade of the clouds and becomes rain, which not only relieves the dryness of the earth but also makes the hungry fields fruitful.

Why should I list the islands, which the sea often puts on like necklaces? On them those who renounce worldly excess and [?], with a faithful resolve of self-control, choose to hide from the world and to turn aside from the uncertain windings of this life. The sea, then, is a hidden place for temperance, a training ground for self-control, a retreat for seriousness, a harbour of safety, the calm of this age, the sobriety of this world. It is also a spur to devotion for faithful and devout men, so that the songs of those singing psalms compete with the sound of the gently washing waves, and the islands applaud with the peaceful chorus of the waves and ring with the hymns of the saints. How can I take in all the beauty of the sea that the Maker saw? And why say more? What is that harmony of the waves but a kind of harmony of the people? That is why the Church is often and rightly compared to the sea. At first, as the crowd of people enters, it pours out waves through all its doorways. Then, in the prayer of the whole people, it roars like waves flowing back, when in the responses of the psalms the singing of men, women, virgins and little children resounds like the harmonious crashing of waves. And what shall I say of this, that the water washes away sin and the saving breeze of the Holy Spirit breathes upon us?

May the Lord grant us these things: [?] to come to rest in a safe harbour; not to know the temptations of spiritual wickedness that are heavier than we can bear; to know nothing of shipwreck in the faith; to have deep peace; and, if at any time the heavy waves of this age rise up against us again, to have the Lord Jesus as our pilot keeping watch for us, who commands by his word, calms the storm and restores the stillness of the sea. To him be honour and glory, praise and everlasting power, from the ages, now and always, and for all ages of ages. Amen.

Once the water had withdrawn, it was fitting that the earth should be given form and beauty, so that it would no longer be invisible and unformed. For many say that whatever has no form is invisible. So they take it that the earth was invisible not because it could not be seen by the most high God or his angels (for human beings had not yet been created, nor even cattle), but because it was without its own form. Now the form of the earth is the sprouting and greenness of the field. So to make it visible and formed, God said: "Let the earth sprout the green plant of grass, bearing seed according to its kind, and the fruit tree bearing fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself."

Let us hear the words of truth, whose sequence is salvation for those who hear them. That first voice of God, given to each creature that was to be brought forth, is a law of nature that has remained with the earth for all time. It was to lay down a rule for future succession, so that the practice of begetting or bearing fruit might grow for all time to come. The first stage, then, is sprouting, when growing things are seen to break out. Next, when the shoot has broken out and advanced, it becomes a green plant. And when the green plant has grown a little further, it becomes grass. How useful, how forceful is that voice: "Let the earth sprout the green plant of grass"! That is, let the earth sprout of itself, seek no one else's help, and need no one's service.

For many people commonly say: "Unless the milder heat of the sun has warmed the lands and in some way cherished them with its rays, the earth cannot sprout." And for this reason the pagans give divine honour to the sun, because by the power of its heat it reaches into the depths of the earth, cherishes the scattered seeds, and loosens the veins of trees stiff with frost. Hear God, then, as if he were saying: "Let the foolish talk of men that is to come fall silent; let the empty opinion be gone. Before the light of the sun is made, let the plant be born; let its privilege be older than the sun's. So that human error may not grow strong, let the earth sprout before it receives the sun's warmth. Let all know that the sun is not the author of growing things." God's mercy loosens the lands; God's kindness makes the fruits burst forth. How can the sun supply the means of life to things that spring up, when they were brought forth by the life-giving power of God's work before the sun came to serve these purposes of life?
It is younger than the plants, younger than the grass.

Perhaps someone may wonder why fodder for cattle was created before food for human beings. Here we should first notice the depth of God, who does not neglect even the smallest things. As the Wisdom of God says in the Gospel: “Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?” Since they are fed by God’s grace, no one should flatter himself about his own industry and ability. Next, God had to put simple fare and natural food before all other foods. This is the food of sobriety; the others belong to delicacy and luxury. This food is common to all animals; that other belongs to a few. So it is an example of frugality and a lesson in thrift: all of us should be content with a diet of simple herbs and cheap vegetables or fruit, which nature offered and the generosity of God first gave. This is healthy and useful food. It wards off disease and cures indigestion. It comes from no human labour but is poured out as a divine gift: crops without sowing, fruit without seed, so sweet and pleasant that it gives pleasure and benefit even to those who have already eaten their fill. Indeed, it was given for the first course and has stayed on for dessert.

But why should I add the marvel of this part of creation and set out the proof of the Wisdom that made it? In this kind of growth, in the gift of green grass, there is an image of human life. A striking mark of our nature and condition can be seen there, and it shines out like a mirror. That grass and the flower of the field are a figure of human flesh, as the good interpreter of the divine expressed with the instrument of his voice when he said: “Cry out. What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the glory of man is like the flower of the field. The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, but the word of the Lord abides for ever.” God’s pronouncement comes in a human voice. God says, “Cry out,” but he speaks in Isaiah himself. Isaiah answered, “What shall I cry?” Then, as though he had heard what to say, he added, “All flesh is grass.” And this is true. The glory of man flourishes in the flesh like grass, and what is thought lofty is as slight as a blade of grass. Early-blooming like a flower and perishable like grass, it puts out greenness in appearance but no solid fruit. Like a flower, it holds up the show of a happier life [?]. Like the grass of the field, it will fall in a short time, for grass withers before it is pulled up. What firmness is there in the flesh? What health can last?

Today you may see a strong young man, blooming with the freshness of youth, handsome to look at and fresh in complexion. Tomorrow he meets you with a changed face and features. The man who yesterday seemed to you so splendid in the grace of his fine form appears pitiable the next day, undone by the weakness of some illness. Many are broken by toil or wasted by poverty. Others are troubled by indigestion, ruined by wine or weakened by old age, or else pleasures unman them and luxury drains their colour. Is it not true that the grass has withered and the flower has fallen? Another man is noble through his grandfathers and great-grandfathers. He is honoured with the insignia of his ancestors and famous for the marks of an ancient lineage. He has many friends, is thronged with clients and guarded on both sides, and a great retinue escorts him out and back. Suddenly some heavy blow of misfortune throws him into confusion. Everyone abandons him, his companions desert him, and those closest to him attack him. See, it is true that human life is like grass, which withers before it is pulled up. There is also the man who until lately was overflowing with abundant wealth. His fame for generosity flew from mouth to mouth. He was distinguished by honours, pre-eminent in power, raised high on the tribunal and exalted on a throne, and the people counted him happy. While he is escorted to the cry of heralds, a sudden reversal of fortune hurries him off to the very prison into which he had thrust others, and among his own defendants he bewails the misery of the punishment that awaits him. How many has a crowd of applauders, the envied procession of a thronging people, escorted home the day before! Then a single night wiped out the splendour of that glorious escort, and a sudden pain in the side mixed the mournful sequel of heavy grief into overflowing joy. Such, then, is the glory of man, like the flower of the field. Even when it is conferred, it adds nothing to one’s deeds, and no fruit is gained in it. When it is lost, it vanishes, suddenly abandoning the whole stage of a man, both what [?] from above and what it animated within.

If only we imitated this grass, of which the Lord says: “Let the earth bring forth the grass of the field, sowing seed according to its kind and according to its likeness.” Let us, then, sow seed according to our kind. To learn what our kind is, listen to the one who says that we ought to seek the divine, if in some way we might grope for it or find it, though it is not far from any one of us. “For in him we live and are and move, as some of your own have said: for we too are his kind.” According to this kind let us sow seed, not in the flesh but in the spirit. We who wish to come to eternal life must sow spiritual seeds, not carnal ones. And you know what the likeness is, since you were made in the image and likeness of God. The grass answers to its kind; you do not answer to yours. A grain of wheat scattered on the earth gives back the grace of its kind, and you degenerate. Crops do not corrupt the purity of their seed; you corrupt the purity of the soul, the vigour of the mind, the chastity of the body.

Do you not recognise that you are Christ’s work? As we read, he formed you with his own hands, and you, Manichaean, adopt another author for yourself. God the Father says to the Son, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” and you, Photinian, say that Christ did not yet exist when the world was established. And you, Eunomian, say that the Son is unlike the Father. But if he is the image, he is certainly not unlike. He expresses the Father completely, and the Father has sealed him with the unity of his substance. The Father says, “Let us make,” and you deny that he had a fellow worker. What the Father spoke, the Son made, and you deny that he is equal, the Son in whom the Father was well pleased.

“Let the earth,” he says, “bring forth the grass of the field according to its kind.” In everything said to grow from the earth, the shoot comes first. When it has raised itself a little, it becomes a blade, then hay, and then comes the fruit. Some growths sprout from a root, such as trees that are not sown but spring from the root of other trees. In the reed we see a kind of knot form on the side near its end, and from there another reed sprouts. So there is a certain seminal power in the root. Grafted plants also sprout in their upper parts. For some, then, the line of succession is gained from the root, and for others by different means. In every growing thing there is either a seed or some seminal power, and it works according to kind. What springs from it grows like the things that were sown, or like those from whose root it comes: wheat from wheat, millet from millet. From [?] the pear bursts forth with white blossom, and the chestnut also springs from the root of a chestnut.

“Let the earth,” he says, “bring forth the grass of the field according to its kind.” At once the earth went into labour and poured itself out in new births. It clothed itself in a mantle of green, took on the grace of fertility, and put on its own ornaments, adorned with all kinds of shoots. We marvel that it brought forth so quickly. But how much greater the marvels are if you look at each thing in turn! Seeds thrown into the earth break down, and unless they die they bear no fruit; but once they have been broken down by a kind of death of their own, they rise again in richer fruit. The crumbling clod receives the grain of wheat. After it is scattered, the harrow covers it, and the earth warms it and holds it close as in a mother’s lap. Then, when the grain has broken down, it puts out a blade, and the very sight of the greening blade is already pleasing. At once the blade reveals the kind of what was sown by its likeness to it, so that you recognise what kind of plant it is at the very start of its stalk, and the fruit shows itself already in the blades. Little by little it grows like hay, comes of age on its stalk, and rises upright. When the ear has lifted itself on the jointed stalk, sheaths are prepared for the coming crop, and inside them the grain is formed, so that [?] may not harm its tender beginnings, the sun’s heat may not scorch them, and harsh winds or the savage force of the rains may not shake them off. Then the rows of the ear follow, formed with wonderful skill. They are pleasing to look at, and for protection they are bound to one another by a kind of natural tie, which divine providence has shaped. And so that the stalks do not give way as supports under the weight of a heavier crop, the stalk itself is enclosed in sheaths. With doubled strength it can then bear the abundant grain and is not bent to the ground, unequal to the burden. Then a palisade of awns is built above the ear itself. It stands out in front as if from a citadel, so that small birds do not peck and harm the ear, or strip it of its fruit, or trample it underfoot.

What shall I say of the way God’s mercy has provided for human benefit? The earth gives back what it received on loan, multiplied by a heap of interest. People often deceive, and [?] their own lender even of the principal. The earth remains faithful. If at any time it has not paid, perhaps because harsh cold, excessive drought or a huge force of rain worked against it, it makes up the previous year’s losses the next year. So even when the harvest disappoints the farmer’s hope, the earth is not at fault. When it smiles on him, the richness of this fertile mother pours itself out in births, so that it never brings any loss to its creditor.

What a sight a full field is! What a scent, what sweetness, what delight for farmers! How could we describe it worthily if we used our own words? But we have the testimony of Scripture, from which we see that the sweetness of a field is compared to the blessing and grace of the saints. Holy Isaac says: “The smell of my son is like the smell of a full field.” Why, then, should I describe the purple violets, the white lilies and the glowing roses, or the countryside painted with flowers now golden, now many-coloured, now yellow, so that you cannot tell whether the beauty of the flowers or their fragrance delights you more? The eyes feast on a pleasing sight, and the scent spreads far and wide and fills us with its sweetness. So the Lord rightly says: “And the beauty of the field is with me.” It is with him because he formed it himself. What other craftsman could express such loveliness in each individual thing? Consider the lilies of the field. How white their petals are! See how the petals, packed together, seem to rise from bottom to top to form the shape of a cup, and how something like gold shines inside. Yet that gold is fenced in all around by the flower as by a palisade, so that it lies open to no harm. If someone plucks this flower and pulls it apart into its petals, what craftsman’s hand is skilled enough to restore the lily’s form? Who imitates nature so well that he would presume to make this flower whole again? The Lord bore such witness to it that he said: “Not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” The richest and wisest of kings is judged inferior to the beauty of this flower.

Why should I list the healthful juices of herbs, or the remedies found in shrubs and leaves? A sick [?] chews small olive twigs and recovers. Locusts, too, are freed from sickness by gnawing olive leaves. Bramble leaves laid on a serpent kill it. Gnats will not touch you if you boil wormwood with oil and anoint yourself with it.

But perhaps some will say: what about the fact that deadly and harmful things are produced along with the useful ones? Along with wheat [?] you find something harmful among the foods of life, and unless it is noticed in time it usually damages health. Hellebore, too, is found among the other nourishments of life. Aconite also often fools and deceives the one gathering it. But this is as if you were to blame the earth because not all people are good. And, what is more, consider that not all the angels in heaven are good. The sun itself parches the ears of grain with too much heat and scorches the first beginnings of growing things. The moon, too, shows travellers their way and reveals the ambushes of robbers. Is it right, then, that we should neglect to acknowledge the Maker’s grace in what is useful, and disparage the Creator’s providence because of a few harmful foods? As if everything ought to have been created for the sake of the gullet, or as if divine kindness had provided only a little for our stomachs! Our foods are fixed for us and known to all, and they bring both pleasure and bodily health.

Each of the things produced from the earth has its own special purpose, and each, according to its share, helps to fill out the fullness of the whole creation. So some things are born to be eaten and others for some other use. Nothing is idle, and the earth brings forth nothing in vain. What you think useless to you is useful to others; indeed, it is often useful to you yourself in another way. What does not serve as food provides medicine. Often the very things that are harmful to you provide harmless fodder for birds or wild animals. Starlings, for example, feed on hemlock, and it does them no harm, because the nature of their bodies lets them escape the poison of its deadly juice. The juice has a cold potency, and they forestall it by quick digestion through the fine passages that lead to the seat of their heart, before it can attack their vital organs. Experts also say that hellebore is food and nourishment for quails, because a natural balance in their bodies lets them avoid the force of the harmful fodder. Indeed, physicians often temper it for the health even of the human body, though it seems contrary to it. How much more, then, can something that the physician’s hand turns to healing serve, by a property of nature, as food! Mandrake, too, often brings on sleep when the sick are troubled by sleeplessness. Need I speak of opium, which has become familiar to us through almost daily use, since it often lulls the most severe pains of the inner organs? Nor should we pass over the fact that hemlock has often withered the frenzies of lust, and hellebore has cured long-standing ailments of the sick body.

So not only is there no ground here for blaming the Creator; there is even more reason for thanks, since what you thought [?] was produced to be a danger works for you as a remedy and brings health. What is dangerous is avoided by foresight, and what is healthful is not lost, thanks to diligence. Have not sheep and goats learned to avoid what is harmful to them? And not by smell alone: through some mystery of nature, though they lack reason, they still recognise how to escape danger and protect their health, and they tell the harmful and the beneficial apart. Often, it is said, when they feel themselves struck by poisoned weapons, they seek out herbs they know and apply them to the wound as a remedy. So their food is their medicine, and you may see arrows spring out of the wound and the poison flee instead of spreading. Indeed, for deer poison is food: the snake flees the deer, and kills the lion. The dragon binds the elephant, but the elephant’s fall is the victor’s death. So both fight with all their strength. The dragon tries to bind the foot in a place where the fall of the bound beast cannot hurt it. The elephant tries not to be caught by the hind foot when it is last in line, or on a narrow path, where it cannot turn around and crush the dragon under its heavy tread, or where it lacks the help of an elephant following behind.

If irrational animals know with what herbs to treat themselves, or how to find help in remedies, does man not know, though he is born with a rational mind? Is he so far from the truth that he barely discovers what suits each use? Or is he so ungrateful for nature’s gifts that, because a draught of bull’s blood is deadly to humans, he thinks this hard-working animal ought never to have been born, or ought to have been made without blood? Yet its strength is useful for tilling the fields and fit for drawing wagons, its meat is pleasant to eat, and it supports farmers by many services. God gave everything to farmers, if only they knew his good gifts, when he said: “Let the earth bring forth the grass of the field, sowing seed according to its kind.” For this includes not only the food that grows of its own accord in grasses and roots and in the fruits of trees and the rest, but also the food that is won by industry and gained by the work of farming.

How fitting it is that he did not command the earth to pour out seed and fruit at once! He decreed that it should first sprout, then that the fields should grow green, and afterward that the seed should mature according to the property of its kind. In this way the grace of the fields would never [?]. First they would supply a pleasing beauty and tranquillity, and later the usefulness of fruit.

But perhaps someone will say: how does the earth bring forth seeds according to their kind, when seeds that are sown often degenerate, and good wheat that has been sown comes back discoloured and inferior in form? But if this ever happens, it seems we should put it down not to a change of kind but to a kind of sickness and unevenness in the seed. Wheat does not stop being wheat if it is burned by frost or [?] by rain. It is changed in appearance rather than in kind, and in colour too, and through decay. In fact, soaked grain often returns to the proper appearance of its kind if it is dried by sun or fire, or if it is entrusted to careful farmers and nourished by a mild climate and rich, fertile soil. So what had degenerated in the parent is restored in the offspring. Therefore we are in no danger that God’s command, whose working has become ingrained in nature, will be left forsaken through some defect in the rest of the succession, since even today seeds keep the purity of their kind.

From the reading of the Gospel we have learned that darnel and the other spurious seeds often mixed in with crops are called tares. But these have a kind of their own. They did not take on a degenerate nature by being changed and discoloured from the seed of wheat into another kind of seed. The Lord teaches this when he says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field; but while people were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat.” We certainly notice that tares and wheat are distinct in kind as well as in name. Then the servants said to the master of the house: “Lord, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where, then, do the tares come from?” And he said to them: “An enemy has done this.” The devil’s seed is one thing; Christ’s seed, which is sown for righteousness, is another. The Son of Man sowed one thing, and the devil another. The nature of the two seeds is so different that their sowers are opposed. What Christ sows is the kingdom of God; what the devil sows is sin. How, then, can the kingdom and sin be of one kind? “The kingdom of God is like this,” he says, “as if a man [?] seed upon the earth.”
There is also a man who sows the word, of whom it is written: “The sower sows the word.”

This man sowed the word upon the earth when he said, "Let the earth bring forth grass"; and at once the seedlings of the earth sprang up and the many kinds of things shone forth. On one side the green beauty of the meadows supplied plenty of pasture; on the other the yellowing ears of the fields, as the rich crop stirred, gave the image of a rolling sea. The earth offered every fruit of its own accord. It could not be ploughed, for there was no one to till it, since the farmer had not yet been formed; yet unploughed it overflowed with rich harvests, and I rather think with a greater yield, since no farmer's idleness could rob the earth of its fertility. For now fruitfulness is gained by each according to the merit of his labour: the tilling of the fields is watched, and neglect or offence is punished with barrenness of rich soil, through floods of rain, droughts, falling hail, or some other cause. But then the earth brought forth fruit everywhere with a spontaneous yield, because he who is the fullness of all things had commanded it. For the word of God was bearing fruit on the earth, and the earth had not yet been condemned by any curse. The first beginnings of the newborn world are older than our sins; the guilt is more recent, and for it we were condemned to eat bread in the sweat of [?], and to know no food without sweat.

In fact, even today the fruitfulness of the earth carries on its ancient abundance through its habit of spontaneous fertility. How many things there are that still grow of their own accord! And even in the things we seek by the work of our hands, the divine gifts largely remain ours, so that the grain itself is brought in while we are at rest. The example in the passage read to us teaches this, where the Lord says that the kingdom of God is like this: as if a man should scatter seed upon the ground, he says, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should sprout and grow, he knows not how. The earth bears fruit of itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. And when it has brought forth the fruit, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come. So while you sleep, O man, and without your knowing, the earth produces its fruits of itself. You sleep and you rise, and you marvel at how the grain has grown through the night.

We have spoken of the grass of the field; now let us speak of the fruit tree yielding fruit after its kind, whose seed is in itself. He spoke, and they were made; and suddenly, just as before it was clothed with flowers and green plants, so now the earth was clothed with woods. Trees gathered together, forests rose up, the tops of mountains were suddenly covered with leaves. Here the pine, there the cypress lifted their crowns on high; the cedar and the spruce came together. The fir, too, came forth, not content with roots in the earth and a crown in the air, but ready to face the hazards of the sea with its trusty oars, and to contend not only with the winds but also with the waves. The laurel too rose up and gave its fragrance, never to be stripped of its covering. The shady holm oaks also put forth their crowns, to keep their bristling foliage even in wintertime. For in each kind, nature has kept for the future what it received at the first stroke of the rising world. And so the holm oaks keep their privilege; it remains that they stay green [?], so that no winds can strip them of the garment of their leafy hair.

Before, the rose had sprung up without thorns, mingled with the flowers of the earth, and that loveliest of flowers bloomed without any deceit; afterwards the thorn hedged in the flower's beauty, as though holding up a mirror to human life, which often pricks the sweetness of its enjoyment with the neighbouring stings of cares. For the elegance of our life is fenced about and hemmed in by certain anxieties, so that sorrow is joined to grace. Therefore whenever anyone rejoices, whether in the sweetness of reason or in the [?] of successes, he ought to remember the sin through which, while we flourished in the delights of paradise, the thorns and briars of mind and soul were rightly assigned to us by sentence of condemnation. So, O man, though you may shine with the splendour of noble birth, or the height of power, or the brilliance of virtue, the thorn is always close beside you, the briar is always there; always look back at what lies beneath you. You bloom upon a thorn, and your beauty does not last long. Each of us, once the brief flower of youth has run its course, withers away.

Indeed, just as you know that you share frailty with the flowers, so too you share gladness with the vines, from which comes the wine that gladdens the heart of man. And O man, I wish you would imitate the example of this kind, so that you might bring forth joy and delight as fruit for yourself. The sweetness of your grace is within you: it springs from you, it abides in you, it dwells inside you; the delight of your conscience must be sought within yourself. That is why it says: "Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells." First of all, nothing is more pleasing than the fragrance of the vine in flower, since the juice pressed from their blossom makes a kind of drink that serves both pleasure and health. Then who would not marvel that from a grape seed a vine bursts forth right up to the topmost crown of a tree, which it cherishes as if in an embrace, binds as with arms, encircles with its limbs, clothes with its leaves, and crowns with garlands of grapes? In imitation of our life, it first sets down a living root; then, because by nature it is pliant and prone to fall, it grips whatever it has seized with its tendrils as though with arms, and by these it raises itself and lifts itself up.

The people of the Church is like this vine. It is planted, as it were, by the root of faith and held down by the layering of humility. Of it the prophet beautifully says: "You brought a vine out of Egypt and planted its roots, and the land was filled. Its shade covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God. It stretched out its shoots to the sea and its runners to the river." And through Isaiah the Lord himself spoke, saying: "My beloved had a vineyard on a hill in a fertile place. And I put a wall around it, and dug around the vineyard of Sorech, and built a tower in the midst of it." For he surrounded it, as with a rampart, with heavenly commandments and the guard of angels; for the angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him. He set in the Church a tower, as it were, of apostles, prophets and teachers, who are accustomed to stand guard for the peace of the Church. He dug around it when he relieved it of the weight of earthly cares; for nothing weighs down the mind more than anxiety for this world and the craving for money or power. This is shown to you in the Gospel, when you read that the woman who had a spirit of infirmity was bent over, so that she could not look up again. Her soul was bent, for it stooped toward earthly gains and did not see heavenly grace. Jesus looked at her and called her, and at once the woman laid down her earthly burdens. He shows that those were weighed down by these cravings too to whom he says: "Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you." So that woman's soul, dug around as it were, breathed again and was raised up.
And the same vine, once it has been dug around, is tied up and raised so that it does not bend back to the ground.

Some shoots are cut back, others are layered: those are cut back that run riot in useless growth, and those are layered that the good farmer has judged fruitful. Why should I describe the rows of props and the grace of the trellis, which truly and plainly teach that equality is to be kept in the Church, so that no one who is rich and honoured exalts himself, and no one who is poor and lowly is cast down and despairs? Let all in the Church have one and the same freedom; let justice and grace be shared in common by all. That is why the tower stands in the midst, to hold up the example of those country folk, of those fishermen, who earned the right to hold the citadel of virtue. By their example let our affection be raised up and not lie on the ground, mean and contemptible; let the mind of each one lift itself toward higher things, so that it dares to say: "But our citizenship is in heaven." So that it cannot be bent back by any storms of this world or dragged down by the tempest, with those tendrils and coils, like embraces of love, it clasps all who are near and rests in union with them. It is love, then, that binds us to the things above and grafts us into heaven. For whoever abides in love, God abides in him. That is why the Lord also says: "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it abides in the vine, neither can you unless you abide in me. I am the vine, you are the branches."

Clearly, then, he has indicated that the example of the vine is to be called upon for the ordering of our life. It is said first to bud when warmed by the mild air of spring, and then from the shoots themselves to put forth all its fruit; from these the grape is formed as it springs up, and growing little by little it keeps the sourness of unripe offspring, and cannot become sweet until it is ripe and mellowed. Meanwhile the vineyard is clothed with green leaves, by which it is given no small protection against cold and every harm, and is shielded from the heat of the sun. What sight is more pleasing, what fruit is sweeter, than to see the hanging garlands like necklaces of a lovely countryside, and to pick grapes glowing with golden or purple colour? You would think hyacinths and other gems were gleaming, Indian stones flashing, the beauty of white gems shining out. Yet you do not notice that through these you are being warned, O man, not to let your last day find your fruits unripe, or the time of full age bring in only meagre works. For unripe fruit is usually bitter, and nothing can be sweet unless it has grown to full ripeness. The perfect man is not harmed by the chill of dreadful death or the sun of wickedness, because spiritual grace overshadows him, puts out all the fires of worldly greed and bodily lust, and wards off their heat. Let all who see you praise you; let the throngs of the Church admire you like garlands of branches; let each one gaze on the beautiful necklaces of faithful souls; let them delight in the ripeness of prudence, the splendour of faith, the grace of confession, the beauty of justice, the abundance of mercy, so that it may be said to you: "Your wife is like an abundant vine on the sides of your house," because by the gift of generous liberality you imitate the overflowing richness of the fruitful vine.
But why do I linger on the vine alone, when every kind of tree is useful? Some were born for fruit, others given for use.

For even those that bear no abundant fruit are of more valuable use. The cedar is suited to supporting the ridges of roofs, because its timber is tall enough to span great distances and not heavy upon the walls. The cypress too is fit for coffered ceilings and for adorning gables. That is why the Church also says in [?]: "The beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress," declaring that the fair adornments of its roof are [?], who like beams sustain the summit of the Church by their virtue and adorn its roof. The laurel and the palm are tokens of victory: the heads of victors are crowned with laurel, and the palm adorns the victorious hand. That is why the Church also says: "I said, I will climb the palm tree, I will take hold of its heights." Seeing the loftiness of the Word, and hoping that it can climb to its height and to the summit of knowledge, it says, "I will climb the palm tree," so as to leave all lower things behind and strive toward the higher, toward the prize of Christ, so as to pick and taste its sweet fruits; for sweet is the fruit of virtue. The poplar too, a shady tree used for victors' crowns, and the pliant willow, suited to tying vines: what else do they declare in a mystery but that the bonds of Christ are good, bonds that do no harm, bonds of grace, bonds [?] of love, so that each may glory in his bonds, as Paul gloried when he said, "Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ"? Bound by these bonds he said, "Who shall separate us from the love of Jesus Christ?"—bonds of self-denial, bonds of love. Bound by these bonds David too says: "On the willows in the midst of it we hung up our instruments." Boxwood too, useful for forming the strokes of letters, with its light wood trains the hand of a child; that is why Scripture says, "Write on boxwood," so that the very material may also remind you—for it is always green and never stripped of its leaves—never to be laid bare by hiding your hope, but that the hope of salvation may always spring up for you through faith.

Why should I list how great the variety of trees is, how different and how beautiful the adornment of each: how spreading the beeches, how tall the firs, how leafy the pines, how shady the holm oaks, how two-coloured the poplars, how bushy and self-renewing the chestnut, which as soon as it is cut down usually sprouts a whole wood from itself; and how in the trees themselves one can detect age, whether old or young? For the younger have slenderer branches, the older have sturdier, knotted limbs; the former have smooth, broad leaves, the latter more shrunken and rough ones. There are also trees which, with an old and dead root, cannot restore a successor if they happen to be cut down; and others, whose youth is still green or whose nature is more fertile, for which cutting is a gain rather than any loss, so that they are renewed in many heirs by a reviving succession.
There is also something to marvel at: there is sex even in fruits, there is a distinction of sex in trees.

For you may see the palm that bears dates often bending its branches and lowering them, as if showing desire and an embrace toward the tree that country boys call the male palm. That palm, then, is female, and it confesses its sex by this show of submission. So those who tend the groves throw seeds of dates, or of the male shoots, onto its branches. By these the female tree receives, as it were, a sense of fulfilment and is granted the favour of the union it sought. Enriched by this gift, it straightens up again, raises its branches and lifts its foliage once more to its former position. The same is believed of the fig, and so many people are said to graft a wild fig beside the cultivated, fruit-bearing fig, because the fruit of that fertile, cultivated fig is said to drop quickly to the ground when it is tried by some breeze or by heat. Those who know this remedy therefore tie the unripe figs of the wild tree to the fruitful one and so cure its weakness, so that it can keep its own fruit, which would soon fall if the remedy were lacking. By this riddle of nature, as it were, we are warned not to shun those who are separated from our faith and fellowship. For a pagan who has been won over may become a more vigorous defender of the faith in proportion as he was a weightier champion of error; and [?] if one of the heretics is converted, he may strengthen the side to which he has come over after changing his opinion, especially if he has some natural uprightness, so that his conviction can be lively, provided that he is supported by careful sobriety and the practice of chastity. Pour out your zeal on him, then, so that, like that fruitful fig, you may strengthen your own virtue by the presence of that wild tree and your union with it. In this way your resolve will not slacken, and the fruit both of your diligence and of grace will be preserved.

How many things there are that teach us that natural hardness can be softened by diligent effort! Farming offers an example of this. Pomegranates often blossom early yet cannot bear fruit unless they are tended with the proper remedies of skilled growers; often the juice inside dries up while the outside [?] keeps up a beautiful appearance. Not without reason is the pomegranate compared to the Church, as you have in the Song of Songs, where it is said to the Church: "Your cheeks are like the rind of a pomegranate," and further on: "if the vine has blossomed, if the pomegranates have flowered." For the Church displays the fine splendour of faith and confession, made beautiful by the blood of so many martyrs and, what is more, endowed with the blood of Christ. At the same time, after the manner of this fruit, she keeps a great many fruits within herself under a single defence and embraces many works of virtue; for "the wise in spirit conceals his affairs." Farmers are also said to treat almonds in a similar way, so that the bitter tree may come to bear sweet fruit: they bore into the root of the tree and insert in the middle a shoot of the tree the Greeks call peukē and we call the pitch pine. When this is done, the bitterness of the sap disappears.
