If, then, farming can change the qualities of plants, can the pursuit of learning and careful discipline not soften any disease of the passions? Let no one, then, who stands on the slippery ground of youth or of intemperance despair of his own conversion. Wood is often turned to better uses:

can the hearts of human beings not be changed? We have shown that fruits differ not only between trees of different kinds, but often even within the same species of tree, where fruits contend with one another. For male fruits are of one kind and female fruits of another, as we have already said above about dates. And who could grasp the variety, appearance and charm of fruits, the usefulness of each, and the properties of their juices, which seem suited to particular purposes: how the more bitter fruits heal the ailing bowels of human beings and temper bloating and inner harshness, and how, in turn, the sharp humours are tempered by sweet fruits? Indeed, the more ancient medicine is the one that used to heal with herbs and juices, and no health is more secure than that which is secured by the rule of diet. So we are taught by nature that food alone is our medicine. Certainly open sores are closed by herbs, and internal ailments are cured by herbs, and so it is the physicians' task to know the powers of herbs; for this is where the practice of healing grew up.

But to bring my pen back to fruits in their simplest form: some are ripened by the sun, others come to maturity enclosed in shells and husks. Apples and pears, and all kinds of [?] too, are exposed bare to the sun. But the fruit of the walnut and the hazelnut, and the pine kernel too, though covered by shell and husk, is still nourished by the heat of the sun; and the more the pine kernel is hidden within the dense cone, the more it is nourished by the sun's heat.

How great, then, is the Lord's providence: where the fruit is softer, the thickness of the leaf provides a stronger covering to protect it, as we see in the fruit of the fig tree. So what is more delicate must be defended by what is stronger, as the Lord himself teaches through Jeremiah, saying: "Like these good figs, so will I acknowledge the exiles of Judah, whom I have sent away from this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good; and I will set my eyes upon them for good." He fenced them about, as delicate ones, with a stronger covering, as it were, of his mercy, so that the tender fruit might not perish too early. Then, in later passages, he says of these same people: "My delicate ones have walked rough roads," and to them he says further on: "Be steadfast, children, and cry out to the Lord." For this alone is a covering that cannot be violated and a defence that cannot be breached against every storm and injury. Where the fruit is tender, then, the coverings and defences of the leaves are thicker; but where the fruit is sturdier, the leaves are more delicate, as the apple tree shows. For the sturdier fruit does not need much help in the way of protection; indeed, the very shade of a thicker protection might harm the fruit more.

Let the vine leaf, then, teach us the grace of nature and the inner mysteries of divine wisdom. We see that it is cut and divided in such a way that it seems to show the form of three leaves; the middle part is so distinct that, were it not attached to the lower parts, it would look to observers like a separate leaf. This arrangement of nature seems to have been kept so that the leaf may both let in the sun more easily and cast shade. The middle part extends farther and narrows at its very tip, so that it shows more beauty than covering. Indeed, it seems to take the shape of a prize, signifying that the grape holds first place among the other hanging fruits; by a silent judgement of nature, yet by clear evidence, the form and privilege of victory are born with it. It carries its prize with it, then, and by this it is given protection against injuries, against the violence both of the air and of the rains, while no obstacle is placed in the way of its receiving the heat of the sun, by whose warmth it is nourished, coloured and enlarged. The leaf of the fig tree, too, is divided almost as the vine leaf is, into four lobes, and this is the more evident the larger the leaf is, though not, like the vine leaf, with a jagged edge all round or a curling tip. For as the fig leaf has greater thickness, so the vine leaf has a more elegant form. The thickness of the leaf serves to ward off the damage of storms; its divisions serve to let the warmth reach the fruit and give it its charm. In the end, this kind of fruit is slow to feel the hail and quick to feel ripeness, because it seems both to be hidden from injuries and to lie open to favour.

Why should I describe the differences among leaves: how some are round, others longer, some pliant, others stiffer, some not easily brought down by any wind, others shaken off by the slight stir of a breeze?

It is beyond explaining to search out the properties of each thing, or to distinguish their differences by clear evidence, or to lay open their hidden and secret causes with proofs that never fail. Water, for instance, is one and the same, and yet it often changes itself into different appearances. Among sands it is golden, among rocks foaming, among groves greener, among flowers many-coloured, among lilies more brilliant, among roses redder, in grass clearer, in a marsh muddier, in a spring more transparent, in the sea darker: it runs on, taking the colour of the places it flows into. In the same way it changes its temperature too: among hot places it boils, in shady places it grows cold, struck by the sun it grows hot, and watered by snows it turns white with icy moisture. And how its very taste is changed, so that now it is sharper, now more bitter, now stronger, now harsher, now sweeter, varying according to the quality of the things it has been poured onto! It becomes sharp with unripe juices, with the pounded husk of the walnut and with crushed leaves; it becomes bitter with wormwood, stronger with wine, harsher with other things, heavy with poison, sweet with honey. And if mastic, or the fruit of the terebinth, or the kernel of a nut is mixed with it, it is easily turned into the smooth nature of oil. And since it is the nurse of all plants, it supplies different services to each. Whether it washes their roots or comes down poured from the clouds, it gives distinct powers to all: it fattens the root, raises the trunk, spreads the branches, makes the leaves grow green, nourishes the fruit, [?] the seeds, and regularly enlarges the fruit. So although the same water is the nurse of all, some kinds of trees produce sourer juices and others sweeter, some late fruit and others early. Their very sweetnesses differ from one another too: there is one sweetness in the vine, another in the olive, another in cherries, another in the fig; it is distinct in the apple and different again in the date.

The very feel of water is in one place soft, in another rougher, and often heavier. It often differs in weight as well as in appearance; for in many places it is judged heavier, in many lighter. It is no wonder, then, that since water itself differs within itself, the [?] of trees that are produced by the washing of the same water also differ among themselves. And though the cause of all is one, the use of each is different and its nature is different. The gum of the cherry tree has one power, that of the mastic tree another. The fragrant woods of the East are said to exude a different drop, that of balsam, and in Egypt and Libya the stalks of the fennel plants weep a different kind of tears by some power of a more hidden nature. And why should I tell you — though the statement may seem [?] — that amber is the tear of a plant, and that the tear hardens into the solidity of so great a substance? Nor is this supported by slight evidence, since leaves, or the tiniest pieces of twigs, or certain small kinds of living creatures are often found in amber; it seems to have taken them in while the drop was still soft and to have held them fast once it had hardened.

But why do I contend in common speech with the lofty and precious order of nature, when this speech of mine is fed by human wit, while divine providence has formed the nature of all things? So my outpouring of words must be checked as if with reins, lest we seem presumptuously to expound the differences of trees and the powers of roots and "whatever things are hidden and unforeseen," as it is written, which seem to have been conferred on Solomon by God as a special gift of wisdom. Yet these things are not reported to have been made known even by him, so that it seems to me he was able to discourse on the kinds of plants, but not able to explain more fully the principles of all creation.

If crops are often more abundant where there is irrigation, and beans are green, and the manifold beauty of gardens springs up and springs up again; if the bank of overflowing rivers is adorned with green beds of growth, how suddenly the whole creation of plants burst into flower at the word of the Lord, which is more abundant than any course of waters! The fields hastened to bring forth crops that had not been sown in them; the gardens hastened to put forth kinds of vegetables unknown before and marvels of flowers; the banks of rivers hastened to clothe themselves with myrtle groves. The trees made haste to rise quickly, quickly to put on their blossom, and to supply food for human beings and fodder for cattle. Their fruit is common to all, and their use too has been given to all. The trees brought forth both at once: one thing for us to eat, another to shield us from the sun with cooling shade. In the fruit there is food, in the leaves the enjoyment of pleasantness. Yet because the providence of the Creator knew beforehand that human greed would claim the fruit chiefly for itself, it provided for the other living creatures, so as to give them a food of their own. So they find no small nourishment in leaves and in the bark of the woods. And what would serve for healing, that is, juices, gums and shoots, was supplied as well. So the things that we later came to know as useful through trial, practice and example, the Creator, in the majesty of his foreknowledge, commanded from the beginning to come out of the bosom of the earth, giving them for the uses they were suited to.

And the Lord commanded that the earth should bring forth the green plant and the fruit-bearing tree yielding fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in it. Someone might perhaps say that in many trees neither fruit nor seed can be seen, and think that the divine command fails in some case, so that its truth is in doubt. Let him note that it is quite impossible for all growing things not either to use seeds or to have something that seems to correspond to the power of seeds; and anyone who pays careful attention will be able to grasp this by clear evidence. Willows seem to have no seed, yet in their leaves they have a kind of grain that has the power of a seed, so that when it is committed to the earth, a tree rises from it as though from a planted cutting and springs up as though from a seed. From that grain the first root grows, and from the root there sprouts a wood not only of willows but also of other trees of a similar kind. The propagation of roots, too, has the power of seed, and so many people have extended their groves by this kind of planting.

Great is the power of God in each thing. Let no one be surprised that I have said God's great power is in plants, since he said that his great power was in the locust and the caterpillar, because the offence against the divine majesty was atoned for by the measured discipline of the barrenness and want of the Jews. For patience is great power, and providence is great power. Those who had offended the Creator of the lands were unworthy to enjoy the earth's fruitfulness. And truly great is he who punishes the crime of such great impiety with wretched famine. So if the earth by the great power of God produced the barren caterpillar, how much more does it bring forth by great power the things that are fruitful!

Who can look at a pine cone without being amazed at the great art instilled and imprinted on nature by the divine command: how from the very centre, at differing distances, it rises with the same resin, with which it cherishes its own fruit? So all around it the same form and order are preserved; in each section a brood of kernels abounds, and the fruit and its grace come round again in a circle. In this pine cone nature seems to express an image of itself, for it guards the privileges it received from that first divine and heavenly command and brings forth its offspring in the regular turn and order of the years, until the end of time is fulfilled.

But just as in this fruit nature marks a pleasing image of itself, so in the tamarisks, that is, low shrubs, it has portrayed a figure of wicked cunning. For just as double-hearted men are present everywhere, putting on a show of grace and simplicity among the good while clinging to the most vicious, so these shrubs grow both in watery places and in deserts, by a kind of contrary habit. That is why Jeremiah compared wavering and insincere characters to tamarisks.
"Let the earth bring forth," he said, and at once the whole earth was filled with springing growth.

And to man it is said: "You shall love the Lord your God," yet the love of God is not poured into the hearts of all. Human hearts are deafer than hard rocks. The earth supplies us with fruits it does not owe, in obedience to its Maker; we refuse the service we owe by not worshipping our Maker.

See what providence God shows in little things, and since you cannot comprehend it, marvel at how he has kept some things always in flower, while he willed that others should undergo changes of stripping and clothing. Amid the whiteness of snow and the frosts of cold the fields keep their greenness, and though they are covered with ice, they still shelter beneath it no small show of green in their offspring. Among the kinds of trees that are clothed with lasting foliage there is also no small difference. The olive or the pine always keeps its clothing, yet they often change their leaves; they display them not as lasting but as replacements for the beauty of their tree, filling in turn the office of an unbroken, continual covering. But the palm remains ever green [?] by the permanence, not the changing, of its leaves; for the leaves it first put forth it keeps without any succession of replacements. Imitate it, then, O man, so that it may be said to you too: "Your stature has become like a palm tree." Keep the greenness of your childhood and of that natural innocence which you received from the beginning, so that, planted beside the streams of water, you may have your fruit ready in your season, and your leaf may not [fall] [?]. Following this greenness of grace ever flowering in Christ, the Church says: "In his shade I longed to sit, and I sat down." The apostles received this privilege of an ever-green gift: not one of their leaves could ever fall, so that even their shadow healed the sick; for the faith of their minds and the flowering merits of their virtues overshadowed the infirmities of the body. Remain, then, planted in the house of the Lord, so that in his courts you may flourish like the palm, and the grace of the Church may rise up in you, and the fragrance of your nostrils may be, as it says, like [?], that you may be drunk in Christ.

This little verse has rightly reminded me to return to a point I had almost passed over: we said that the vine too sprouted at the Lord's command, though we know that it was later planted by Noah after the Flood. For so you have it: "Noah was a tiller of the soil, and he planted a vine, and drank of its wine, and fell asleep." Noah, then, is the originator not of the vine but of its planting; for he could not have planted it unless he had found it already brought into being. He was the cultivator of vines, not their author. But God, who knew that wine drunk soberly would give health and increase prudence, but taken immoderately would give occasion for vices, gave the created thing and left abundance to human choice, so that the sparingness of nature might be a teacher of sobriety, and the human condition might blame itself for the harm of excess and the fall into drunkenness. Indeed, Noah himself became drunk and fell asleep, overcome by wine. He who through the Flood had grown to glory was, through wine, exposed to shame. But the Lord preserved the grace of his creature even in this, by turning its fruit to our salvation, so that through it forgiveness of sins might come to us. Hence Isaac said devoutly: "The smell of Jacob is like the smell of a full field," that is, a natural smell. For what is sweeter than a full countryside, what more delightful than the scent of the vine, what more pleasing than the flower of the bean? So although someone before us has ingeniously said: "The patriarch did not smell of vine or fig or grain, but breathed forth a [?] grace," I nevertheless take the simple and pure scent of the earth itself as the grace of the blessing. No deceit composed it; the truth of heavenly favour poured it forth. Indeed, it is counted among the most sacred blessings that the Lord should grant us, from the dew of heaven, an abundance of wine, oil and grain. To him be honour, praise, glory and eternity from the ages, now and always and for all ages of ages. Amen.
THE FOURTH DAY

Anyone who gathers in the grape harvest usually cleans the vessels into which the wine will be poured beforehand, so that no impurity spoils the wine's quality. What is the use of planting vines in rows, digging round them every year or ploughing furrows with the plough, pruning them, propping them up, tying them to elms and joining them in a kind of marriage, if wine produced with so much labour turns sour in the jar? Likewise, anyone who wants to watch the sun rise in the morning cleans his eyes, so that no dust or dirt lodges in them to dull his gaze, and no misty haze clouds the bodily sight of the onlooker. In our reading the sun must now rise, which did not exist before. We have already passed the first day without a sun, spent the second without a sun, completed the third without a sun: on the fourth day God commands lights to be made, the sun and the moon and the stars. The sun begins. Cleanse the eyes of your mind, O man, and the inner gaze of your soul, so that no speck of sin dims the keenness of your understanding and disturbs the sight of a pure heart. Cleanse your ear, so that you may receive the bright streams of divine Scripture in a clean vessel and no contamination may enter. The sun comes forth with great radiance, filling the day and the world with great light and warming it with its heat. Beware, O man, of weighing its greatness alone, lest its excessive brilliance blind the sight of your mind. For someone who looks straight into its rays suddenly loses all sight because the light is thrown back at him, and unless he turns his face and eyes towards other directions he thinks he sees nothing and has been robbed of the gift of seeing; but if he turns his gaze aside, his sight stays whole. Beware, then, lest its rising ray confound your sight as well. And so look first at the firmament of heaven, which was made before the sun; look at the earth, which began to be visible and ordered before the sun came forth; look at its plants, which came before the light of the sun. The locust [?] is earlier than the sun, the grass older than the moon. So do not believe to be a god something that you see God's gifts were given precedence over. Three days have passed: no one looked for the sun, and the brightness of light was abundant. For the day too has its own light, which goes before the sun.

So do not rashly expose yourself to such great splendour of the sun — for it is the eye of the world, the delight of the day, the beauty of heaven, the grace of nature, the most excellent of created things — but when you see it, consider its maker; when you admire it, praise its creator. If the sun, which is a fellow member and sharer of creation, is so pleasing, how good is that Sun of righteousness! If this sun is so swift that in its rapid course it passes over everything by day and night, how great is he who is everywhere always and fills all things with his majesty! If the one that is commanded to go forth is wonderful, how far beyond wonder is he who, as we read, speaks to the sun and it does not rise! If that is great which day by day, as the hours succeed one another, approaches some places or withdraws from them, what must he be who, even when he emptied himself so that we could see him, was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world! If that is most excellent which often suffers eclipse when the earth comes in its way, of how great majesty is he who says: Yet once more I will shake the earth! The earth hides the one; it cannot bear the motion of the other unless it is propped up by the substance of his will. If it is a loss to a blind man not to see the grace of this sun, how great a loss it is for the sinner, robbed of the gift of the true light, to endure the darkness of everlasting night!

So when you see the sun, consider the earth, which was founded before it; consider the grass of the field, which has the privilege of coming first in order; consider the trees, which clap their hands because they began to exist before the lights of heaven. Are the merits of the grass then greater than those of the sun, or is the standing of the tree higher? Far be it from us to prefer insensible things to the minister of so great a gift. What, then, did the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God foresee in having the trees begin to exist before those two lights of the world, those heavenly eyes, as it were, of the firmament, unless that all should learn from the testimony of the divine reading that the earth can be fruitful without the sun? For the earth that could bring forth the first seeds of things without the sun can certainly nourish the seeds it receives and, by its own warmth, without the heat of the sun, give birth to its offspring.

Thus nature cries out, as it were, with the voice of her own gifts: The sun is good indeed, but as a servant, not as a master; a good helper of my fruitfulness, but not its creator; a good nourisher of my fruits, but not their author. Sometimes it even scorches my offspring; often it does me harm, and in many places it leaves me barren. I am not ungrateful to my fellow servant; it was given to me for my use, it has been bound over to labour with me, with me it has been made subject to vanity, with me it has been subjected to the bondage of corruption. With me it groans, with me it is in travail, so that the adoption of sons and the redemption of the human race may come, by which we too may be set free from bondage. Standing beside me it praises the creator, with me it sings a hymn to the Lord our God. Where its favour is greater, there it shares a common fellowship with me. Where the sun blesses, there the earth blesses, the fruit-bearing trees bless, the cattle bless, the birds bless with me. The sailor out at sea blames the sun and longs for me; the shepherd in the mountains shuns it and turns to my plants. He hurries to my trees, to be shaded by them when he is burning with heat, and to my springs when he is thirsty and weary [?].

But lest the testimony of the eyes seem too slight to you, cleanse your ear and bring it close to the heavenly oracles; for every word is established by two or three witnesses. Hear him who says: Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven to give light upon the earth. Who says this? God says it. And to whom does he say it, if not to the Son? So God the Father says, 'Let there be a sun,' and the Son made the sun; for it was fitting that the Sun of righteousness should make the sun of the world. He himself, then, brought it into light, he himself illuminated it, he himself gave it the power to pour out light. So the sun was made; therefore it too serves, since it is said: You have founded the earth, and it abides; by your ordinance the day continues, for all things serve you. Indeed, if the day serves, how does the sun not serve, which was made to rule the day? How do the moon and stars not serve, which were made to rule the night? For the greater the grace the creator has bestowed on them — so that the air shines more than usual with the brightness of the sun, the day gleams more clearly, the darkness of night is lit up by the brilliance of the moon and stars, and the sky, as if crowned with flowers, sparkles with fiery lights so that you would think it shone like a paradise in spring, adorned with living garlands of fragrant roses — the more beauty, then, that seems to have been conferred on them, the more they owe; for one to whom more is entrusted owes more. And so many have rightly called it the ornament of heaven, because it is a precious necklace of stars.

And so that we may know that the fertility of the earth is not to be ascribed to the heat of the sun but credited to divine kindness, the prophet says: All things wait on you to give them food [?] in due season: when you give it to them they will gather it, when you open your hand all things will be filled with goodness. And further on: Send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth. And in the Gospel: Consider the birds of the air, for they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them. So it is not the sun or the moon that are the authors of fruitfulness, but God the Father, through the Lord Jesus, bestows the bounty of fertility on all things.

The prophet has beautifully explained to us what he means when he says that God made the sun to rule the day and the moon to rule the night. For in that same Psalm 103, of which we spoke above, he wrote: He made the moon for seasons; the sun knows its setting. For when the day has begun to complete its hours, the sun recognizes the setting owed to it. So the sun is under the rule of the day, and the moon under the rule of the night; the moon is compelled to obey the changes of the seasons, and is now filled with light and now emptied. Many, it is true, seem to take this passage mystically as referring to Christ and the Church: that Christ recognized the passion of his own body, saying, Father, the hour has come: glorify your Son, so that by his own setting he might give eternal life to all who were being pressed down by the setting of everlasting death; and that the Church has her seasons, namely of persecution and of peace. For she seems to wane like the moon, but she does not fail. She can be overshadowed; she cannot fail. In persecutions she is indeed diminished by the departure of some, so that she may be filled up by the confessions of martyrs and, made glorious by the victories of blood shed for Christ, may pour out over the whole world a greater light of her devotion and faith. For the moon suffers a loss [?] of light, not of body, when in its monthly changes it seems to lay aside its light in order to borrow it from the sun; this can easily be observed when the air is pure and clear and no mist is drawn over it to darken it. For the moon's disc remains whole, even if not all of it shines in the same way as a part of it, and it is as large as it usually appears when it is full of light, but through a kind of shadow it appears bereft of its light. That is why its horns shine: because its body is spread out in a circle and is, as it were, drawn in where the light of a portion fails.

It may perplex someone that he says, Let there be lights to give light upon the earth, to divide between day and night, since Scripture had already said, where he made light: God divided between the light and the darkness. And there was evening and there was morning, one day. But let us consider that the light of day is one thing, and the light of the sun and moon and the light of the stars another, because the sun itself seems to add brilliance to the daylight with its rays, as either the dawn or the close of day can show. For before sunrise the day is indeed light, but it does not shine brightly, since it gleams more fully still under the midday sun. The prophet shows this when he says: And he will bring forth your righteousness as the light and your judgment as the noonday. For he compared the righteousness of the saint not merely to light but to the light of noon.

Next, he willed that there should be not just one sign but two to distinguish day from night, so that both the light and the rising of the sun mark the distinction, and again the failing of the light and the rising of the stars distinguish between the end of the day and the beginning of the night. For when the sun has set, some remnant of the day still remains until darkness covers the earth, and then the moon and the stars rise. As for the night, this is plainly clear, since the illumination of the moon and stars testifies to the hours of night, seeing that by day the risen sun hides the brilliance of the moon and of all the stars. As for the day, the very burning of the sun is enough to teach that the nature of daylight and that of the sun are different, and that their very appearance differs. For the nature of light is simple, namely to give light; but the sun has not only the power of illuminating [?] but also of heating, for it is fiery, and fire both illuminates and burns. Hence God, wishing to show Moses the wonder of his working, by which to rouse Moses to eagerness to obey and to kindle his heart to faith, appeared in fire in the bush, and the bush was not burned up but only seemed to shine with the appearance of fire. So one function of the fire was idle [?], the other was at work. The power of burning was at rest; the power of illuminating was at work. That is why Moses was amazed: because, contrary to its nature, the fire did not burn the bush, though fire usually burns up even tougher material. But the Lord's fire is accustomed to illuminate, not to burn.

And perhaps you will say: How then is it written, I am [?] a consuming fire? You have reminded me well: it is accustomed to consume nothing but sins. In the rewarding of merits, too, we gather what the nature of the divine fire is: that it illuminates some and burns [?] others, illuminating the righteous and burning the wicked. It does not burn the same people it illuminates, nor illuminate those it burns; rather, its illumination is unquenchable for the [?] of the good, and its burning fierce for the punishment of sinners.
But let us return to the distinction between day and night. When the light of day rises, the night is put to flight; when the day departs, night spreads out.

Light can have no fellowship with darkness, since the Lord established this by a law of nature in the working of living things. When he made the light, he also made a division between light and darkness. Even in daytime, once the sun has spread over the earth, we see the shadow of a person or of some shrub kept apart from the light. In the morning it is cast toward the west, in the evening it turns back toward the east, and at midday it leans toward the north. Yet it is never mingled or mixed with the light; it gives way and retreats. In the same way night [?] seems to give way to day and to turn aside from its light. For, as those more learned than we, who went before us in age or in office, have shown, night is the shadow of the earth. By nature a shadow clings to a body and is joined to it. So painters too strive to depict the shadows of the bodies [?] they portray, and they insist that it belongs to their art not to pass over the force of nature, and a picture that does not also show its own shadow is regarded as a breach [?] of natural law. Just as in the daytime, when some body stands opposite the sun, a shadow falls on the side away from which the light is thrown back, so when day departs and the mass of the earth comes between us and the light of the sun, the air is cast into shadow.

From this it is plain that the shadow of the earth makes the night. So God made the sun, the moon and the stars, and set measures of time for them: the hours of day for the sun, the hours of night for the moon and stars. The sun was to increase the beauty of the day, while they were to [?] the shadows and darkness, and they were to serve for signs and for seasons and for days and for years. The sun and the moon with the stars divide the seasons between them and keep equal measures as the months come round, and they serve for signs. We cannot deny that certain signs are drawn from the sun and the moon. The Lord himself said, “And there will be signs in the sun and moon and stars,” and when the apostles asked for a sign of his coming, he answered, “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven.” He said these would be signs of the coming end of the world, but [?] goes beyond the measure of our concern.

Some people have tried to set out the qualities of births, that is, what each person who is born will become. Yet this is not only [?] but also useless to those who inquire and impossible for those who promise it. What could be more useless than for each person to persuade himself that he is simply what he was born to be? On that view no one should change his life, his condition and his habits or strive to become better. He should simply rest in that belief. You could neither praise the upright nor condemn the wicked, since each would seem only to be answering to the necessity of his birth. And how could the Lord have set rewards before the good and punishments before the wicked, if necessity forms our conduct and the course of the stars shapes our way of life? What is this but stripping a human being of his humanity, if nothing is left to character, nothing to training, nothing to effort? How many we see snatched from crimes and sins and turned to a better state! The apostles were redeemed and gathered from among sinners, certainly not by the hour of their birth [?]. It was the coming of Christ that sanctified them, and the hour of the Lord's passion that redeemed them from death. That condemned thief who was crucified with the Lord passed into eternal [?] not by the favour of his birth but by confessing his faith. It was not the force of his birth that hurled Jonah into the sea, but the offence of ignoring God's command. The whale took him in and, as a sign of a mystery to come, cast him up again after three days, and preserved him on account of the grace of prophecy. When death was hanging over Peter, it was an angel [?] that freed him from prison, not the order of the stars. Blindness turned Paul to grace, and when he was struck by a viper and tossed in shipwreck, it was not the remedies of his birth but the merits of his devotion that [?]. What shall we say of those who rose again at the apostles' prayers after they had died? Was it their birth that called them back, or the grace of the apostles? What need was there for the apostles to commit themselves to fasting and dangers, if they could reach what they wanted by the favour of their birth? Had they believed that, and waited on the necessity of fate, they would never have attained such great grace. This belief, then, is useless.

What is more, it is also impossible. To take something from their own reasoning, for the sake of refuting it, not proving it: they say that birth has great power, and that it must be calculated from certain minute moments, and that unless it is calculated exactly, the difference is enormous. For they say the birth of a poor man and a powerful one, of a needy man and a rich one, of an innocent man and a guilty one, are separated by a tiny instant, a brief moment. Often, they say, one born destined for long life and one who will die in early childhood are born in the same hour, if the other factors differ and are separated by some point of time. Let them tell us how they can calculate this. Picture a woman giving birth. The midwife first takes the child from the womb, listens for its cry, by which it is known that the newborn is alive, and checks whether it is a boy or a girl. How many moments do you suppose have [?] amid these delays? Suppose the astrologer stands ready. Can a man be present at a childbirth? While the midwife sends word and the Chaldean hears it and sets up the horoscope, the fates have already passed to the lot of another child, born just after. The inquiry is about one child, and the nativity of another is set out. Suppose their opinion about the necessity of births is true: the calculation still cannot be accurate. The points of time pass by, and time flees beyond recall. I am led to believe that there is no doubt that time is divided into an instant and the twinkling of an eye, since we shall all be raised in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, as the Apostle declares: “Behold, I tell you a mystery. We shall all rise again, but we shall not all be changed, in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet; and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” How many instants pass between the birth, the receiving of the child, the laying of it down, its crying and the report! And that is to put it simply. For they themselves divide that vital circuit of the twelve signs into twelve parts. Because the sun takes thirty days to pass through a twelfth part of that sphere which is held to be [?], so that the sun's circuit is completed in the course of a year, they divide each of those twelve portions into thirty little portions, which the Greeks call moirai. Each little portion they also divide into sixty, and again they cut each of those sixty into sixty [?]. How impossible to grasp it is that they should fix the moments of a birth to a sixtieth of a sixtieth of a little portion, and determine what the motion or the aspect of each sign is at the birth of the newborn! Since it is impossible to grasp such fine fractions of time, and the slightest change brings error into the whole, the whole business is full of [?]. Their disputants do not know their own affairs: how then do they know other people's? They do not know what threatens themselves: can they foretell to others what is to come? It is ridiculous to believe it, for if they could, they would rather look out for themselves.

Then how foolish it is that if someone says he was born under the sign of the Ram, he should be judged, from the habits of the beast, to be outstanding in counsel, because a beast of this kind leads the flock; or to be wealthier, because the ram has natural clothing and gains [?] from its covering, so that ready profits are thought to come naturally to that man. They argue in the same way about the signs of the Bull and the Fishes, supposing that the motions of heaven and the powers of the signs are to be interpreted from the nature of common animals. So our food sets the decrees of our life, and our meals, that is, the ram, the bull and the fish, stamp the pattern of our character on us! How then can they derive the causes of things and the substance of this life from heaven, when they assign to the heavenly signs themselves the causes of their movement from the qualities of cheap food? They say that one born under the sign of the Ram is generous, because the ram gives up its wool without reluctance. They prefer to credit this virtue [?] to the nature of a common animal rather than to heaven, from which the clear sky shines on us and the rain often falls. Those on whom the Bull looked at their birth, they say, are hardworking and gentle in service, because a hardworking animal willingly bows its neck to servitude to take on the yoke; and the sheep likewise [?]. One whose birth the Scorpion has embraced with its part they declare [?] to be spewing out the poisons of malice, because it is a venomous creature. Why then do you claim that you will give authority for how to live from the dignity of the heavenly signs, and draw the proof of your claim from trifles? If such traits of character, taken from animals, are stamped on the motions of heaven, then heaven itself seems to be subject to the power of a beastly nature, from which it would have received the causes of the vital substance that it imparts to human beings. If that is far from the truth, it is much more ridiculous that, lacking the support of the truth, they should seek credibility for their argument from this source.

Next let us consider that they call “planets” those signs by whose motions, they claim, the necessities of our life are formed. Whether they always wander, as the name suggests, or, as they themselves say, are carried along with swift motion and change their aspect ten thousand times a day, or, if that seems incredible, change it many times over by their countless revolutions, it is not credible that by such wandering and such swift motion they should decree for us a fixed and unchangeable [?] and lot in life. They say, however, that the motions of all of them are not equal, but that some have swifter circuits and others slower, so that in the same hour they often see one another and often hide from one another, as one passes another by.

They say that it matters a great deal whether beneficent or maleficent and harmful signs look upon the moment of birth, and that the difference between births lies in this: the aspect of a beneficent sign confers very much, while that of a maleficent and harmful one does very great harm. For this is how they are accustomed to name the very signs they worship. I must use the names of those whose claims I am dealing with, so that they cannot say their arguments were misunderstood rather than emptied and destroyed. Since they cannot grasp that wandering and swift motion, it often happens that, through that incomprehensible fineness of a point and a moment, they posit the aspect of a beneficent sign where in fact the hostile encounter of a grievous and harmful one occurs. And what wonder if human beings are deceived, when harmless signs are slandered? If they are believed to be harmful by their own nature, then the supreme God is accused of having made what is evil and of being the author of wickedness. But if they are thought to have taken on by their own will the power to harm the innocent, who are not yet conscious of any wicked deed and to whom punishment is assigned before guilt, what could be so irrational, surpassing even the savagery of irrational beasts, as that the experience of harm or favour should be assigned not to human merits but to the motions of the signs? “He did no wrong,” someone says, “but a harmful star looked upon him. They look for Saturn's star [?] for him: it turned away a little, took away his misfortune and acquitted him of his crime.”

But this wisdom of theirs is like a spider's web. If a gnat or a fly falls into it, it cannot free itself; but if any kind of stronger creature is seen to run into it, it passes straight through, tearing the flimsy net and the empty snares [?]. Such are the nets of the Chaldeans: the weak stick in them, while those who are stronger in understanding cannot be caught. So you who are stronger, when you see astrologers, say: “They are weaving a spider's web.” It can have no use and no binding power, provided that you do not, like a gnat or a fly, blunder into it through your weakness, but, like a sparrow or a dove, break the feeble net with the speed of your swift flight. Indeed, what sensible person would believe that the motions of the signs, which often change in a single day and return upon themselves in many ways, confer the marks of power? If that were so, how many configurations of royal births there would be each day! Kings would then be born every day, and royal succession would not pass to sons; instead, men would keep arising from every other station to acquire the right to power. What king, then, calculates his son's nativity to see whether the throne is due to him, and does not rather pass on the succession of the kingdom to his own by his own decision? Certainly we read that Abijah begot Asa, Asa begot Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat begot Joram, Joram begot Uzziah, and so on: the whole succession down to the captivity was carried on through kings of the same line and the same rank. Just because they were kings, could they command the heavenly signs to shape their motions? What human being can have dominion over them?

Again, if our actions and deeds are to be referred to the necessity of birth rather than to the shaping of character, why have laws been set up and statutes proclaimed, by which punishment is decreed for the wicked and safety granted to the innocent? Why is pardon not given to the guilty, when, as these people say, they sinned not by their own will but by necessity? Why does the farmer labour, instead of waiting to bring fruits he has not worked for into his barns by the privilege of his birth? If he was born such that riches flow to him without work, let him by all means wait for the earth to bring forth crops of its own accord for him without any seed. Let him not press the ploughshare into the fields, nor put his bent hand to the sickle, nor bear the cost of gathering the vintage; let the flowing wine pour into all his jars of its own accord, and let the berry of the wild olive sweat out oil for him unbidden, without being grafted on any stock. Nor need the anxious merchant, crossing the wide sea, shudder at the danger to his life, since a treasure of riches can slip into his lap while he sits idle, by some lot of birth, as they say. But this is not what everyone thinks. The farmer tirelessly cuts the earth with the plough pressed down; naked he ploughs, naked he sows, naked he threshes on the floor the grain parched by the blazing sun. And the trader, impatient of his own [?], furrows the sea, often in an unsafe ship. Condemning their importunity and rashness, the prophet says, “Be ashamed, O Sidon, says the sea.” That is: if dangers do not move you, let shame at least restrain you and modesty confound you. Be ashamed, Sidon, where there is no place for courage, no care for safety, no youth devoted to war and trained [?] to keep watch for its country, but all anxiety is about gain and all zeal for trade. “The seed of merchants,” he says, “is like the harvest.” But what reward is there for a Christian if he orders his cares and works not by will but by necessity?

For where necessity is decreed, effort goes without honour. We have said much; we do not wish to say more, lest anyone think that what we have taken from their claims for refutation was taken up for learning. For how can we, as old men, recount the things we laughed at [?]? Now let us turn our pen to what remains of the reading.

“Let the lights be,” it says, “for signs and for seasons and for days and for years.” We have spoken of signs. As for seasons, what are they but the changing turns of winter, spring, summer and autumn? In these seasons the sun's passage is either swifter or slower, for some places it merely touches with its rays, others it scorches with its heat. So when the sun lingers in the southern regions, it is winter for us. When the sun is farther away, the earth grows stiff with frost and is bound by cold, and the long shadow of night covers the land, so that the nights are much longer than the days. This is why in winter [?] great quantities of snow and rain pour down. But when the sun leaves the southern regions and returns above the earth, it makes night and day equal. The longer it draws out its course, the more it gradually restores the mildness of the air and recalls the gentleness of the breezes. These warm all things and drive them to bring forth again, so that the earth sprouts, the seeds come back to life in the loosened furrows, the trees [?], and, for the lasting preservation of the species of creatures that live on land or delight in the waters, a succession is propagated by yearly offspring. But when the sun rises toward the north at the summer solstice, it lengthens the days and shortens and contracts the nights. The more closely it joins and mingles with this air by constant presence, the more it heats the air itself, dries up the moisture of the earth, makes the seeds grow, and ripens the fruits of the woods, as it were, into mature juices. Then, because it burns more fiercely, it makes shorter shadows at noon, since it lights up this region from high overhead. That is why the synagogue says in the Song of Songs:

“Tell me, you whom my soul loved, where you pasture your flock, where you rest at noon, lest perhaps I become one who goes veiled beside the flocks of your companions.” That is: Tell me, Christ, whom my soul loved. Why not rather “whom it loves”? Because the synagogue loved [?], but the Church loves, and never changes her affection toward her Christ. “Where,” she says, “do you pasture [?], where do you rest at noon? I long to follow you as a foster-child, I who before held you as one joined to you, and to seek your flocks, because I have lost my own.” You pasture in [?], in the place of the Church, where [?] shines, where judgment gleams like noonday, where no shadow is seen, where the days are longer, because the Sun of righteousness lingers with them longer, as in the summer months. Indeed, the day of the Lord is not short but great, for it is written, “Until the great day of the Lord comes.” So Jacob too says, “All the days of my life that I spend are few and evil,” for uncertain light is evil. Short days, then, are days of uncertain light and full of shadow. Great days are without shadow, as very many have learned from experience in certain hotter regions. So the synagogue, in short and evil days, whose type [?] Jacob often expresses in his own person or in that of his people, had a great deal of shadow. It did not see the Sun of righteousness, and when it did see him, it saw him not from on high above its head but from the south of [?], when it was winter for [?]. But to the Church it is said, “Winter is past, [?]; flowers have appeared on the earth; the time of harvest has come.” Before the coming of Christ it was winter; after the coming of Christ came the flowers [?] of spring and the harvest of summer. So the synagogue, seeing him shine from the south and from the turning of [?], is overshadowed. But the people of the Gentiles, which was in confusion [?], the Gentiles who sat in darkness, have seen a great light; on those who sat in the region of the shadow of death a light has dawned, the great light of the Godhead, which no shadow of death interrupts. He therefore shines from on high, as [?] says: “By which the Dayspring from on high has visited us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death.” There is, to be sure, also a shadow of salvation, not of death, as it is written instead: “Under the shadow of your wings you will protect me.” It is a shadow because it is of the body, a shadow because it is of the cross, but a shadow of salvation, because in it was the forgiveness of sins and the raising of the dead.

We can take an example from this: winter days are short but have longer shadows, while summer days are longer but have shorter shadows. At midday, too, the shadow is shorter than at the beginning or end of the day, and this holds for us in the western part of the world. But there are people in the southern regions who [?] are without shadow on two days of the whole year, because, having the sun directly above their heads, they are lit up all round. This is why in Greek they are called ascii. It is even said that the sun stands so directly overhead that it shines brightly down narrow wells on the water deep below. In the south, it is said, there are people called amphiscii, because they cast their shadow on both sides. For when people walk toward the sun, the shadow is behind them: for example, if you walk toward the east in the morning hours, toward the south at midday, or toward the west at sunset. So the sun meets you from three directions: from the east, from the south and from the west. In the morning and the evening the shadow is behind you, and at midday it is to one side. But the sun is never in the north, and so if you head north, whether in the morning, the evening or at noon, the shadow cannot be behind you. In this part of the world that we inhabit, only those who live toward the south are seen to cast their shadow toward the south. This is said to happen at the height of summer, when the sun moves toward the north. Afterward autumn receives us and breaks the force of the heat; then, the warmth relaxed and laid aside little by little, it hands us over to the winter winds through a moderate, middling mildness, without treachery or any harm.

“Let them be,” it says, “also for days”: not that they make the days, but that they hold rule in them, so that the sun may light up the dawn with richer grace and may have, by the service of its course, the power to mark the whole day. This is how some understand what the prophet says: “The sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night,” since they carry the light around. The sun and the moon are also ordained for years. The moon completes its course twelve times in periods of thirty days and so completes the year, according to the Hebrews with some days added, and according to the Romans with one day added in the leap year, kept once every four years. There is also the solar year, when the sun, having completed its circuit through all the signs, returns [?] to the point from which it began its course; for its passage through the whole circuit is said to take a year.

So God made these two great lights. We can take them as great not so much by comparison with other things as by their function, just as the sky is great and the sea is great. For the sun is great, since it fills the whole world with its heat, and the moon with its light; and they fill not only the lands but also the air around us, the sea and the face of the sky. In whatever part of the sky they are, they [?] all things and are seen equally by all. Each people believes that they linger over its own regions alone, and are present and shine for it alone, when in fact they shine alike for everyone, so that no one thinks anyone else is nearer to them than he is himself. There is clear proof of their greatness: the moon's disk looks the same to everyone. Its light sometimes grows and sometimes shrinks, yet on any given night it looks to everyone just as it looks to me. If it seemed smaller to those far away and shone larger to those nearer, that would show it to be narrow and small. With all other things, we judge them smaller when we are far off and larger when we look at them from close by. The nearer you are, the more the size of the thing [?] grows for you. But the sun's ray is nearer to no one and farther from no one, and likewise the moon's globe is the same for all. The sun looks the same to Indians and to Britons at the same moment when it rises. When it sinks in the west, it does not look smaller to the people of the east than to those of the west, and when it rises the people of the west do not think it lower than the people of the east do. "How far," it says, "is the east from the west!" East and west are far from each other, but the sun is far from no one.

It is more present to no one and more remote from no one. Do not be troubled that the sun's disk looks to you about a cubit across when it rises. Consider instead how much space lies between the sun and the earth, a distance that our weak sight cannot cross without great loss. Our sight grows dim, but does the sun grow dim, or the moon? Our gaze is narrow, but does it make the things it sees any narrower? Their appearance is reduced; their size is not taken away. We must not attribute the weakness of our own condition to the lights themselves. Our sight deceives us, so do not trust its judgment. The heavenly bodies look smaller as a spectacle, not in their own form. If you stand on a high mountain peak and look down at the plain below and the herds grazing there, will you not think their bodies like ants? If you look out over the sea from some lookout [?], do not the gleaming white sails of the largest ships among the blue waves seem from far off to cover the sea like a flight of doves? And what of the islands that spread out fields of land [?] in the sea? How narrow are the bounds that seem to enclose them! How round rough things look, and how dense things that are scattered! Weigh these weaknesses of your sight, then, and as a fair judge you will find in yourself the proof of what we are saying.

But do you want to judge the sun's greatness not only with the eye of the mind but also with the eye of the body? Then consider this. A great many globes of stars seem to be woven across the vault of the sky and adorn it with countless lights, and yet they cannot clear away the darkness of night and the clouds of the sky. But as soon as the sun sends ahead the signs of its rising, all the fires of the stars vanish in the brightness of that single light. The air opens, and the face of the sky is flooded with a purple glow. The sun is still only beginning to breathe forth its light, and already, in an instant, the splendor of its full light flashes out, and the sweet breeze that goes before the rising sun begins to blow. Tell me, please: if its disk were not great, how could it light up the great disk of the world?

And what shall I say of the Creator's careful tempering and control? He [?] just the right measure to the sun's health-giving [?] heat. So its fiery heat, fierce as it seems, does not pour into the veins of the earth and the forms of things and burn them up. Nor, on the other hand, does it cool so much across the vast spaces of the world that it gives the earth no seed of warmth, leaving it barren and poor in fruit and warming it to no fruitful purpose.

What we have said about the moon's consort and brother applies in much the same way to the moon itself, since it has taken on the same ministry as its brother: to light up the darkness, to nurture seeds, to increase crops. But in many things it also differs from its brother. The moisture of the earth that the heat has dried up all day long is restored by the dew in the short time of the night, for the moon itself is lavish with dew [?]. Indeed, when the night is clear and the moon shines all night long, the dew is said to soak the fields more abundantly. And many who sleep in the open air have found that the longer they had lain under the light of the moon, the more moisture had gathered on their heads. That is why in the Song of Songs Christ says to the Church: "For my head is filled with dew, and my locks [?] with the drops of the night." Then the moon wanes and waxes, so that it is smaller when it rises new and is filled up again when it has been diminished. In this there is a great mystery. For the elements share in its waning, and as it waxes the things that were emptied are filled up again, such as the brains of animals and the moist parts of sea creatures. Indeed, oysters [?] and many other things are said to be fuller when the moon's globe grows. Those who [?] from their own experience report the same of the inner parts of trees. So we see that its rising and its waning are a matter of design, not of weakness. It would never bring about so great a change in things unless it had outstanding power and a grace conferred on it by the Creator.

Some men, learned men and even Christians, have claimed that the weather usually changes when the moon rises. But if this happened through some force in the moon's changing, the sky would cover itself with clouds and rain would pour down every time the moon rose. Indeed, when a few days ago there was talk of rain, which people said we needed, someone remarked: "Look, the new moon will bring it." Much as we longed for showers, I did not want claims of that kind to prove true. And in the end I was glad that no rain fell until it was given in answer to the prayers of the Church, and so made it plain that rain is to be hoped for not from the beginnings of the moon but from the providence and mercy of the Creator. It is true that straits overflow on every side during the moon's other phases, and [?] the waves they receive, or are themselves carried along with great force. Yet when the moon rises they lie still, as long as it is without light; but when the passing days uncover it again, they return to their ebbing and flowing courses. The tide too, which is said to occur in the Ocean, is said to keep its regular order on other days, but at the moon's rising it is reported to give clear signs of change. The western sea itself, where this tide is observed, then advances and retreats more than usual and surges more strongly, as though it were drawn back by certain breathings of the moon, and then, driven forward and drawn back by the same force, poured back into its proper measure.

So if you wonder how the moon comes to wane when it has such power to change things, consider that in this too there is a great mystery. By its example you learn, O man, that nothing in human affairs or in the whole created world can exist that will not at some time be dissolved. Even the moon, to which the Lord has entrusted so great a ministry, to light up the world, waxes and wanes. For all things fail that have arisen from nothing and come to perfection, and once perfected they decrease again: heaven and earth will pass away. Why then do we not adopt the same moderation? We should not lose heart in adversity, for he who made all things from nothing can easily raise you, too, to the highest and most perfect state. Nor again should we be puffed up in prosperity, or boast of any power or wealth, or glory in bodily strength or beauty, in which change is easy [?] and frequent. Instead we should pursue the grace of the soul, which lasts into the future. [?] If the setting of the moon saddens you, though it is always restored and renewed, it ought to sadden you much more if the soul, once filled with progress in virtue, later turns aside from its purpose through inconstancy and carelessness and keeps changing its pursuits. That is a mark of folly and of fearfulness [?]. That is why Scripture says: "The [?] changes like the moon." So the wise man does not change with the moon, but will abide in wisdom [?] with the sun. The moon, then, has no share in folly, for it is not the moon that changes like the fool, but the fool who changes like the moon. Indeed, the seed of the righteous abides forever like the moon made perfect in strength [?], and is a faithful witness in heaven. For it is one thing to carry out a ministry, another to be carried this way and that by one's temperament and, through weakness of understanding, to hold no fixed opinion. The moon labors for you and has been made subject because of the will of God, for the creation was subjected to futility not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope. So the moon changes unwillingly; you change willingly. It groans at the change in its beauty [?]; you do not understand, and you rejoice in your [?]. It waits constantly for your redemption, so that it may be set free from the common servitude of the whole creation; you put obstacles in the way both of your own redemption and of its liberty. So it is your folly, not its own, that while you are waited for and do not turn back even late, it still goes on changing.

So do not judge the moon with the eye of your body, but with the alertness of your mind. The moon wanes so that it may fill the elements. This, then, is a great mystery. He who gave grace to all things gave this to the moon. He emptied it so that it might fill, he who also emptied himself so that he might fill all things. For he [?] himself so that he might come down to us, and he came down to us so that he might ascend for all; for, it says, "he ascended above the heavens, that he might fill all things." And so he who had come emptied filled the apostles from his own fullness. That is why one of them says: "For from his fullness we have all received." So the moon has proclaimed the mystery of Christ. No ordinary thing is it on which he has set his sign; no ordinary thing that bears the type of the beloved Church. The prophet signifies this when he says: "In his days righteousness will arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away." And in the Song of Songs the Lord says of his bride: "Who is this who looks forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?" And the Church is rightly like the moon, for she has shone out over the whole world and, lighting up the darkness of this age, says: "The night is far gone; the day has drawn near." It says, beautifully, "looks forth," as though she were looking out over her own from above, as you have it: "The Lord looked forth from heaven upon the children of men." So the Church, as she looks forth, has frequent wanings and risings like the moon. But by her wanings she has grown, and through them she has earned her increase, while she is diminished by persecutions and crowned by the martyrdoms of her confessors. She is the true moon, which borrows the light of immortality and grace from the everlasting light of her brother. For the Church shines not with her own light but with the light of Christ, and draws her splendor from the Sun of righteousness, so that she says: "I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me." Truly blessed are you, moon, to have earned so great a distinction! So I would call you blessed, not for your new moons but because you are a type of the Church. In the one you serve; in the other you are loved.

How ridiculous it is, then, that people commonly believe you can be drawn down by magic spells! These are old wives' tales and popular notions. For who would think that a work of God appointed to so great a ministry could be assailed by Chaldean superstitions? The one who disguises himself as an angel of light did fall, but he was brought down by his own will, not by the power of spells [?]. In the same way, Church, people think that you too can be drawn down, as it were, from your place and station. Many assail the Church, but the spells of the witch's art cannot [?] harm her. Enchanters have no power where the song of Christ is sung every day. She has her own enchanter, the Lord Jesus, through whom he has made void the spells of the magicians' incantations and the venom of serpents. Like the serpent that was lifted up, she herself devours the snakes; and though the Egyptians murmur their deadly spell, it is blunted in the name of Christ. So too Paul [?] the magician, not only by exposing the weakness of his sorcery but also by taking away his sight [?]. So Peter, breaking the power of spells, cast down Simon as he sought the heights of heaven in magic flight, and laid him low.

The fourth day, I think, has turned out beautifully. Why then are many people in the habit of [?] the fourth day, and why do they think it useless to begin anything on this number, the day on which the whole world shone out with new light? Did the sun begin under evil omens? And how can it mark good things for others if it could not [?] choose a day for its own rising? How can they approve its signs if they do not approve its rising? And what do we say of the moon, which began on the fourth day and on the fourteenth marks the day of salvation? Or is the number displeasing by which the mystery of redemption is celebrated? That is exactly why the demons urge people to avoid that number, the number by which their wickedness was destroyed. That is why the pagans say nothing should be undertaken on it: they know that this was when their arts first began to lose their power and the pagan peoples moved over to the Church. Certainly they hold that a moon on its fourth day, if it is clear and its horns are not blunted, is a sign of fair weather for the rest of the days until the month is out. So they refuse to begin things on the very day when fair weather begins. But now we must take care that the fourth day does not set on us while we are still speaking. The shadows are falling longer from the mountains; the light [?] is waning and the shadow is growing.
THE FIFTH DAY

[?] The whole earth was now green with all kinds of growing things, and the sky too shone, marked out by the sun and the moon, the twin lights of its face, and adorned with the beauty of the stars. A third element remained, namely the sea, so that it too might receive [?] by God's gift. For all the offspring of the earth are nourished by the air of heaven, and the earth too, as it releases its seeds, gives life to everything; and above all at that moment, when first commanded by the word of God to grow green, it was sprouting forth by the gift of its [?]. The water stood idle and seemed to be left without the benefit of God's work. But the Creator still had something to bestow on it, by which it could equal the services of the earth; he was keeping something in reserve for it, so that it too might claim for itself some special privilege of its own in the gift conferred on it. The earth had given life first, but to things that had no breathing soul. The water is commanded to bring forth creatures that would display the vigour and dignity of a living soul, and would receive the sense to protect their own safety and to flee death.

So God said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls according to their kind, and flying things that fly beneath the firmament of heaven.” The command came, and at once the water poured itself out in the births it had been ordered to produce. The rivers began to beget, the lakes to give life, and the sea itself to bring forth the various kinds of creeping things and to pour out, each according to its kind, whatever it had formed. Not even the small pools or the muddy marshes stayed idle; all of them took up the power of creating that had been given to them. Fish leapt out of the river, dolphins sported in the waves, shellfish [?] clung to the rocks [?], sea urchins grew. Woe is me! Enticement began before man did, the mother of our luxury; delicacies existed before man. So man's temptation came before his creation. But nature did no wrong: she provided food; she did not prescribe vices. She gave these things for all in common, so that you would not claim any of them for yourself as if they were your own. For you the earth brings forth its fruits; for you the waters produce parrot-fish [?] and all their offspring. And not content with these, you tasted the food that was forbidden you. Everything is heaped up to your reproach, so that the guilt of your greed may weigh the more heavily.

But we cannot even list how many species and names there are, all of which were given life in the moment of the divine command. The form of the body came together and at the same moment the soul was at work, and the vital vigour [?] some power [?]. The earth was filled with growing things, the sea filled with living creatures. There, things without sensation sprout; here, things with sensation move about. Even on land the waters claim their own portions. The fish of the waters lick the land and seek their prey from it; gnats too buzz around you near the marshes that bred them. They too heard the command of the Lord when he said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls.”

We know that the kinds of serpents are called creeping things because they creep over the earth; but much more does everything that swims have either the appearance or the [?] of creeping. For although some creatures seem to fall into the water when they plunge into the depths, yet when they swim on the surface they creep with their whole body, which they drag over the backs, as it were, of the waters. That is why David said: “This great sea and [?]; there are creeping things without number.” Indeed, although many have feet and the use of walking, because they are amphibious and live either in water or on land, such as seals, crocodiles, and the river horses [?] they call hippopotamuses, because they are born in the river Nile [?], yet when they are in deep water they do not walk but swim. They do not use the foot as a step for walking, but as an oar for creeping, just as a ship glides along driven by oars and its prow cuts through the waters.

“Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” said the Lord. A short word, but powerful and far-reaching, it pours a common nature into the smallest and the greatest alike. The whale [?] is brought forth in the same moment in which the frog is born by the working of the same power. God does not labour over the greatest things, nor does he disdain the smallest. Nature felt no pain in giving birth to dolphins, just as she felt none when she produced tiny murex shells and snails. Consider, O man, how many more creatures there are in the sea than on land. Count, if you can, the kinds of all the fish, both the tiny and the very largest: octopuses, oysters [?], crayfish, crabs, and among these countless others of their own kind. What shall I say of the kinds of serpents, the dragons that Job speaks of [?]? Nor shall I pass over scorpion-fish, frogs, turtles, as well as sea weasels and dogfish, sea calves, huge sea monsters, dolphins, seals, sea lions. What shall I say [?] of the sea blackbirds, thrushes, and peacocks, whose colours we also see reproduced in birds: black like the blackbird, their backs and necks painted in changing colours like the peacock's, their bellies speckled like the thrush's, and so on? Whose species and names have the land creatures claimed for themselves? For these things began first in the sea [?], since it was the water that first, at God's bidding, brought forth the creeping things with living souls that it was commanded to produce.

Add this charm too: the things we fear on land we love in the water. What is harmful on land is harmless in the water, and even the snakes there have no venom. The lion is fearsome [?] on land, but sweet in the waves. The moray, which they say has something harmful about it, is a costly delicacy. The frog, repulsive in the marshes, is comely in the waters and surpasses almost all other foods. If anyone is keen [?] to learn more, let him ask the fishermen of different places, for no one can know everything. Beware of the dogs, however, even in the sea; the apostle teaches that they are troublesome even in the Church and must be guarded against, saying: “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers.” The weasel's smell is foul on land, but in the water it is [?]. The land weasel knows how to avenge itself with its stench; this one is no less pleasing when caught than when free. Nor shall I let you go unhonoured in my account, grayling, whose name grew out of a flower. Whether the waters of the Ticino or of the lovely Adige have nourished you, you are a flower. Indeed, there is a common saying, wittily applied to someone who gave off a pleasing sweetness: “He smells either of fish or of flower.” Thus the smell of a fish was declared to be the same as that of a flower. What is more pleasing than your appearance, more delightful than your sweetness, more [?] than your scent? What the honeycomb gives off, you breathe out from your body. What shall I say of the sea ravens, or of the sea wolves [?]? The lamb does not know to fear these wolves. So great is the charm of the waters, whose sea calves [?] even lions flee [?], that the prophet's words about the holiness of the Church rightly fit them: “The wolves and the lambs shall graze together; the lion and the ox shall eat straw together.” Nor is it any wonder, since in the Church too the waters bring it about that robbers, their wickedness washed away, are ranked with the innocent. Why should I mention the purple shellfish, which adorn the banquets of kings and dye their robes? What is revered in kings, then, comes from the waters; that splendour which shines is from the waters. Add the sea pigs, pleasing even to the Jews: since nothing is unclean that water washes, they cannot regard these as unclean as they do those born on land.

There are countless uses, then, and countless kinds of fish. Some lay eggs, like the larger speckled fish they call trout, and entrust them to the waters to be nurtured. The water, then, gives life and creates, and still carries out the duty of that first command as if it were a perpetual law, a kind of gentle mother of living things. Others bring forth living young from their own bodies, like sea weasels, dogfish and huge sea creatures, dolphins and seals and other sea creatures of that sort. When they have given birth, if they happen to sense any danger or threat around their young [?], in order to protect them or to calm the fear of their tender age with a mother's love, they open their mouths and hold their young suspended in their harmless teeth, and they are even said to take them back inside their bodies and hide them in the womb that bore them. What human affection could imitate this devotion of fish? Kisses are enough for us; for them it is not enough to open their insides, to take their offspring back and restore them unharmed, to warm them again with the heat of their own body, to quicken them with their own breath, and for two to live in one body, until either they bring them to safety or shield their young from danger by putting their own bodies in the way. Who that sees this, even if he could manage it [?], would not yield to such great devotion in fish? Who would not stand amazed that nature keeps in fish what it does not keep in men? Many have killed their own sons, set upon from suspicion with a stepmother's hatred; other women, as we read, have eaten their own children in a famine. For human children the mother has become a tomb; for the offspring of fish the parent's womb, like a wall with a rampart of its inmost organs, keeps the young unharmed.

The various kinds of fish, then, have various ways: some lay eggs, others give birth to young that are alive and fully formed. Those that lay eggs do not weave nests like birds, do not take on the labour of long brooding, do not rear their young with trouble to themselves. The egg drops, and the water receives it into the lap of its own nature like a gentle nurse and, warming it quickly, turns it into a living creature. For the egg, quickened at once by the parent's touch, drops, and out comes a fish.

And then how pure and undefiled is their succession! None mates with another kind, but only with its own: grayling with grayling, bass with bass. The scorpion-fish too keeps the chastity of an unstained union with its own kind. So it has the modesty of its kind but not the venom of its kind; for the scorpion-fish does not sting, but nourishes. They know nothing, then, of adulterous unions with a partner of another kind, like those brought about with great care by men when donkeys and mares are mated together, or again when she-asses are mixed with horses, which are truly adulterations of nature; for surely it is a greater thing to commit an offence that pollutes nature than one that wrongs a person. And you, O man, arrange these things as the go-between of an adultery among beasts of burden, and you think that animal [more valuable] [?] which is adulterous than one which is genuine.
