You yourself confound different kinds, you mix different seeds, and you often force unwilling animals into forbidden matings, and you call this skill. Since you cannot do this with men, so that a mixture of different kinds [?] might produce offspring, you take from a man what he was born as, you strip manhood from a man, and by cutting off a part of the body you deny him his sex and make a eunuch, so that audacity might accomplish in men what nature refused.

Consider from this too how good a mother water is. You, O man, have taught fathers to disown their sons, have taught separations, hatreds, quarrels; learn what [?] the bond between parent and children is. Fish cannot live without water, nor be separated from the company of their parent, nor be parted from the care of their nurse; and by a kind of nature it happens that, once separated, they die at once. For they do not live, as all [other creatures] do, by breathing this air, because they lack the natural ability to draw in breath and breathe it out; otherwise they could not live always under water, since they take in no breath. What air is to us, water is to them. As the air supplies us with the stuff of life, so water supplies them. When the passage of breath is cut off, we die at once, because we cannot go without the breath of life for even a short time; so too fish taken out of water cannot exist without what sustains them.

And the reason is plain. In us the lung takes in air through the roomier inner spaces of the chest and, since it is permeable through many pores, cools the inner heat with the inflow of air. For the chest, just as it receives food, so it separates the surplus of food from the wholesome juices and the blood [?]: [?] the lung has gathered, so that the inbreathing of air can reach it more easily. Fish, however, have gills, which they now fold and draw together, now unfold and open out. So in this closing and opening, while water is taken in, passed through and penetrates, the function of breathing appears to be carried out. Fish therefore have a nature of their own, not shared with the others; a particular way of life, a substance of living set apart and distinct from the rest. That is why they are not tamed, and do not, like land animals, take pleasure in the touch and caress of a human hand, even though they live when kept in their ponds.

What shall I say of how thick their teeth are? They do not have teeth on one side only, like sheep or cattle; both jaws are armed with teeth, because they live in water, and if they chewed their food for long and did not swallow it quickly, it could be carried off and dissolved from their teeth by the water [?]. So they have thick, sharp teeth, so that they can bite quickly, make quick work of their food, and swallow it easily, without any pause or delay. In fact they do not chew the cud; only the parrot-fish among them is said to ruminate, as those report who have had the chance, the experience or the interest to learn such things.

Yet they too have not escaped the violence of power among their own kind, and everywhere the weaker are subject to the greed of the stronger. The weaker each one is, the more exposed it is to being preyed upon. Most of them feed on plants and tiny worms; but there are some that devour one another and feed on their own flesh. Among them the smaller is food for the larger, and in turn the larger is attacked by a stronger one, and the plunderer of another becomes another's food. So it happens that, having devoured one, it is devoured by another, and both end up in a single belly, the devoured with its own devourer, and in a single gut prey and punishment share company. Perhaps this wrong grew up among them of their own accord, just as in us it did not begin from nature but from greed; or else, since they were given for the use of men, they were also made as a sign, so that in them we might see the vices of our own ways and take warning from their example, lest a stronger man attack a weaker, only to give a still stronger one [an example] of wrong to use against himself [?]. So he who harms another sets a snare for himself, into which he himself may fall.

You too are a fish, you who invade another's insides, who drag down the weak, who pursue the one who yields all the way into the depths. Beware lest, while you pursue him, you yourself fall upon one stronger, and he who escapes your snares lead you into the snares of another, and the one who feared his own ruin when you pursued him see your misfortune first. What difference is there between a rich man who swallows up the inheritances of the weak with the gluttony of wicked desire, and a sheatfish whose belly is filled with the insides of smaller fish? The rich man died, and his spoils did him no good; rather, the infamy of his plundering made him all the more detested. The sheatfish was caught and its useless prey was discovered. How many are found in it that had devoured others! And you, rich man, hold in your bosom the plunderer of another. He held the goods of the poor man whom he had attacked; you, crushing him, have added two inheritances to your wealth, and still you are not satisfied with so great an increase. And you say that you have punished others, when you commit the very things you avenge, more unjust than the unjust, more wicked than the wicked, more greedy than the greedy. See that the same end does not find you as found that fish: the hook [?] and the nets. But you presume on your power, thinking no one can resist you. The sheatfish too presumed that no one would cast a hook for it, no one would set nets, and that if it fell into them it would break through them all; and yet it did not escape the trident, or it ran into the knots of a stronger net from which it could not free itself. No doubt the wickedness of men too, the more grievous the crimes it has committed, the less it can be safe in its crime, and it will at last pay what, as the price of crimes, is agreed to be hard to escape [?].

You are a fish, then, O man. Hear why you are a fish: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, which gathered fish of every kind. When it was full, they drew it to the shore and sat down and chose the best into their vessels, but threw the bad away. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the wicked from among the righteous and throw them into the furnace of fire.” So there are both good and bad fish. The good are kept for their value; the bad are burned at once. The nets do not entangle the good fish but lift it up, and the hook does not kill and destroy it but bathes it in the blood of a precious wound; in the confession of its mouth a good price is found, with which the apostolic tribute and Christ's own tax are paid. For so it is written, where the Lord says: “From whom do the kings of the earth take tribute or tax? From their own sons or from strangers?” And when Peter answered, “From strangers,” the Lord said: “Go to the sea and cast a hook, and take the fish that comes up first; and when you open its mouth you will find a stater there. Take it and give it for me and for you.”

So do not fear Peter's [?] hook, O good fish; it does not kill, it consecrates. Do not despise yourself as worthless because you see that your body is weak. You have in your mouth something to offer both for Peter and for Christ. Do not fear the nets of Peter, to whom Jesus says: “Put out into the deep and let down the nets.” For he does not cast them on the left side but on the right, as Christ commanded him. Do not fear his embrace, for it was said to him: “From now on you will be catching men alive.” So he cast his nets and took in Stephen, who was the first to come up out of the Gospel, holding in his mouth the stater of righteousness. In his steadfast confession he cried out, saying: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” For this fish the Lord Jesus stood, for he knew that in his mouth was the price of his own tax. And so by his glorious martyrdom this rich champion fulfilled both Peter's judgment and teaching and the grace of Christ.

Do not be troubled that I have put the Gospel in place of the sea. The Gospel is the sea on which Christ walked; the Gospel is the sea on which Peter, though he faltered when he denied, yet through the right hand of Christ found the support of faith and the grace of standing firm; the Gospel is the sea from which the martyr came up; the Gospel is the sea in which the apostles fish, into which the net is cast that is like the kingdom of heaven; the Gospel is the sea in which Christ's [mysteries] [?] are prefigured; the Gospel is the sea in which the Hebrew escaped and the Egyptian was destroyed; the Gospel is the sea, because the Church is the bride of Christ and the fullness of divine grace, which was founded upon the seas, as the prophet said: “He himself founded it upon the seas.” Leap up above the waves, O man, for you are a fish. Do not let the waves of this world overwhelm you. If there is a storm, make for the deep water; if it is calm, play in the waves; if there is a gale, beware the rocky shore, lest the raging surge dash you against a cliff. For it is written: “Be wise as serpents.”

And since the example set before us is of wise serpents, let us be wise in seeking and keeping marriages; let us love the partnerships granted to us. If those who were born far apart, separated by distant regions [?], have come together, and if one [?] has set out for foreign parts, let no [?], no absence diminish the love once agreed upon. The same law binds those present and those absent; the same bond of nature has tied the rights of love between those far apart and those at home; the necks of both are joined under the same yoke of blessing, even if one travels the long separations of distant lands, for they have received the yoke of grace not on the neck of the body but on the mind. The viper, the most wicked kind of beast and more cunning than all of the serpent kind, when it conceives the desire to mate, seeks out a familiar union with the sea moray or prepares a new one; it goes to the shore, announces its presence with a hiss, and calls her out to the conjugal embrace. The moray, thus invited, does not fail to come, and grants the venomous serpent the longed-for union. What does such an account mean, if not that the ways of a spouse must be borne with, and that if he is absent, his presence must be waited for? He may be harsh, deceitful, unrefined, unstable, drunken: what is worse than venom, which the moray does not shrink from in her mate? Called, she does not fail to come, and embraces the slippery [?] one with devoted love. He bears your faults and the fickleness of a woman's levity; can you not, woman, bear with your husband? Adam was deceived by Eve, not Eve by Adam. It is right that she take as her guide the one whom, as a woman, she drew into sin, lest she fall again through a woman's weakness. “But he is rough and unpolished.” He pleased you once. Is a husband to be chosen again and again? The ox seeks its partner and the horse loves its own, and if one is changed, the other does not know how to draw the yoke with a stranger and feels itself incomplete. You reject your yoke-mate and think he should often be replaced; if he is away for a single day, you bring in a rival, and at once, without knowing the cause, as though you knew it, you avenge a wrong to your honour. The viper seeks the absent one, calls the absent one, and summons him with a coaxing hiss; and when she senses her mate approaching, she spits out her venom, showing respect to her husband and reverencing the grace of marriage. You, woman, drive away with insults the husband coming home from far away. The viper watches the sea and searches out her mate's path; you block your husband's way with abuse, you stir up the venom of quarrels rather than casting it out; at the time of the marriage embrace you boil over with deadly poison, and you neither blush for your marriage nor respect your husband.

But you too, husband (for we may also take it this way), lay aside the swelling of your heart and the harshness of your ways when your attentive wife [?] shows you respect. Drive away indignation when your gentle wife invites you to love. You are not her master but [?] her husband; it is not a slave-girl that has fallen to your lot, but a wife. God willed you to be the guide of the weaker [?] sex, not its overlord. Return her devotion, repay her love with kindness. The viper pours out its venom: can you not lay aside the hardness of your mind? But you have a natural sternness: you ought to temper it out of regard for marriage, and lay aside your fierceness of spirit out of reverence for your union. It can also be taken this way: husbands, do not seek another man's bed; do not lay snares for another's union. Adultery is a grave thing; it is an injury to nature. In the beginning God made two, Adam and Eve, that is, a husband and a wife, and he made the wife from the husband, that is, from Adam's rib, and he commanded both to be in one body and to live in one spirit. Why do you sever the one body, why do you divide the one spirit? It is adultery against nature. This is what the embrace of the moray and the viper teaches, sought not by the right of kind but by the heat of lust. Learn, husbands: the man who seeks to defile [?] another's wife, whose companionship does he seem to be taking to himself, and to what serpent must he himself be compared? He hastens to a viper, which [?] into a man's lap not by the straight path of truth but by the slippery way of wayward love. He hastens to one who takes back her venom like the viper, which is said, once the act of union is done, to swallow again the venom it had spat out; for the adulteress is a viper. That is why Solomon too says that the drunkard, when lust has grown used to boiling up through wine, is laid out as if by the bite of a snake, and venom spreads through him as if from a horned serpent. And so that you may know he spoke of the adulteress, he added: “When your eyes see a strange woman, your mouth will speak perverse things.”

Let no one think that we have put forward contradictory things in using this viper as an example both of good and of evil, since both serve for instruction: that we should be ashamed either not to show faithfulness to one we love, when a serpent shows it, or to forsake holy marriage and prefer what is slippery and harmful to what is wholesome, as one does who mates with a serpent.

And since we have begun to weave our discourse on cunning, by which each man strives to get round his brother and deceive him, and fits himself for new frauds, so as to cheat by guile one he cannot overcome by force and to cloak him over with some disguise of art, I will not pass over that deceitful trick of the octopus. Finding a rock on a shallow shore, it fastens itself to it, by its shadowy cunning takes on the rock's colour, and, its back covered with a like appearance, it shuts within the nets of its stealthy art the [?] fish that glide up to it without any suspicion of deceit, supposing it to be [?] a rock, and catches them in a kind of fold of its own flesh. So the prey comes of its own accord. And it is caught by stratagems like those of men who often change their character and set in motion various arts of doing harm, so as to probe the minds and feelings of each person: when they are among the continent they preach continence, but in a gathering of the intemperate they behave as though they had strayed from the pursuit of chastity and were sunk in the wallows of excess. So those who hear or see them trust themselves to them with careless readiness and fall all the more quickly, because they do not know how to turn aside or how to beware of what does harm; for wickedness is graver and more harmful when it is shaded by a [?] veil. Therefore we must beware of those who spread the tresses and arms of their fraud far and wide, or who put on a many-shaped appearance. For such men are octopuses, with many coils and the marks of crafty wits, by which they can entangle whatever falls upon the reefs of their fraud.

And what tricks the crab too contrives for the sake of food! It also delights in the oyster and seeks a feast of its flesh. But since [?] to contrive its food, because the hunt is both difficult and dangerous — difficult because the food inside is shut in by very strong shells (for nature, interpreter of the imperial command, has fortified the softness of the flesh as with walls, nourishing and cherishing it in a hollow fold in the middle of the shells and spreading it out as in a valley, and so all the crab's attempts are vain, since it cannot by any force open the closed oyster), and dangerous if the oyster should shut upon its claw — it takes refuge in stratagems and plots an ambush with a new kind of trickery. Since every kind of creature is soothed by pleasure, it watches for when the oyster, in places remote from every [?], opens that double door of its own toward the sun's rays and unbars its shell-gates, to take some pleasure for its inner parts in the free air. Then it slips in a pebble by stealth, prevents the oyster from closing, and so, finding the gates open, safely inserts its claws and feeds on the flesh within.

There are men, then, who after the crab's fashion creep into the practice of cheating others, prop up the weakness of their own strength with a kind of cunning, weave a trap for their brother, and feed on another's misfortune. But you, be content with your own, and let others' losses not be your food. Simple innocence is good food. Content [?] with its own goods, it does not know how to lay snares for those of others, nor does it burn with the torches of greed. To it every gain is a loss to virtue and a kindling of desire. And so poverty with truth is blessed, if it knows its own goods, and is to be preferred to all treasures, because “better is a little given with the fear of God than great treasures without fear.” For how much does it take to feed a man? Or if you seek something that will also be enough to show kindness to others, that too is not much; for “better is hospitality with herbs and goodwill than a feast of fatted calves with strife.” Let us therefore use our wits to seek goodwill and to guard our salvation, not to cheat another [?]. We may use the examples of the sea for the furthering of our own salvation, not for the danger of another's.

9.24. The sea urchin — I mean the sea creature — a tiny animal, cheap and despised, is often a sign to sailors of a coming storm or [?]. For when it senses a gale of winds coming, it seizes a heavy pebble and carries it like ballast and drags it like an anchor, so as not to be dislodged [?]. So it does not balance itself by its own strength but steadies and governs itself by another weight. From this sign sailors take a warning, as it were, of coming turmoil and take precautions [?], so that a sudden whirlwind may not find them unprepared. What mathematician, what astrologer or Chaldean, can so grasp the courses of the stars, the motions and signs of the sky? By what wit did it gather these things, from what teacher did it learn them? Who was its interpreter of so great an omen? Men see a disturbance in the air and are often deceived, because it often clears without a storm; the urchin is not deceived, its signs never escape the urchin.

Where does so tiny an animal get such knowledge that it can foretell the future? The more there is nothing in it by which it could have such [?], the more you should believe that this creature too has received this [?] gift of foreknowledge through the kindness of the Lord of all things. For if God so clothes the grass that we marvel at it; if he feeds the birds and has prepared food for the raven [?] (for its young cry to the Lord); if he has given women skill in weaving; if he has not left without wisdom the spider, which so finely and skilfully hangs its loose nets in doorways; if he himself has given strength to the horse and loosed fear from its neck, so that it exults in the plain and, running to meet [?], scents the battle from afar and is roused by the sound of the trumpet; if he has filled so many of these irrational creatures, and other insensible things such as grass and lilies, with the ordering of his wisdom, why do we doubt that he has bestowed on the sea urchin too this gift of foreknowledge? For he has left nothing unexamined, nothing overlooked. He who feeds all things sees all things; he who made all things in wisdom fills all things with wisdom, as it is written. And so, if he has not passed over the sea urchin as having no share in his care, if he takes thought for it and instructs it with signs of things to come, does he not take thought for your affairs? Indeed he does, as his divine Wisdom bears witness when it says: “If he looks upon the birds, if he feeds them, are you not worth more than they? For if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the fire, how much more will he clothe you, you of little faith?”

Or do we suppose that it is without some endowment of nature that fish also have this gift, that each kind of fish has its appointed dwelling-places, which none of its own kind leaves and no stranger invades? What geometer divided their habitations for them, never at any time to be broken? We have heard of a geometer, a land-measurer, but never of a sea-measurer; and yet the fish know their measure — not one prescribed by city walls and gates, nor bounded by buildings of houses or the boundaries of fields, but the measure of what is fitting, so that each has enough for its use, not as much as some immoderate greed would claim for itself. It is a kind of law of nature to seek only as much as suffices for living, and to reckon the size of one's estate by the measure of one's food. This kind of fish is fed and bred in that bay of the sea, that kind in another. Indeed you will not find the kinds of fish mixed together; what abounds here is lacking elsewhere. One bay of the sea feeds grey mullet, another sea bass, another [?], another spiny lobsters. They have no free power of roaming, and yet their numbers are not shut in by mountains nor is their passage blocked by rivers flowing between; rather, a habit stamped on them by nature keeps each within bounds as if of its homeland, and to go out beyond its fellow inhabitants [?] is regarded with suspicion.

But our way of thinking is far different: to change our homes by exile, to be gripped by disdain for the natives, to court the favour of newcomers, to move the ancient boundaries which our fathers set, to join field to field and house to house. [?] the land for men, and even the seas are laid flat; again the land is cut through at the whim of individuals and the sea is let in, so that they may make islands and possess straits. They claim stretches of the sea for themselves by right of ownership, and speak of their rights over the fish as subject to them like slaves born in their household. “This bay of the sea is mine,” says one, “that one is another's”: the powerful [?] the elements among themselves. For some, oysters are reared in the waves; for others, fish are shut up in a fishpond. Even the sea is not enough for luxury unless they have storehouses of oysters. So they count the oysters' ages and build tanks for fish, lest the banquet [?] cannot be filled. And with what ears they hear the name of a neighbour, with what eyes they look on his possessions! How they plot day and night to take something from those near them! “Will you alone dwell upon the earth?” cries the prophet. The Lord takes note of these things and reserves them for punishment.

How foreign to the fish is the plunder of greed! They seek out nature's hidden places and know a sea beyond the bounds of the world, broken by no islands, with no land lying in between or set anywhere beyond it. There, then, where the sea spread far and wide shuts off all use of sight and the daring of sailing for profit [?], the great sea creatures are said to hide themselves — those immense kinds of fish with bodies like mountains, as those who have been able to see them have told us. There they pass a quiet life, apart from islands and separated from all contact with coastal cities; they have their own regions and allotted dwellings. In these they remain without trespassing on their neighbours' boundaries, nor do they seek changes of place by wandering, but they love them as their native soil and think it sweet to linger there. They have chosen these places so that they may lead a solitary life, far from the interference of onlookers.

There are, however, some kinds of fish that change their places not from fickleness of temperament but from the need to rear their young. Seeing to this at the fitting and appointed time, they gather from many places and from various bays of the sea as if by common counsel, and in a united column make for the seas of the north, hastening toward that sea [?] by a certain law of nature. If you saw them going up, you would say it was a kind of current, so do they rush forward and cut through the waves, streaming through the Propontis into the Euxine with violent force. Who tells the fish of these places, who prescribes the times? Who gave them the plan of their journey, the order of their company, the limits and times of their return? Men, of course, have an emperor whose command is awaited; the watchword goes out, edicts are posted for the provincials to assemble, letters are sent to the military tribunes, a day is fixed — and many cannot arrive by the appointed day. What emperor gave the fish their command, what teacher imparted this discipline, what quartermasters lay out their routes, what leaders direct their march, so that no one fails to meet? But I recognize who that emperor is who by divine ordinance pours his command into the senses of all creatures, who silently gives to dumb animals the order of natural discipline, who not only pervades great things but spreads himself through even the smallest. The fish obeys the divine law, and men contradict it. The fish faithfully heeds heaven's commands, and men make God's precepts void. Or does the fish seem contemptible to you because it is dumb and without reason? But take care that you do not begin to be more contemptible to yourself, if you are found [?] more irrational than it. What is more reasonable than this passage of the fish? They do not explain its reason in words, but they speak it in deeds. For in summertime they make for the strait of the Pontus because this bay is sweeter than the rest of the sea. The sun does not linger over its waters as long as over the others, and for this reason it does not draw off all the water that is sweet and drinkable. Who does not know that even sea creatures often delight in fresh water? Indeed, while they follow the rivers and swim upstream, fish of the sea's kinds are often caught [?]. Since, then, this reason makes the Pontus more pleasing to them — or else because the regular north wind there tempers the heat — they judge it more suitable than the others for spawning and for rearing all their young there, because the tender offspring could scarcely bear the hardship of a foreign region, while there the gentle mildness of the air cherishes them. And so, their task done, they all return together in the column in which they came.

Let us consider what reason this is. The bay of the Pontus is exposed to the most violent blasts of the north wind and the other winds; so if a heavy gale rages there, storms are stirred up so that the sand is churned up from the bottom. A sandy swell is the sign of this: rising higher at the wind's movement, and then heavier with its weight, it is without doubt held to be unbearable not only for sailors but even for the sea creatures themselves. Add to this that, since very many and very great rivers mingle with the Pontus, in wintertime the bay itself grows colder and its whole [?] freezes stiff. Therefore the fish, as judges of the waters, seek there in summer the mildness of the [?] northern breeze, and having enjoyed its pleasantness, they hasten in turn to avoid the harshness of winter; fleeing the cruelty of the northern region, they betake themselves to the other bays, where either the calm of the winds is gentler or the warmth of the sun is wont to make it like spring. So the fish knows the time for giving birth, which the wisdom of Solomon spoke of as a great mystery; it knows the time for going and returning, it knows the time for [?] and for [?], and it knows these so that it cannot be deceived, because it uses not the estimate of reason and the arguments of disputation but the inspiration of nature, which is the true teacher of devotion. Indeed all living creatures have fixed [?] times for giving birth; man alone has them indiscriminate and confused. The other kinds seek a mild season; women alone bring forth their offspring at an unkind season, for a wandering and intemperate lust for begetting produces a wandering season of childbirth. The fish crosses such great [?] there so that it may seek some benefit for its kind; we too cross wide seas, but how much more honourable is a voyage undertaken for love of posterity than for greed of money! Indeed, for them the crossing is reckoned to devotion, for us to gain. They bring back offspring [more precious than?] all merchandise; we, in wretched lust for profit, bring back merchandise far unequal to the danger we ran. So they return to their homeland, while we abandon ours; by swimming they increase their kind, while by sailing ours is diminished.

Who then would deny that such instinct and power have been poured into them by God, when he sees these fish arranging with lively instinct so regular a pilgrimage to the north to fulfil their fertility, and others taking on such strength in a tiny body that they can stop the greatest ships running under full sail in mid-ocean? So the remora, a little fish, is said to halt a huge ship with such ease that you would see it cling to the sea as if rooted and be unable to move; for it holds it motionless for some time. Or do you think that so much strength could have been supplied to this creature too without the Creator's gift? Why should I speak of swordfish, sawfish, dogfish, whales or hammerheads, or of the sting of the stingray, even when it is dead? For just as, if anyone treads on a viper's [?], it is said to do more harm than venom, though only when fresh, and to spread an incurable wound, so too the stingray is said to bring more danger with its sting when dead than when alive. The sea hare too, a timid animal on land but formidable in the sea, brings a swift corruption that cannot easily be [?]. For your Creator willed that you should not be quite safe from those that lie in wait even at sea, so that because of the few things that do harm you should, as if posted on watch, always hope for the protection of salvation from your Lord [?] with the arms of faith and the shield of devotion.

Let us come to the Atlantic Ocean. How huge are the sea creatures there, of boundless size! If ever they swim on the surface of the waves, you would think islands were walking, or the highest mountains were rising with their summits to the sky. They are said to be seen not on beaches or shores but in the depths of the Atlantic Ocean, so that at the sight of them sailors are deterred from presuming to sail in those parts, and do not dare to approach the secret places of the elements without the utmost terror of death.

But now let us ourselves rise from the depths of the sea; let our discourse emerge a little and lift itself to higher things. Let us consider only those things that are familiar to many and full of charm: how water is turned into solid salt, so that it is often cut with iron — which is no wonder in the case of British salt, which shines with the snowy whiteness of that same mineral [?] in the likeness of solid marble, wholesome as food for the body and very pleasant in drink; how coral too, a not unlovely stone, is a plant in the sea, but if it is brought out into the air it hardens with the firmness of stone; whence nature has set in oysters the most precious pearl, and how the water of the sea [?] it in such soft flesh. Things that are hard to find even among kings lie commonly on the shores as if [?] and are gathered on rough rocks and crags. Water also nourishes a golden fleece, and the shores produce a wool resembling that metal, whose colour none of those who coat fleeces with various dyes has yet been able to imitate. So far does human industry fall short of matching the beauty of the sea's nature. We know with what care the fleeces of sheep are tended, even less precious ones; yet however excellent they may be, no dye grows naturally in them. Here the colour is natural, and no dye has yet equalled it. This too is a fish's fleece. And the purple shellfish themselves, which provide the royal insignia, belong to the sea.

And what charm of meadows or loveliness of gardens can equal the painted beauty of the blue sea? Though flowers gleam [?] in the meadows, this wool too shines with the gleam of gold [?]; and they quickly wither, while this lasts a long time and is kept. [?] gleam from afar in gardens, sails on ships; there a fragrance breathes, here a wind. What use is there in a leaf? But how much commerce in ships! Lilies bring sweetness to the nostrils, sails bring safety to men. Add the leaping fish and the playing dolphins, add the waves sounding with their hoarse murmur, add the ships running to the shores or putting out from them. And when chariots are let out of the starting gates, with what zeal and passion the spectators contend! Yet the horse runs in vain, but ships do not sail in vain: the one in vain because it is empty, these to good purpose, being full, as it were, of grain. What [?] more pleasing than ships driven not by the whip but by the breath of the winds, where no one is an opponent but all are supporters, where no one who arrives is defeated but all the vessels that complete the voyage are crowned, where the prize is the reward of safety and the victory is the price of return? How great the difference between straight courses and those that turn back! The one [?], the other [?]. Add the shores woven over with oars, for which the signal to set out is a breeze from heaven. And so charioteers bring back empty applause, while these, having been kept safe, pay their vows.

What can I say that is worthy of Jonah, whom the whale took in to life and gave back to the grace of prophecy? The water set right the man whom earthly things had led astray. He who had mourned on land sang psalms in the whale's belly. And so that the redemption of neither element should be passed over, the salvation of the lands went ahead first in the sea, because the sign of the Son of Man is the sign of [?] Jonah. As he was in the belly of the whale, so Jesus was in the heart of the earth. There was a remedy in both, yet the greater example of mercy was in the sea, since fishes took in the one whom men rejected, and fishes saved the one whom men crucified. Peter too staggers on the sea, but he does not fall; and though he confessed in the waves, he denied on land. So there, as one devoted, he is grasped by the hand; here, as one who has forgotten, he is [?] by a stern look. But now let us ask the Lord that our discourse, like Jonah, may be cast up on land, so that it does not toss any longer on the deep. And well did the gourd also spring up, to shade us from our ills. But it too, withering as the sun climbs, warns us to rest, so that we do not begin to grow overheated in mind on land and our words also fail us. Certainly more has been given to us than to the Ninevites: in the waters, the forgiveness of sins.

And when he had been silent for a little while, he began his discourse again and said: Dearly beloved brethren, the necessary discussion of the nature of birds had escaped us, and a discourse of this kind had flown away from us along with the birds themselves. For it happens [?] by a certain law of nature that those who look at something, or who wish to express it in speech, take on the quality of the things they look at or speak of. So with the slower things we [?], and with the swift we are carried off by a quick gaze, and in our style too we are either slower or rapid. So while I was taking care that things sunk in the sea should not pass me by and things covered by the waters should not escape me, I [?] every winged creature; for while I bent down and searched the lowest depths of the waters, I did not look back at the flights of the air, nor [?] even the shadow of a swift wing, which could have gleamed in the waters. But when I thought all the business finished, believed I was done, and judged the fifth day complete, the birds came to my mind, which, when they go to rest, are accustomed to soothe the sky with song, glad as if their task were done. This they are accustomed to renew, as if by solemn rite, at the rising and the setting of the day, so as to render to their Creator praises for the time of night and of day, both the time now past and the time about to begin. I had therefore lost a great incentive for stirring up our devotion. For who, having the understanding of a man, would not blush to close the day without the celebration of psalms, when even the tiniest birds attend the beginnings of days and nights with solemn devotion and sweet song?

Let our winged discourse, then, come back to us. It had almost slipped out of our sight and, like an eagle seeking the heights, had hidden its [?] in the clouds, had we not, as we raised our eyes, washed with water, from the depths toward heaven, seen the air empty of flights [?] and thought that it must be called back to the service of the pen. You will be the judges, you who are fowlers of the word, whether it flies off uselessly [?] or has usefully fallen back into your nets. Nor do I fear that weariness will creep over us in seeking out flights, since it did not creep over us in searching the depths, or that any of us will fall asleep during the discussion, since he can be woken by the songs of birds. Surely I do not doubt that one who stayed awake among mute fishes cannot feel sleepy among singing birds, when he is summoned to wakefulness by such charm. Nor should this be thought trivial on the ground that it could have been passed over, since it is the third part of creation among living things. For there is no doubt that there are three kinds of living creatures: those of the land, those of the air, and those of the water. Thus it is written: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls according to their kind, and winged creatures flying above the earth along the firmament of heaven according to their kind.”

We are called back to what we passed, like forgetful travellers who, having gone past heedlessly, retrace their steps and pay a heavy penalty for their carelessness in the labour of repeating the journey. Yet there is also the good traveller who makes up for the loss of turning back by the quick speed with which he covers the rest of the way. This I think I must do, especially since the discourse is about birds, which are wont to dazzle men's eyes with their swift flight. For why should we linger over things in which speed is usually what pleases? So let our discourse, leaving the beaten track and unused to this kind of writing, resound and ring with singing birds.

But where am I to find swans' songs, which delight even under the heavy terror of approaching death? Where am I to find those natural measures of song with which even the marshes resound and give forth melodies of the sweetest charm? Where the voices of the parrot and the sweetness of blackbirds? Would that the nightingale might sing this, which wakes the sleeper from his sleep; for that bird is wont to signal the [?] of the rising day and to bring a more abundant joy at dawn. Yet if their sweetness is lacking, there are the moaning turtledoves and the hoarse doves, and the crow too, which calls for rain at the top of its voice. So, in a rustic discourse, let us follow as best we can the knowledge that country folk have taught us.

And since we have spoken of the creeping things of the waters, it is hard for our discourse to rise all at once to the birds of the sky. So let us first speak of the birds that dwell around the waters of the sea and the rivers, with which we can come up out of the water. Let us therefore begin our discourse with the halcyon. It is a sea bird that is wont to bring forth its young on the shores, laying its eggs in the sand at about midwinter. For it has set apart for hatching its young the very time when the sea rises highest and dashes most violently on the shores, so that the grace of this bird might shine out all the more through the solemn wonder of a sudden calm. For when the sea has been heaving with waves, as soon as the eggs are laid it suddenly grows gentle; all the storms of the winds subside, the blasts of the breezes are still, and the sea lies calm, untouched by the winds, while the halcyon warms her eggs. The warming lasts seven days, at the end of which she brings out her chicks and completes the brood. At once she adds another seven days in which to nourish her young until they begin to grow up. And do not wonder that the time of nurture is so short, since the completion of the brood takes so few days. Such grace has this tiny bird received as a gift from God that sailors watch for these fourteen days, which they count on for fair weather and call halcyon days, during which they dread no stirring of stormy weather. “Are you not of more value than sparrows?” says the Lord.

If, then, out of regard for a tiny bird, though the sea rises [?] amid the harshness of winter, amid heavy storms and tempests of wind, a calm is suddenly poured over all the elements, wipes the clouds from the sky and settles the waves, you recognize, O man made in the image of God, how much you ought to hope for, if only you imitate the faith of this little bird with devout zeal. She, seeing the storms rise and the winds rage amid the fierceness of winter, is not called back or turned aside, but driven on. So she sets her eggs on the shore, where the sand, still wet from the ebbing wave, receives them; nor does she dread the rising waves which she sees murmuring and washing up.

And lest you think she seems to treat her eggs with contempt, as soon as she has laid them she builds a nest and warms her brood with her own body. Nor does she fear for her own safety from the flooding of the shore, but, secure in the grace of God, she entrusts herself to the winds and the waves. And that is not all. She adds as many days again for nurture, and does not fear that in so many days the calm of the treacherous sea will be broken, and she puts to the test her [?], now established by the solemn custom of nature. She does not hide her tender young in any hiding places or under roofs, nor shut them up in caves, but entrusts them to the bare and [?] ground. She does not protect them from the cold with [?], but reckons that they will be safer under the divine warmth, the more she disregards everything else. Which of us does not cover his little ones with clothes and hide them under a roof? Who does not shut them in enclosed bedrooms, who does not block up the windows on every side so carefully that not a breath of air can get in even slightly? Rightly, then, the very ones we clothe and cherish so anxiously we strip of the covering of heavenly mercy; but [?] those whom she casts out naked, God clothes with a divine garment.

Nor shall I pass you by, divers, whose name has stuck to you from your constant diving. How you are always diving and gathering the signs of the breezes, and, foreseeing a coming storm, quickly fly back from mid-sea and retreat with cries to the safety of the shores! How you too, coots, who delight in the deep sea, flee the commotion of the sea that you foreknow and play in the shallows! The heron itself, which is wont to keep to the marshes, [?] its familiar haunts and, fearing the rains, flies above the clouds so as not to feel the storms of the clouds. Let us consider the various birds of the sea, how, when a stirring of the winds threatens, they betake themselves to safer pools, which are sweeter to them at that time, and search out familiar food in some hidden bay of the land.

And who would not marvel at the night watches of the geese, which bear witness to their vigils by their constant cries? Indeed, by this very means they saved the Roman Capitol from the Gallic enemy. Rightly do you owe it to them, Rome, that you reign. Your gods were asleep, and the geese were keeping watch. That is why on those days you sacrifice to the goose and not [?]; for your gods give way to the geese, by whom they know they were defended so that they themselves were not captured by the enemy.

It is fitting that after the description of fishes the discourse has passed to the birds that are accustomed to the waters, since they too likewise delight in the practice and function of swimming. Hence there seems to be a first kinship between these birds and fishes, since a certain fellowship in swimming seems to be common to both kinds. There is a second kinship between birds and fishes too, in that the practice of flying is a form of swimming. For as the fish cuts the water by swimming, so the bird cleaves the air with swift flight. And both kinds alike are furnished with a tail and with oars of wings, so that fishes raise themselves forward as if with a rein and advance farther, and with the rudder of the tail either easily turn wherever they wish or with a rush direct their course straight ahead. Birds too swim in the air with their flights as if in water, and stretch out what are, as it were, arms, and with the tail either raise themselves upward or plunge downward. Hence, since in some respects their practice and form are the same, the birth of both kinds came forth from the waters by divine command. For God said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living [?] souls according to their kind, and winged creatures flying along the firmament of heaven according to their kind.” Not without reason, then, since both kinds are brought forth from the waters, is the property of swimming [?] common to both.

Indeed, while the slippery snake [?] and serpents (for the serpent was given its name because they cannot walk but creep) and dragons likewise, like most fishes, are without feet, no kind of bird lacks the service of feet, because all get their food from the land. And so they are supported by the gift of feet, because they need such service to seek their food. Thus some birds are armed with talons for seizing [?], such as hawks and eagles, which practise the plunder of the hunt; others put them to suitable use and service either for walking or for procuring their food.

Birds have one name, but who could take in their different kinds by memory or by knowledge? There are birds that [?] on flesh. So they have rough talons, a hooked and sharp beak, and swift flight, because they live by plunder, so that they can easily seize the prey they pursue and quickly tear out its entrails with beak or talons. There are also birds that feed on seed they find, and others on varied and chance food. There is also a difference in their way of flocking together, a grace that those bent on plunder lack. For because of their greed for prey, or because of [?] ambush, they do not agree even among themselves, and so they avoid the company of their own kind (for greed shuns the fellowship of many), and besides, a gathering of many would easily give itself away. For these birds, then, there is no companionship except the bond of mating. This, then, is the way of life of eagles and hawks; but doves, cranes, starlings, ravens and crows, and thrushes too, on the contrary, delight greatly in company.

Some kinds of birds, again, are native, which always stay in the same places; others are visitors, which go off to other regions and return when winter is over. There are others which come back in winter and go abroad from us in summer, either because some betake themselves to warmer parts in wintertime, or because many in turn spend the summer in these places, which they know to be more pleasant. Thrushes, for instance, come back at the end of autumn, on the edge of winter, as if summer were over. Against them we, with inhospitable cruelty, contrive snares, and in various ways we strive now to deceive them with a treacherous perch, now to trick them with whistling, now to catch them in nooses. The stork's return raises the banner of spring. Cranes, because they seek the heights, love to travel often.

Some birds submit to the hand, grow used to the table and are soothed by stroking; others shy away. Some delight in the same dwellings as men; others love a secluded life in the wilderness, making up for the difficulty of seeking their food by their love of freedom. Some only [?] with their voices, others delight with sweet and melodious song. Some by nature, others by training, utter distinct and differing sounds, so that you would think a man had spoken when it was a bird. How sweet is the voice of the blackbird, how clear that of the parrot! There are also some that are simple, like doves, and others that are cunning, like partridges; the cock is more boastful, the peacock more beautiful. Among birds there are also differences of life and of works: some love to take counsel in common, and with combined strength to look after something like a commonwealth and to live as if under a king; others each look out for themselves, refuse rule and, if they are captured, long to escape from unworthy servitude.

Let us begin, then, with those that have offered themselves to our use as a model. For in them there is a kind of polity and a natural military service; in us these are forced and servile. With what unbidden and voluntary practice do cranes keep anxious watch at night! You may see sentries posted, and while the rest of their kind [?], some go round and scout, lest an ambush be attempted from any side, and [?] provide protection with tireless vigour. Then, when the time of its watch is completed, having done its duty, it settles down to sleep after first giving a cry, to wake the sleeper to whom it is going to hand over its turn of duty. And that one willingly takes up its lot: it does not, as is our way, give up sleep unwillingly and sluggishly, but briskly shakes itself out of its bed, carries out its turn, and repays the favour it received with equal care and dutifulness. So there is no desertion, because the devotion is natural; so the watch is safe, because the will is free.

They keep this order also when flying, and by this arrangement they lighten all their labour, taking turns in the office of leadership. For one goes ahead of the others for a time appointed to it and flies in front, as it were, before the standards; then it turns back and yields to the one following the lot of leading the column. What could be more beautiful than this: that both the labour and the honour are common to all, and that power is not claimed by a few but passed on to all by a kind of voluntary lot?

This is the office of the ancient commonwealth and the image of a free state. Thus from the beginning men had begun to practise the polity they received from nature after the example of the birds: that labour should be common and dignity common, that individuals should learn to share cares in turn and [?] obedience and command, that no one should be without a share of honour and no one exempt from labour. This was the finest state of affairs. No one grew insolent through perpetual power, nor was anyone broken by long servitude, since promotion was conferred without envy, by the order of office and the measure of time, and the lot which shared the duty of watching seemed more bearable. No one dared to oppress another with servitude, since he would have to bear in turn the disdain of the one who would succeed to the honour; nor [?] was labour heavy, since the dignity that would follow relieved it. But once the lust for domination began to claim the powers it had won and to refuse to lay down those it had taken up, once military service began to be not a common right but a servitude, once the taking up of power became a matter not of order but of [?] ambition, the performance of labour itself began to be borne more harshly, and what is not voluntary soon gives way to carelessness. How unwillingly men take on the duties of the watch! How grudgingly each man in camp, having drawn the danger by lot, keeps the watch that is entrusted to his guard by royal command! A penalty for slackness is set out, and yet carelessness often creeps in and the watches are not kept. For necessity, which imposes obedience on the unwilling, often brings distaste with it; for nothing is so easy that it has no difficulty when you do it unwillingly. So unbroken labour turns away goodwill, and continuous, long-lasting power begets insolence. Where among men would you find one who would of his own accord lay down command, give up the insignia of his leadership, and willingly become last in rank instead of first! We, on the other hand, often contend not only for the first place but even for the middle one; we claim the first couches at a banquet, and once a place has been given us, we want it to be ours forever. So among cranes there is equanimity in labours and humility in power. They have to be reminded to take their turns of watch; they do not have to be reminded to step down from power, because in the one case the natural rest of sleep must be interrupted, while in the other the grace of voluntary diligence must be shown.

They say that storks set out in an assembled column whenever they think they must travel somewhere, and that they are carried together into many places around the East, and all move as one, as if at a military signal. You would think it an army marching with its standards: so do they all keep the order of travelling, of accompanying and of leading the way. Crows lead and guide them and escort them like a kind of [?] bodyguard, so that they are believed to bring them help as they fight against hostile birds, and to take up the wars of others at their own peril. Proof of this is that none are found staying in those places for some time afterward, and that, returning with wounds, they declare by a kind of plain voice of blood [?] and other signs that they have endured the clash of grievous battles. Who, then, laid down for them a penalty for desertion? Who prescribed fearful punishments for abandoning service, so that none tries to slip away from the hospitable squadrons, but all eagerly perform the duty and office of escort?

Let men learn to keep the laws of hospitality, and let them learn from birds what reverence is owed to guests and what services must be rendered to them, since crows are not wont to deny them even their own dangers. We, then, shut our doors on those to whom birds devote even their lives; those whom they accompany, sharing their peril, we bar from the hospitality of our roof; and those whose wars they take up, we often make war upon. I am lying if this was not the cause of the Sodomites' punishment, or if the fury of Egypt, while it tried to make war on a nation that was its guest, did not pay the penalty for its inhospitality in the drowning of a faithless people.

But let us consider how far [?] the kindness of this bird surpasses the piety and prudence of rational beings, a kindness that none of us could imitate even after seeing the example. For when the father's limbs are worn out by long old age and stripped of the covering of feathers and the oars of wings, the offspring stand around him, warm him with their own feathers and—what shall I say?—feed him with food they have gathered together, while it too repairs the losses of nature, so that, holding up the old bird on this side and that with the support of their wings, they train him to fly and bring back to their former use the now unaccustomed limbs of their dutiful father. Which of us would not shrink from lifting up a sick father? [?] Who would lay a weary old man on his shoulders, a thing that among [?] would be thought scarcely credible? Who, dutiful though he be, would not hand this service over to his slaves? But to birds what is full of devotion is not heavy, and what pays the debt of nature is not burdensome. Birds do not refuse to feed their father, which many men have refused to do even under a prescribed necessity and the terror of punishment. Birds are bound by a law not written but inborn; no precepts bring birds to this duty, but the offices of natural grace. Birds do not blush to carry the limbs of a venerable old father. For this is a conveyance of piety, and it has become so widely known through frequent testimony that it has [?] the reward of a fitting recompense: in Roman usage the stork is called the dutiful bird, and what is said to have been conferred by decree of the senate on scarcely a single emperor, these birds have earned in common. So these birds have decrees of the Fathers as the mark of their own kindness; for it was fitting that dutiful children should first be proclaimed by the judgement of the Fathers. They also have the votes of all; for the repaying of benefits is called antipelargosis, since the stork is called pelargos. So the virtue took its name from them, since the returning of thanks is named with the stork's name.

We have an example of the devotion that the young of birds show in honouring their parents. Now let us take a great lesson in a mother's care for her children. The swallow is tiny in body but lofty in its remarkably devoted affection. Though it lacks everything, it builds nests more precious than gold, because it builds wisely, and a nest of wisdom is better than gold. What could be wiser than to enjoy the roaming freedom of flight and yet to entrust its little ones and its home to the dwellings of men, where no one will attack its young? It is a fine thing, too, that from their very birth it accustoms its chicks to the company of human beings and makes them safer from the snares of their enemies. Then it is remarkable how gracefully it builds its home by itself without any helper, as if it were skilled in the craft. It gathers straws in its beak and smears them with mud so that it can glue them together. But because it cannot carry mud in its feet, it dips the tips of its wings in water, so that dust easily sticks to them and turns into mud. With this mud, little by little, it gathers the straws or tiny twigs and makes them hold together. In this way it builds the whole structure of the nest, so that its young can move about inside their house without harm, as on a paved floor. None of them catches a foot in the chinks of the weaving, and no cold creeps in upon the tender brood.

This kind of industry is common to many birds. But one thing is unique to the swallow, and it shows a remarkable devoted care and a mark of wise understanding and knowledge, even a kind of medical skill. If its chicks are blinded or have their eyes pierced, it has a certain way of healing them by which their sight can be restored to the use it had lost. So let no one complain of poverty because he has left his house empty of money. The swallow comes first: empty of money, it abounds in industry. It builds and spends nothing. It raises a roof and takes nothing from its neighbour. Need and poverty do not drive it to harm another, and it does not despair when its young are gravely sick. But poverty afflicts us and the pressure of want torments us. Need drives many into wickedness and pushes them into crime. Out of love of gain we turn our wits to fraud and bend our feelings to it. In the gravest sufferings we lay hope aside, and broken in spirit [?] we lie there, improvident and idle, when we ought to hope all the more in God's mercy at the very moment that human supports have failed.

Let men learn to love their children from the custom and devotion of crows. Even [?] these birds follow their young with attentive company. Anxious lest the tender ones should perhaps fail, they bring them food, and for a long time they do not give up the work of nourishing them. But the women of the human race quickly wean even the children they love, or, if they are richer, they disdain to nurse them. The poorer women cast off their little ones and expose them, and when the children are found they disown them. The rich too, so that their patrimony may not be divided among many heirs, [?] in the womb, and with murderous potions they snuff out the pledges of their own womb inside the very belly that conceived them. Life is taken away before it is given. Who but man taught that children should be disinherited? Who devised such harsh paternal laws? Who made brothers unequal in the brotherly fellowship of nature? The sons of one rich man are dealt [?] different lots. One is flooded with the whole of his father's estate by the terms of the will. Another bewails his drained and meagre portion of his father's rich inheritance. Has nature divided the merits of children? Like a midwife [?] she gives all alike the substance they need to be born and to live. Let her teach you not to treat unequally in your estate those whom you have made equal by the title of brotherhood. You gave them all in common the fact that they were born. You ought not to begrudge them a common share in that to which nature has made them heirs.

Hawks are said to show harsh unkindness toward their own young. When they notice them attempting their first flights, they throw them out of their nests and drive them away at once. If the young linger, the parents push them with their feathers and hurl them down, beat them with their wings and force them to dare what they fear, and afterward give them no more food. Yet what wonder is it if creatures used to plundering disdain to nurture? Let us consider that they were created for this purpose, so that fear might train even birds to be on their guard, and they would not slacken their vigilance everywhere but would look ahead to the dangers to be avoided from predators. Then, since the work of plundering has grown into them by a kind of nature, they seem rather to be training their chicks for prey from an early age than denying them the benefits of feeding. They take care that the young do not grow lazy at a tender age, are not weakened by soft living, do not waste away in idleness, do not learn to wait for food rather than seek it, and do not lay aside the vigour of their nature. They break off the work of feeding to force the young to dare to practise seizing prey.

The eagle too is much talked about as disowning its young, not both of them, but one of its two chicks. Some have thought this happens because it dislikes having to provide double food. But I do not think this should be readily believed, especially since Moses bore such great witness to this bird's devotion to its young as to say: As an eagle protects its nest and is confident over its young, it spread out its wings and took them up and bore them on its shoulders. The Lord alone led them. How then does it spread out its wings, if it kills one of them? So I think it becomes harsh not out of stinginess in feeding but through a test of judgment. For it is said always to test the young it has hatched, so that the deformity of a degenerate offspring may not tarnish the royal eminence of its race among all birds. So it is asserted that it holds its chicks up to the rays of the sun and suspends the little ones in midair with its talon. If any of them meets the reflected light of the sun and keeps [?] the keenness of its eyes undaunted, with its power of sight unharmed, it is approved, because the steadiness of its clear gaze has shown that its nature is genuine. But the one whose eyes are dazzled by the sun's ray [?] is rejected as degenerate and unworthy of so great a parent. It is not thought worthy of being reared, since it was unworthy of being acknowledged. So the eagle condemns it not out of a harsh nature but by the integrity of its judgment. It does not disown it as its own but refuses it as a stranger.

Yet, as some report, the kindness of a common bird excuses [?] this conduct of the royal bird. For the bird called the coot, which in Greek is called phene, takes in that eaglet, whether disowned or simply not recognized, and joins it to its own brood. Mingling it with its own, it feeds and rears it with the same motherly care that it gives its own young and with an equal supply of food. So the phene nourishes the young of others, while we cast out our own with pitiless cruelty. The eagle, if it casts one out, does not cast it out as its own but fails to recognize it because it is degenerate. We, what is worse, disown those whom we recognize as our own.

But let us come to the turtle-dove, which the law of God chose as the offering of a chaste sacrifice. So when the Lord was circumcised, it was offered, because it is written in the law of the Lord that they should give as a sacrifice a pair of turtle-doves or two young pigeons. For this is the true sacrifice of Christ: chastity of the body and grace of the spirit. Chastity belongs to the turtle-dove, grace to the dove. For it is said that when the turtle-dove has been widowed by the loss of its mate, it grows weary of the marriage bed and even of the name of marriage [?], since its first union proved faithless in its lasting and bitter in its sweetness, having caused more grief by death than delight by love. So it refuses to enter a union again. It does not break the laws of modesty or the bonds of its departed husband. It keeps its love for him alone and keeps for him alone the name of wife. Learn, women, how great is the grace of widowhood, when it is proclaimed even among birds.

Who, then, gave these laws to the turtle-dove? If I look for a man, I do not find one. No man has dared to do it, since not even Paul dared to lay down laws for remaining a widow. Indeed he says [?]: I want, therefore, the younger women to marry, bear children, and manage their households, and give the adversary no occasion. And elsewhere: It is good for them if they remain as they are; but if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry, for it is better to marry than to burn. Paul wishes for in women what the turtle-doves practise without fail. And elsewhere he urges the younger women to marry, because our women can hardly attain the chastity of turtle-doves. So it was God who poured this affection into turtle-doves and gave them this virtue of continence, for he alone can lay down what all may follow. The turtle-dove is not inflamed by the bloom of youth and is not tempted by the lure of opportunity. The turtle-dove does not know how to break its first pledge of faith, because it knows how to keep the chastity it promised when the authority of marriage allotted it a mate.

We have spoken of widowhood among birds, and of how this virtue first arose among them. Now let us speak of virginity, which is asserted to exist in many birds, so that it can be found even in vultures. For vultures are said not to indulge in intercourse or to unite in any conjugal practice or marital coupling. So they are said to conceive without any seed from males and to give birth without mating. Their offspring are said to live on to a great age, so that their lives stretch out to a hundred years, and the end of a short life does not easily overtake them.

What do they say who are accustomed [?] to laugh at our mysteries when they hear that a virgin gave birth, and who think it impossible for an unmarried woman to give birth when no intercourse with a man had violated her chastity? Is something thought impossible in the mother of God that no one denies is possible in vultures [?]? A bird gives birth without a male and no one disputes it. Yet because Mary gave birth while betrothed, they call her chastity into question. Do we not notice that the Lord set forth many examples beforehand from nature itself, by which he might show the fittingness of the incarnation he took upon himself and establish its truth?

Come now, I will explain which birds seem to manage a kind of commonwealth and to live out their lives under laws. What comes to mind first is that the practice of a commonwealth requires that the laws be common to all and be observed by all with common devotion, so that all are held by one bond. No one should have a right that another knows is not lawful for himself. What is lawful should be lawful for all, and what is not lawful should be lawful for none. There should also be a common reverence for the fathers, by whose counsel the commonwealth is governed, one common dwelling in the city for all, one common duty of living together, a rule laid down for all, and a single counsel.

These things are great, but how much more excellent are they in bees! Bees alone of all kinds of living creatures have offspring common to all. They all live in one dwelling and are shut within the threshold of one homeland. Labour is common to all, food is common, work is common to all, use and fruit are common, flight is common. What more need I say? Generation is common to all, and you will find that the integrity of a virgin body is common to all as well. For they do not mingle with one another in any intercourse, nor are they [?] by lust, nor are they shaken by the pains of childbirth. Yet suddenly they send forth a vast swarm of children, gathering their offspring with their mouths from leaves and plants.

They appoint their own king and create their own peoples, and though they are placed under a king, they are still free. For they hold the prerogative [?] and the affection of faithful devotion, because they love the king as one appointed by themselves and honour him with so great a swarm. Their king is not chosen by lot, for in a lot there is chance, not judgment, and often by the irrational fall of the lot the worst is preferred to the better. Nor is he marked out by the common clamour of an ignorant multitude, which does not weigh the merits of virtue or look into the advantages of public benefit but sways with uncertain fickleness. Nor does he sit on the royal throne by the privilege of succession and birth, since one who is ignorant of public life cannot be prudent and learned. Add the flatteries and luxuries which, ingrained in the tender years, usually enervate even a keen mind, and then the teaching of eunuchs, most of whom bend the king's mind more toward their own profit than toward the public good. But among bees the king is formed by clear marks [?] of nature, so that he excels in size of body and in appearance, and then, what matters most in a king, in gentleness of character. For although he has a sting, he does not use it to punish. There are laws of nature, not written in letters but impressed on character, that those who hold the greatest power should be gentler in punishing. And the bees that have not obeyed the king's laws punish themselves with a penitent sentence, dying from the wound of their own sting. The Persian peoples are said to keep this custom even today: as the price of their offence they carry out on themselves the sentence of their own death. So no one, not the Persians, who have the harshest laws over their subjects, not the Indians, not the Sarmatian peoples, reveres a king with such devotion as the bees do. None of them dares to go out of their homes or to go forth to any pasture unless the king has gone out first and claimed the lead in flight.

Their procession goes through fragrant countryside, where gardens breathe with flowers, where a stream runs through the grass, where the riverbanks are pleasant. There is the play of lively youth, there is exercise in the open field, there is relief from cares. The work itself is sweet. From flowers and from sweet plants the first foundations of their camp are laid. For what else is a honeycomb but a kind of camp? Indeed the drone is kept away from these hives of bees. What square military camp can have as much skill and grace as the frames of the combs have, in which the small round cells support one another? What architect taught them to build hexagonal cells with all their sides exactly equal, to hang thin wax between the walls of their dwellings, to pack in honey, and to fill their granaries, woven of flowers, with a kind of nectar? You can see them all vying in their tasks. Some keep watch as they seek food, others keep anxious guard, others scout for coming rain and watch the clouds gathering, others shape wax from flowers, others gather with their mouths the dew that has settled on the flowers. Yet none of them lies in wait for the labours of others or seeks a living by robbery. If only they did not have to fear the ambushes of robbers! Still, they have their stings, and if they are provoked they pour out venom amid the honey, and in the heat of revenge they lay down their lives in the wound. So that moist dew is poured into the hollows within the camp, and little by little, over time, it thickens into honey, though at first it was liquid. Through its blending with the wax and the scent of the flowers it begins to give off the sweetness of honey.

Rightly does Scripture praise the bee as a good worker, saying: Go to the bee and see how she is a worker, and how worthy of honour is the work she carries on, whose labour kings and common people use for their health; for she is desired by all and renowned. Do you hear what the prophet says? He sends you, surely, to follow the example of that little bee and to imitate its work. You see how hard-working it is and how pleasing. Its fruit is desired and sought by all and makes no distinction between persons. With impartial grace it is equally sweet to kings and to common people alike. And it serves not only pleasure but health. It sweetens the throat and heals wounds, and it also brings medicine to internal ulcers. So, though the bee is weak in strength, it is strong in the vigour of wisdom and in the love of virtue.

Indeed, they defend their king with the utmost protection and think it noble to die for him. While the king is safe they do not know how to change their judgment or [?] their mind. When he is lost, they abandon their faithfulness [?] to their task and themselves plunder [?] the honey, because the one who held the leadership of the work has been killed.
So, while other birds scarcely produce a single brood in a year, bees produce two, and outweigh the others by their double fertility.

Let us now consider what is meant by the words: Let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls, and winged creatures flying above the earth according to their kind, and along the firmament of heaven. Why it said “above the earth” is clear: because they seek [?] their food from the earth. But how “along the firmament of heaven,” when eagles fly higher than other birds and yet even they do not fly along the firmament of heaven? The answer is this. What we call caelum in Latin is called ouranos in Greek, and ouranos is [?] named from horasthai, that is, from seeing, because the air is transparent and clearer for seeing. So Scripture spoke of the kinds of living creatures that fly in the air. Nor should anyone be troubled that it says “along the firmament of heaven.” It did not use “firmament” here in the strict sense but loosely, because compared with that ethereal body even this air of ours, which our eyes can perceive, is thick, as it were, and denser, and so takes the place of a firmament.

Now we have said what winged creatures there are and what nature or grace they have, and these only a few out of many, for there is no time to describe them all, since they are alike and of the same [?]. Still, let us consider how the birds themselves differ from one another. We find that the crow's feet are separated and divided into what are like distinct fingers, that nature has formed the feet of the raven and of chickens in yet another way, and that the feet of birds that eat flesh are curved and [?], as if ready for prey. But those more graceful birds that have the use and habit of swimming have broad feet, with their toes joined and linked by a kind of membrane. Here the admirable plan of nature lies open to view. The former are equipped with a fitting use for flying or seizing food, and the latter have suitable aids for swimming, so that they can float better on the waters and, as with oars, master the flowing waters with their feet broadened by the spread of that membrane.

It is also obvious why the swan has a longer neck. Since it is somewhat sluggish of body and cannot easily reach into the depths of the waters, it stretches out its neck for prey. The neck goes ahead, as it were, of the rest of the body, seizes the food it has found, and draws it up from the depths. Add to this that a melody is shaped more sweetly and tunefully through a long neck, and after longer practice it rings out far purer.

How sweet, too, is the song from the tiny throat of the cicadas, whose singing makes the groves burst in midsummer! They are more tuneful in the midday heat, because the purer the air they draw in with their breath at that hour, the clearer their songs ring out. Nor do the bees themselves sing anything unpleasant. There is a pleasing sweetness in that hoarse murmur of their voice, which we seem first to have imitated, more slowly, in the broken blare of trumpets; nothing is thought better suited than that noise to rouse spirits to vigour. And this grace remains to them, since most of them are said to have no lungs and no function or use of breathing, but to feed on a breath of air. In fact, if someone pours oil over them, they die quickly, because their pores are blocked and they cannot draw in that breath of air. And if someone pours vinegar over them at once, they immediately [?] revive, because the force of vinegar is said to open quickly the pores that the congealed oil has blocked.

And since we are speaking of winged creatures, we do not think it out of place to include what history relates, or those who have been able to see it report, about the Indian worm. This horned worm is said first to be turned into the likeness of a stalk and changed into the same nature, and then, by a further progression, to become a bombylius. Yet it does not keep that form and shape either, but seems to take on wings with loose and broader leaves. From these leaves the Seres comb those soft fleeces which the rich have claimed for their own use. So the Lord also says: What did you go out into the desert to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Look, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings. The chameleon too is said to feign different appearances with its changing colour. Certainly there is no doubt that hares turn white in winter and return to their own colour in summer, as we have easily learned close at hand.

I have touched on these things so that these examples too may stir us to faith in the change that is to come in the resurrection. But we must speak of that change in the way the apostle clearly expressed it, when he said: We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed.
