And further on he says: And the dead will rise incorrupt, and we shall be changed [?]. For this corruptible body must put on incorruption [?], and this mortal body must put on immortality. For many have interpreted a kind of change and forms that they had not received, and they have by no means escaped the unfitting usurpation of undue presumption.

The phoenix, too, is said to live in the regions of Arabia and to reach the great age of five hundred years. When it notices that the end of its life is near, it makes itself a casket of frankincense, myrrh and other spices. When its lifetime is complete it enters the casket and dies. From the moisture of its flesh a worm rises up and gradually grows, and in the course of the appointed time it puts on the oars of wings and is restored to the appearance and form of the bird it was before. So let this bird teach us, by its own example at least, to believe in the resurrection. Without any example, and without any grasp of reason, it renews for itself the signs of resurrection. And certainly birds exist for the sake of man, not man for the sake of birds. Let it be an example to us, then, that the author and creator of birds does not allow his saints to perish for ever, since he did not allow even a single bird to perish, but willed that it rise again and be propagated from its own seed. Who, then, announces to this bird the day of its death, so that it makes itself a casket, fills it with sweet scents, enters it and dies there, where the stench of death can be wiped out by pleasing fragrances?

You too, O man, make yourself a casket: strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new. Your casket, your sheath, is Christ, who protects you and hides you in the evil day. Do you want to know that the casket is one of protection? Scripture says: “In my quiver I have protected him.” Your casket, then, is faith. Fill it with the sweet scents of your virtues, that is, of chastity, mercy and justice, and enter wholly into the inner sanctuary of faith, fragrant with the sweet odour of excellent deeds. May the end of this life find you clothed in that faith, so that your bones may grow fat and be like a well-watered garden, whose green shoots spring up quickly. Know, then, the day of your death, as Paul also knew it. He said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. There is laid up for me the crown of righteousness.” So he entered his casket like a good phoenix, and he filled it with the good odour of martyrdom.

I will question you, and you answer me: how is it that vultures customarily announce the death of men by certain signs? By what indication have they been taught and instructed so that, when hostile armies draw up against each other for a lamentable war, these birds follow in a great flock, and so signify that a multitude of men will fall in battle and become the vultures' prey? They seem to gather this by some kind of reasoning from the look of the human battle array.

Divine grace has reached even the locust. When locusts in a dense swarm have covered the whole breadth of some region, at first they rest in a harmless lodging and do not devour the crops in an inhospitable raid, unless they have received the signal of a divine command. For, as we read in Exodus, the locust too carries out the punishment for an offence against heaven, as the servant of a righteous vengeance.

The locust, in turn, is devoured by the seleucis bird (for that is what this bird is called in Greek), which has been given as a remedy against the harm the locust usually brings. The creator gave it an insatiable nature for devouring, so that by its unending feeding it can put an end to the plague I spoke of above.

But what is this? While we draw out our sermon, look, the night birds are already flying around you, and by the very fact that they warn us to end the sermon, they also prompt us to take them up and speak of them. The various birds that evening drives to make way for night are returning to their roosts. They hide themselves in their shelters, escorting the setting of the day with a tuneful song, so that the day does not go away without its share of the thanks with which all creation praises its creator.

The night too has its songs, with which it is used to soothe the wakefulness of men, and the owl has its own songs as well. And what shall I say of the nightingale? A watchful guardian, while she warms her eggs in the hollow and lap of her body, she consoles the sleepless toil of the long night with the sweetness of her song. It seems to me that her highest aim is to bring the eggs she is warming to life no less by her sweet melodies than by the warmth of her body. Imitating her, a poor but chaste woman, pulling the chiselled millstone with her arm so that her little children may not lack bread for food, soothes the sorrowful feeling of poverty with a song in the night. Although she cannot imitate the nightingale's sweetness, she imitates her in the diligence of her devotion.

Consider the owl itself. With the large, grey-blue pupils of its eyes it does not feel the dread of the murky darkness of night, and the darker the night, the more freely it flies without striking anything, contrary to the habit of all other birds. But when day has dawned and the brightness of the sun is spread all around, its sight is dulled, and it wanders as if in some darkness. By this sign it shows that there are some who, though they have eyes to see, do not usually see, and use their sight only in darkness. I am speaking of the eyes of the heart, which the wise men of this world have and yet do not see. In the light they discern nothing; they walk in darkness, while they probe the dark things of demons and believe they see the heights of heaven, tracing the world with a measuring rod and calculating the dimensions of the very air. But, having strayed from the faith, they are entangled in the darkness of perpetual blindness. They have the day of Christ and the light of the Church close at hand and see nothing. They open their mouths as if they knew everything: sharp for vain things, dull for eternal ones, and through the winding course of long disputation betraying the blindness of their own knowledge. And so, while they long to flutter about in subtle arguments, like owls in the light they have vanished.

The bat, a lowly creature, takes its name from vesper, the evening. It is [?] and at the same time a four-footed animal, and it has teeth, which you do not usually find in other birds. Like four-footed animals, it gives birth not to eggs but to living young. It flits through the air in the manner of birds, but it usually spreads itself abroad in the evening twilight. It flies, however, not borne up by oars of feathers but by those of its membrane, held up by which it is carried round and sustained as though flying on feathers. This lowly creature also has this trait: they cling to one another and hang from some spot in the shape of a cluster of grapes, and if the last one lets go, they all come loose. This comes from a kind of gift of love, which is hard to find among the people of this world.

There is also the cock's crowing, pleasant in the night, and not only pleasant but also useful. Like a good housemate, it wakes the sleeper, warns the anxious and comforts the traveller, announcing the progress of the night with its tuneful signal. When it crows, the robber abandons his ambush; roused by it, the morning star itself rises and lights up the sky. When it crows, the fearful sailor lays aside his sadness, and every storm and squall stirred up by the frequent evening winds grows calm. When it crows, the devout soul leaps up to pray and takes up again the duty of reading. Finally, when it crowed, the very rock of the Church washed away his fault, which he had incurred by denying before the cock crowed. At its song hope returns to all, the sick man's trouble is relieved, the pain of wounds is lessened, the burning of fevers is soothed, faith returns to the fallen, Jesus looks upon those who waver and sets right those who stray. Indeed, he looked at Peter, and at once his error left him, his denial was driven out, and confession followed. Scripture teaches that this did not happen by chance but by the Lord's decree. For it is written that Jesus said to Simon: “The cock will not crow before you deny me three times.” Peter, so brave by day, is troubled at night; before the cock crows he falls, and falls a third time, so that you may know that he slipped not through a thoughtless outpouring of words, but because his mind too was shaken and troubled. Yet after the cock crowed the same man becomes stronger, and [?] worthy for Christ to look upon, for “the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous.” He recognized that the remedy had come, after which he could no longer go astray, and, changed from error to virtue, he wept most bitterly, to wash away his error with his tears.

Look on us too, Lord Jesus, so that we too may recognize our own errors, wash away our guilt with devout tears, and be found worthy of the forgiveness of sins. That is why I deliberately [?] my sermon, so that the cock might crow for us as well and come to our aid as we speak, so that if any fault had crept into my words, you, O Christ, might forgive the guilt. Give me, I pray, the tears of Peter; I do not want the joy of the sinner. The Hebrews wept, and they were set free through the sea as the waves parted. Pharaoh rejoiced that he held the Hebrews hemmed in, and he perished, drowned in the sea with his people. Judas too exulted in the reward for his betrayal, but he strangled himself with the noose bought with that very reward. Peter wept for his error and was found worthy to blot out the errors of others.

But now it is time for us to finish and close the sermon. It is a time when it is better to be silent or [?]; it is a time when [?] forgiveness is celebrated. Let that mystical cock crow for us too in the sacred rites, since Peter's cock has crowed in our sermon. Let Peter, who wept well for himself, weep for us, and turn the gracious face of Christ towards us. Let the passion of the Lord Jesus draw near, which daily pardons our sins and accomplishes the gift of forgiveness.

The good Lord does not want to send people away hungry, lest anyone faint on the way. He says: “I have compassion on this crowd, because they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat, and I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” Mary, intent on his word, refused the preparation of a meal. If he speaks so, how much more ought we to consider that not many live by the word of God, and that the body therefore longs for refreshment. Certainly this following day of ours is more laborious than those three days.

And so we, who have played with the birds and sung with the cock, should now sing the mysteries of the Lord. Let the eagles gather to the body of Jesus, renewed by the washing away of sins. For now that great sea monster has given back to us the true Jonah. Let us give thanks that evening has come for us, and let morning come, the sixth day.
THE SIXTH DAY

This is the sixth day, on which the origin of the world's creation is brought to its close, and so the end of our discourse also draws near, a discourse we undertook with some difficulty, since it concerns the beginnings of things. Although it has already carried us through five days with no small labour, today it grows with a heavier interest of cares, because on this day lies the risk of all the earlier days and the sum of the whole contest. For in contests of the lyre or of song, and in the bouts of athletes, frequent and great as the games may be, the earlier days pass without any loss of the crown; but the last day holds the crown's lot: on it lie the risk of the decision, the disgrace of giving way, and the prize of victory. How much more, then, in this great contest of wisdom, so great, held not before a few but before all [?], on which we now dwell: since today something like the crown of the contest comes before us, a greater anxiety presses on us, lest we both pour away the labour of the earlier days and incur shame for the present one. For the conditions of speaking are not the same as those of singing and wrestling: in those a failure is a matter of sport, but in this a slip is death. There, if you make a mistake, the spectators are put off, and the loss is only the coldness of the audience.

Stand by me, then, as judges, like a ring of spectators, and enter with me into this great and wonderful theater of the whole visible creation. Suppose someone who knows a city well [?] leads newly arrived guests around its whole circuit and shows them all its finest works: he does them no small favor. How much more readily, then, should you accept being led around your homeland, as if by the hand of my words, in this fellowship of ours, while I show you the kinds and classes of each thing. My aim is to gather from them all how much richer a grace the Creator of all things has given to you than to everything else. This crown, then, is set before you; today I want to be crowned by your verdict. We do not ask for the withering garlands of athletes but for the fresh judgment of your holiness, by which you may decide this: that divine providence does indeed reach through every creature, and you share with the rest the frailty of the body, yet you surpass the rest by the virtue of the soul, which alone has nothing in common with them.

Come, then, let us speak of the natures of the beasts and of the making of man. For I have been hearing for some time now that some people are whispering: "How long are we to learn about other things and remain ignorant of our own? How long are we to be taught about the other living creatures while we do not know ourselves? Let him say something that will profit me, so that I may know myself." The complaint is fair. But we must keep the order which [?] has laid out, and besides, we cannot know ourselves more fully unless we first know the nature of all living things.

"Let the earth bring forth," it says, "the living creature according to its kind: four-footed animals and serpents and beasts of the earth and cattle according to their kind, and all creeping things according to their kind. And God made the beasts of the earth and all cattle according to their kind and all the creeping things of the earth according to their kind. And God saw that they were good, and God said: Let us make man." I am aware that at this point some have taken the kinds of beasts, cattle and creeping things of the earth as references to the savagery of crimes, the folly of sins and the wickedness of thoughts. I, however, take them as the plain natures of each kind.

Nor am I afraid that anyone will think me like the presumptuous poor host who, in a spirit of kindness, invites a great many people and then sets before them nothing but cheap, ordinary food, so that the meager furnishings of his poor table earn him more blame from his fastidious guests than thanks for his hospitality. After all, Elisha's friends did not reject him as a bad host when he served them wild herbs. Like empty tales is that elaborate, carefully prepared, sumptuous banquet where something that looks like a pheasant or a turtledove is served and a chicken is eaten inside it, or a chicken is brought in stuffed with oysters or mussels, or a cup is drunk which changes, with its varied color and smell, into foreign flavors. Things of the sea are mixed with things of the land, things of the land with things of the sea. This is to find fault with [?] the Creator, who gave us all things for food, because he did not mix them himself. Such dishes seem sweet at first and afterward turn bitter, for the more lavish the luxury, the more ruinous the excess. Elisha, however, served bitter things, but afterward they became sweet. Those who at first thought there was death in that food afterward found in it the grace of sweetness and of life.

Nor, again, am I afraid that I may seem to have invited more people than I can feed, and that the loaves of my words will run short for you. Elisha, whom we rightly cannot equal but should imitate in faith, did not consider how many loaves he had. He chose to share what he had with everyone and judged that it would be enough for all. So he ordered his servant to distribute ten barley loaves among the people. And the servant said, "What, shall I set this before a hundred men?" And he answered, "Give, and let them eat, for thus says the Lord: They shall eat and have some left over." Your faith, then, will make the banquet of a poor tongue abound. Nor am I afraid that fasting will make you so hungry that you go home empty and still famished instead of filled, for it is written: "The Lord upholds the righteous, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied." It is far finer not to be ashamed of barley loaves and to serve what you have than to refuse. Elisha, who kept nothing for himself, had plenty for the multitudes. So Elisha was not ashamed to serve barley loaves, yet we are ashamed to understand simply [?] the things that are declared in simple and proper words. We read "heaven"; let us take it as heaven. We read "earth"; let us understand the fruitful earth.

Why should I ask what the measure of its circumference is, which the geometers have reckoned at one hundred and eighty thousand stadia? I gladly admit that I do not know what I do not know, or rather that I know that knowing it would do no good. It is better to know the kinds of lands than their extent. How could we take in that extent, with the sea poured around it, barbarian regions lying in between, and ground waterlogged and made impassable by marshes? Scripture shows that this is impossible for human beings, since God says: "Who has measured the water in his hand and the heaven with his span, and the whole earth with a closed hand? Who has set the mountains on a scale and the rocks in a balance and the forests on a yoke?" And further on: "He who holds the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like locusts; who has set up the heaven like a vault." Who, then, dares to claim knowledge equal to God's, presuming that he can come to know what God has marked out, by his own oracle, as belonging to his majesty?

Moses was certainly learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. But because he received the Spirit of God, he, as God's minister, ranked that empty, usurping teaching of philosophy below the reason of truth, and he described for me the things he judged suited to our hope: that God made the earth, and that, at the command of almighty God and through the working of the Lord Jesus, the earth brought forth plants from the ground and every living creature according to its kind. He did not think he needed to say how much of the expanse of the air the earth's shadow takes up when the sun withdraws from us and takes the day away to light the lower part of the axis, or how the globe of the moon, passing into this region of the world, causes eclipses. He passed over things that matter nothing to us as things that would profit us nothing. For he saw in the Holy Spirit that we should not pursue the vanities of a wisdom already withering, which fill our minds with insoluble questions and waste our effort, but should rather set down what bears on progress in virtue.

Let us hold fast, then, to the words of the prophet, and not despise the utterances of the Holy Spirit as though they were cheap. "Let the earth bring forth," it says, "the living creature of cattle and beasts and creeping things." Why do we argue about other things when the nature of the earthly creatures is plainly being formed here? The word of God runs through every creature in the depths of the world, so that suddenly from [?] all the kinds of living things that God appointed are brought forth, and by a law laid down for the future they all follow one another according to their kind and likeness: the lion begets a lion, the tiger a tiger, the ox an ox, the swan a swan, the eagle an eagle. A command given once has become ingrained in nature forever, and so the earth never ceases to render the service of its ministry, so that the species of the original order are renewed by succession [?] into new generations.

But do you want to turn the things that were brought forth to human use? Do not deny each kind the truth of its own nature, and you will fit them all the better to human benefit. First of all, nature laid [?] all kinds of cattle, beasts and fish face down, so that some crawl on their bellies, while those held up on feet seem, by the four-footed gait of their bodies, to be bent downward and as if fastened to the earth rather than free. Since they have no power to raise themselves, they look for their food from the ground and follow only the pleasures of the belly, toward which they are bent. Beware, O man, of being bowed down like the cattle; beware of bending toward the belly, not so much with your body as with your desire. Look at the shape of your body and take on a bearing that fits its lofty vigor. Let only the animals feed face down. Why do you bow [?] yourself down in eating, you whom nature did not lay prone? Why do you take delight in what is an outrage against nature? Why do you graze on earthly things night and day, intent on food like the cattle? Why do you dishonor yourself by giving yourself up to bodily enticements, while you serve the belly and its passions? Why do you rob yourself of the understanding your Creator gave you? Why do you compare yourself to beasts of burden, from which God wished to set you apart when he said, "Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding"? Or if the horse's unrestrained greed delights you, and it gives you pleasure to neigh after women, then let it please you to have your jaws bound with [?] and halter. If cruelty feeds you, that is the madness of wild beasts, which are slaughtered for their savagery: see that the monstrousness of your cruelty is not turned against you as well.

The donkey is sluggish, an easy prey and slow of sense. What does it teach us, except that we ought to be livelier, not grow sluggish through idleness of body and mind, and take refuge in faith, which is accustomed to lighten heavy burdens?

The crafty fox, which buries itself in dens and hiding places, is surely a sign of an unprofitable animal: hateful because it plunders, despised because it is weak, and therefore careless of its own safety while it lies in wait for others.

[?] has shaped the partridge, which steals the eggs of another, that is, of another partridge, and warms them with its own body, but cannot enjoy the fruit of its fraud. When it has hatched the chicks, it loses them, because as soon as they hear the voice of the one that laid the eggs, they leave the thief and go, by a kind of natural gift and love, to the one they recognize from the laying of the eggs as their true mother, showing that the one has only performed the office of a nurse and the other that of a parent. So she pours out her labors in vain and is punished by the price of her fraud. This is why Jeremiah says: "The partridge has cried out and gathered what she did not bring forth." That is, she gathered the eggs and cried out as if exulting in the success of her fraud, but she wastes her effort, because with all her labor she raises for another the young that she herself [?] warmed with long and careful brooding. The devil imitates her. He strives to snatch away the offspring of the eternal Creator, and if he manages to gather some who are foolish and lack the strength of their own sense, warming them with bodily enticements, then as soon as the voice of Christ has been poured into the little ones, they depart and go to the mother who embraces her young with a mother's love, like a bird. For the devil gathered the Gentiles, whom he had not created. But when [?] sent forth his voice in his Gospel, they betook themselves above all to him who received them under the shadow of his wings and gave them to their mother the Church to be nourished.

The lion, proud in the fierceness of its nature, will not mix with other kinds of wild beasts, but like a king it scorns the company of the many. It even disdains yesterday's food and turns away from the leftovers of its own meal. And what beast would dare to keep company with it, when its voice naturally carries such terror that many animals which could escape its attack by their speed are, at the sound of its roar, as if struck by some force [?] and give out?

As for the leopard, Scripture has not been silent either: it reveals the varied movements of its spirit by the variety of its color. For Jeremiah says: "If the Ethiopian will change his skin and the leopard his spots [?]." This is understood not only of its appearance but also of the changeableness of its rage: because of the dark, restless and shifting changes of a faithless mind and spirit [?], the Jewish people can no longer hold to the grace of a good purpose or return to any amendment or correction, once they have put on the savagery of a wild beast.

Yet there is something in the nature of four-footed creatures too which the word of the prophet urges us to imitate, so that by its example we may guard against idleness and not be turned aside from the pursuit of virtue by smallness or weakness of body, nor be called back from the greatness of that purpose. The ant is small, yet it dares things beyond its strength. It is not forced to work as a slave, but of its own accord and foresight it lays up for itself provisions of food for the future. Scripture urges you to imitate its industry, saying: "Go to the ant, O sluggard, and imitate its ways, and be wiser than it." For it owns no farmland; it has no one to compel it and works under no master, yet how it prepares its food, storing up for itself a harvest from your labors! And while you are often in need, it lacks nothing. For it no granaries are locked, no guards are impassable, no heaps inviolable. The watchman looks on and does not dare prevent the theft; the owner sees his loss and does not avenge it. The plunder is carried across the fields in a black column; the paths seethe with the company of travelers, and large grains that cannot be gripped in their narrow mouths are shoved along on their shoulders. The master of the harvest watches this and is ashamed to deny such dutiful industry its frugal gains.

And what shall I say of dogs, in whom it is implanted by a kind of nature to show gratitude and to keep anxious watch for the safety of their masters? This is why Scripture cries out to those who forget kindness, to the idle and the cowardly: "Dumb dogs, who do not know how to bark [?]." They are dogs, then, who know how to bark for their masters and how to defend their homes. So you too should learn to use your voice for Christ when savage wolves attack Christ's sheepfold. Learn to keep the word in your mouth, so that you may not seem, like a dumb dog, to have abandoned the guardianship of the faith entrusted to you by a kind of treacherous silence. Such a dog is the travel companion of an angel. In the prophetic book, Raphael thought it not without reason to take one along with himself and the son of Tobit when he set out to drive away Asmodeus and confirm the marriage; for by [?] mindful gratitude the demon is driven out and the marriage made firm. So by the example of a dumb beast the holy angel Raphael taught the young Tobias, whom he had taken into his protection, the disposition to return a kindness. For who would not be ashamed not to repay those who have done him good, when he sees that even beasts shun the crime of ingratitude? They keep the memory of the food they were given; do you not keep the memory of the salvation you received?

The she-bear lies in wait, as Scripture says, for it is a beast full of cunning. Yet it is said to bear its young shapeless from the womb, and then to mold its cubs with its tongue and form them into its own shape and likeness. Do you not marvel at such a devoted service of the mouth in a wild beast, whose devotion gives shape to nature? The bear, then, molds her young into her own likeness; can you not train your children to be like you?

What of the fact that it has not neglected the skill of healing either? When it has been badly hurt and covered with wounds, it knows how to heal itself by applying its sores to an herb whose name is [?], as the Greeks call it, so that they are cured by its mere touch. The serpent too drives off the blindness it has contracted by feeding on fennel. So when it feels its eyes clouding over, it seeks the remedy it knows and is not cheated of its effect. The tortoise, when it has fed on a serpent's entrails and notices the poison creeping through it, applies marjoram as the medicine of its health. Though it lives sunk in marshy wallows, it still knows how to cure itself with its own antidote, and by this sure aid to health it proves that it too knows the powers of herbs. You may also see the fox healing itself with pine resin and by such a remedy putting off the approach of death.

The Lord himself cries out in the book of Jeremiah: "The turtledove and the swallow and the sparrows of the field have kept the times of their coming, but my people has not known the judgments of the Lord." The swallow knows when to come and also when to return; the faithful bird also knows how to announce the sign of spring by the witness of its arrival. The ant too knows how to watch for times of fair weather. When it notices that its stores are damp and soaked with rain, it studies the sky carefully for when the mild weather will hold steady, then opens up its heaps and carries the grain out of its holes on its shoulders, so that its own corn may be dried by constant sun. Indeed, on all those days you will never [?] see rain burst from the clouds until [?] it has brought its [?] back into its hole. Oxen know to keep to their stalls when rain threatens. And when they have sensed by natural instinct a change in the weather, they look outside and all stretch their necks beyond the stalls in the same way, showing that they want to go out. At the approach of winter the sheep seizes grass insatiably, never filled with food, because it foresees that the grass will fail in the harshness of winter, and so it stuffs itself with grass for fodder before the burning frost destroys it all. The land hedgehog, commonly called the urchin, if it senses any danger, shuts itself up in its spines and gathers itself within its armor, so that whoever thinks to touch it is wounded. This same hedgehog, foreseeing the future, provides itself with two breathing holes: when it [?] that the north wind is going to blow, it blocks the northern one, and when it learns that the clouds of the air are being swept away by the south wind, it moves to the northern one, so as to avoid winds that blow against it and would harm it head-on.

Hence the prophet offered the Lord worthy praise, saying: "How great are your works, O Lord! In wisdom you have made them all." Divine wisdom penetrates all things and fills all things, and this is gathered more richly from the instincts of irrational creatures than from the reasoning of rational ones, for the testimony of nature is stronger than the argument of learning. What animal does not know how to protect its own safety: by resisting, if it has strength; by fleeing, if it has speed; by taking precautions, if it has cunning? Who taught them the use of healing and gave them knowledge of herbs? We are human beings, and we are often deceived by the look of herbs, and often find harmful those we thought wholesome. How often has deadly food crept in among sweet dishes, and poisoned fare reached the vitals of kings even past the watch of court servants! Wild beasts know by smell alone what is harmful and what is beneficial; with no one going before, no one tasting first, they crop the herb and it does them no harm. For nature is a better teacher of truth. Without anyone's instruction she pours the sweetness of health into our senses, and she also teaches us that the bitterness of pain is to be avoided. Thus life is sweeter, and death more bitter. It is nature that commends the cubs to the lioness and softens a savage beast with a mother's love. It is nature that checks the ferocity of the tigress and turns her back from the prey she is about to seize. For when she finds her lair empty and her cubs carried off, she at once follows the robber's tracks. He, though mounted on a swift horse, sees that he can be overtaken by the beast's speed and that no means of escape is left to him, so he contrives a trick of this kind. When he sees that she is about to reach him, he throws down a glass ball. She is then fooled by her own reflection and thinks it is her cub. She checks her charge, wanting to pick up her young. Then, having been held back by an empty image, she again pours all her strength into catching the horseman and, spurred on by rage, closes on him faster as he flees. Again he delays his pursuer by throwing down a ball, and yet the memory of the trick does not shut out the mother's devotion. She turns over the empty image and settles down as if to suckle her young. So, deceived by her own devotion, she loses both her revenge and her offspring. This Scripture sets before us when it says:

"Children, love your fathers; parents, do not provoke your children to anger." Nature instills this in the beasts, that they love their own cubs and cherish their young. They know nothing of a stepmother's hatred; parents are not turned against their offspring by a change of partner, nor do they know how to prefer the children of a later union and neglect those of an earlier one. They know their own young; they know nothing of differences in affection, the kindling of hatreds or distinctions of resentment. The nature of wild beasts is [?] simple; it knows nothing of slanders against the truth. For the Lord has so balanced all things that to those to whom he gave less reason he granted more affection. What beast does not offer itself to death above all for its cubs? What beast, though hemmed in by countless troops of armed men, does not shield its young with its own body? Though a harvest of spears may rain down on her, she keeps her little ones safe from danger, fenced in by the wall [?] of her body. What does man say, who neglects the commandment and blots out nature? The son despises the father, the father disowns the son, and they think this is a right, when fruitfulness is condemned. Rather, the father condemns himself, since he makes void what he begot; and this is thought to be authority, when nature is punished with barrenness.

No one will doubt that the dog lacks reason. Yet if you consider how keen its senses are, you would think that by the shrewdness of its perception it takes on the power of reason. Few people in the world, even after spending their whole long lives in study, have managed to learn how to link the parts of a syllogism together. Yet a dog, one may well judge, can easily grasp this by its natural training. When it has found a hare's track by day and comes to a turning in the path, a kind of crossroads that splits into several ways, it goes to the start of each path in turn and silently works the matter out for itself, as though it were uttering [?] a statement by its skill in gathering the scent. "Either it turned off this way," it says, "or that way, or else it took itself into this bend. But it did not go into this path or into that one. It remains, then, that it has certainly gone this way." What men can hardly put together after long study of a constructed art, dogs have by nature: first they detect what is false, and then, having rejected the falsehood, they find the truth. Do not philosophers spend whole days dividing propositions in the dust, drawing each one with a rod? Out of three, since one of them must be true, they first dispose of two as fitting with falsehood, and so they conclude that the force of truth lies in the one that is left. Who can be so tenacious in remembering a kindness and so mindful of a favour? For dogs know how to leap on robbers in defence of their master, to keep strangers from approaching at night, and they are ready to die for their masters and to die with their masters. Often, too, when a murder has been committed, dogs have furnished evidence to convict the guilty, so that their mute testimony has frequently been believed.

They say that at Antioch, in an out-of-the-way part of the city, a man who had a dog with him was killed at dusk. A certain soldier, eager for plunder, had committed the murder. Under cover of the day's still dark beginning, he had withdrawn to another part of the city. The corpse lay unburied, a large crowd of onlookers stood around it, and the dog with tearful whining mourned its master's misfortune. As it happened, the man who had done the killing, with the cunning typical of human nature, came up to that ring of people looking on and approached the body as though in pity. By boldly mingling among them he hoped to win credit for his innocence. Then the dog left off its cry of grief for a moment and took up the arms of vengeance. It seized the man and held him fast, and, murmuring a pitiful song like a kind of closing speech, it moved everyone to tears. It made its proof believable, because out of so many it seized him alone and would not let him go. The man was thrown into confusion, because he could not discredit so plain an accuser by charging it with hatred, enmity, envy or some injury, and he could no longer deny the crime. So the dog achieved the harder thing: it secured vengeance, since it could not provide protection. What fitting return do we make to our Creator, whose food we eat? We overlook the wrongs done to him, and often we serve up to God's enemies the very feasts we receive from God!

What is more innocent than lambs, which we compare to the tender infancy of little children? Often in a great flock a little lamb wanders through all the folds and strays from its mother. When it cannot find her, it calls the absent one with repeated bleating, to draw out her answering voice, so that it may retrace its wandering steps toward the sound. Though it moves among many thousands of sheep, it recognizes its mother's voice, hurries to her, and seeks the springs of its mother's milk that it knows. However much it is gripped by the desire for food and drink, it runs past other udders, heavy and brimming with milk; it seeks its mother alone, and shows that for it only its mother's udder, though its supply is scanty, overflows. She too, among many thousands of lambs, knows only her own young. Many bleat as one, all look the same; yet she distinguishes her offspring from the rest and recognizes her own child alone by the silent witness of a mother's love. The shepherd makes mistakes in telling sheep apart; the lamb does not make mistakes in recognizing its mother. The shepherd is deceived by appearance, but the ewe is not deceived in her love. All have one smell, yet nature has its own scent, which the dear offspring seems to give off with a certain particular quality.

Nature has its own practices and its own native instincts. A little child's teeth have scarcely begun to break through, and already it knows how to try out its weapons. A puppy has no teeth yet, and still, as if it had them, it tries to take revenge with its mouth. A fawn has no antlers yet, and still it practises with its forehead, threatening with weapons it has not yet tried. If a wolf sees a man first, it takes away his voice and looks down on him as the victor who has robbed him of speech; but if it senses that it has been seen first, it lays aside its ferocity and cannot run. The lion fears the cock, especially a white one. A wounded goat seeks out dittany and drives the arrows out of its wound. The beasts too know their own remedies. A sick lion looks for a monkey to devour so that it may be healed. [?] drinks the blood of the wild roe and escapes the force of illness. Every sick wild beast is cured by drinking a dog's blood; a sick bear eats ants; a stag chews little olive twigs.

So wild beasts know how to seek what is good for them; and you, O man, do not know your own remedies. You do not know how to rob your adversary of his strength, so that, like a wolf seen first, he cannot escape you; how to detect his treachery with the eye of your mind, check the flow of his words first, and blunt his impudence and the sharpness of his arguing. But if he gets in first, he will take away your voice. And if you are struck dumb, loosen your garment so that you may loosen your speech; and if the wolf rises up against you, take up a rock, and he flees. Your rock is Christ. If you take refuge in Christ, the wolf flees and will not be able to frighten you. Peter sought this rock when he was faltering on the waves, and he found it, for he grasped the right hand of Christ.

What shall I say of the fact that men delight in garlic and take as food the very thing the leopard flees from? In fact, if anyone thinks fit to rub garlic somewhere, the leopard leaps away from the place and does not stay. Something whose smell a venomous wild beast cannot bear, you take as food and pour into your innermost parts! But it does sometimes serve as a medicine for pains. Then let it be taken as a medicine, not as food; let it be taken by the sick, not by those who are feasting. You look for medicine and run from fasting, as though you could find any greater remedy. If a serpent tastes the spittle of a fasting man, it dies. You see how great the power of fasting is: with his spittle a man kills an earthly serpent, and rightly also the spiritual one.

How much good sense the Lord has poured even into the smallest creatures! The turtledove covers its nest with squill leaves so that the wolf will not attack its young, for it knows that wolves are accustomed to shun such leaves. The little fox knows how to cherish its offspring; and do you not know, do you neglect to learn, how to keep the offspring of this life safer against the wolves of spiritual wickedness?

But let us return to the order of creation and consider why some animals have shorter [?] necks, such as lions and tigers, and bears too, and others longer ones, such as elephants and camels. Is not the reason plain, that wild beasts that feed on flesh had no need of a long neck? For they do not lower their necks and mouths to the ground to graze; rather they attack a stag, or seize [?] an ox or a sheep. But the camel, being taller, how could it graze on the tiniest plants unless it stretched a longer neck all the way to the ground for grazing? So the camel has been given a longer neck in proportion to its [?] build; so too the horse in proportion, and the ox likewise, for these feed on grass.

The elephant, moreover, also has a projecting trunk, because, being taller than all the others, it cannot bend down to graze. So it uses the trunk's service to gather its food. The trunk pours abundant drink into that enormous beast, and for this reason it is hollow, so that it can draw up whole pools to quench the thirst of so huge a creature and, having gathered up a river, can flood the drinker with it. Its neck is indeed [?] shorter than the bulk of so great a body would require, so that it too should not be more a burden than a use. For the same reason it does not bend its knees, because it needed stiffer legs, so that so vast a structure of limbs could be held up as if on columns. It bends its heel slightly; the rest of the foot is rigid from top to bottom. Nor can so great a beast lower itself as we often do onto our [?], and so it rightly cannot share with the other animals the ability to roll over or crouch. It is propped up on either side by very large beams, so that in sleep it may lean [?] a little without danger, since its foot is not divided by any joint. For tame elephants, then, props of this kind are provided by the ingenuity of those who make use of them. But for wild ones, since no one sets up such props to support them, danger results.

For they lean against a tree, either to rub their sides or to rest in sleep. Sometimes the tree gives way, bent by so great a body, and breaks, and the elephant that had leaned its weight on it falls and cannot raise or lift itself up. Lying there, it either dies, or, betrayed by its groaning, it is struck down, since its belly and the other softer parts nearby lie open to wounds; for weapons do not easily pierce its back or the rest of its outer parts. There are some who lay these traps for them for the sake of ivory. They weaken [?] the trees the elephants are used to lean against, on the other side where the animals make less use of them, so that the trees cannot bear the weight of its limbs and bring about its fall.

But if anyone finds fault with these things, let him also find fault with the height of [?] buildings, because they threaten a heavier fall the sooner and are more difficult to repair once collapsed. But if we often raise buildings high, either for beauty or as lookouts, we ought to approve these qualities in elephants too, for they are of great use in warfare. Hence the [?] of the Persians, fierce in war, strong with arrows and every kind of missile, because weapons are hurled downward from above with greater force. Their battle line advances as if surrounded by walking towers. In the middle of open plains they fight as though from a wall, and, stationed as if in a citadel or watchtower, they watch the battle rather than undergo it, and so, kept out of danger, they seem safe on the bulk of the beasts. For who would dare approach them, when from above he is easily pierced by javelins, and below he is trampled by the charge of the elephants? So battle lines give way before them, and wedges of armed men, and those square formations of standards. With unbearable force they rush upon the enemy, so that no column of fighters, no close-packed mass of soldiers, no wall of shields holds them back. Like moving mountains they wheel about in battle, tower like hills with lofty peaks, and with the crash of their trumpeting shatter everyone's confidence. What can a foot soldier do against them, however strong his arms and quick his hand, when a wall surrounded by throngs of armed men comes at him on the march? What can a horseman do, when his horse is terrified and flees from the hugeness of so great a beast? What can an archer do, when the iron-clad bodies of the men above cannot feel the blow of a dart, and the beast itself is not easily pierced by steel even when bare, and, protected by armour, cuts through the opposing lines without danger to itself and tramples the squadrons?

So, like huge buildings, elephants are held up by stronger foundations; otherwise, supported by feet unequal to their bulk, they would collapse within a short span of life. As it is, they prolong their life to three hundred [?] years, because all their limbs are suited to their size. That is why their joints are not divided as ours are, but compacted, so that they may be sturdier. How quickly people's knees and soles suffer if they stand for long, or run too fast, or walk without stopping! For what is jointed and articulated admits the sensation of pain or the occasion of injury more easily than what is solid and compact.

And why are you amazed that they are feared when clad in armour, since they are always armed with their tusks as with natural spears? Whatever they wrap their trunk around, they break; whatever they press beneath their foot, they crush to death as if by the fall of some enormous building. They wrap their trunks around groves to feed themselves and, like very tall serpents, lash whatever they catch in their snake-like coils. Usually they curl it into a ring, especially when food is gathered from the ground or water is drawn up. So they are proof to us that nothing has been created superfluous. And yet this beast of such great bulk is subject to us and serves at the command of humans.

Indeed, since we are about to speak of the creation of man, we ought to prepare the way and give a foretaste of his excellence. Nothing among creatures seemed sturdier than the elephant, nothing so fearsome or tall, nothing so wild as lions and tigers are. And these serve man and lay aside their nature through human training. They forget what they were born as and take on what they are told. In short, they are taught like little children, they serve like the weak, they are beaten like the fearful, they are corrected like subordinates; they pass over into our ways, since they have lost their own impulses.

Nature, then, is wonderful in the greatest things, for the Lord is wonderful on high; and it is wonderful in the smallest as well. For just as we marvel no less at level plains than at lofty mountains, nor [?] are we more amazed at the height of the cedar than at the low-growing fruitfulness of the vine or the olive, so I do not admire the elephant [?] more because it is tall than the mouse because it is fearsome to the elephant. This, then, is the power of nature: the same creatures are fearsome to some and fearful of others. For each creature has been given a certain advantage, so that it is supported by privileges of its own. The elephant, fearsome to bulls, fears the mouse. The lion, king of beasts, is driven wild by the tiny sting of a scorpion and is killed by a serpent's venom. The lion's beauty is outstanding: he shakes the brawn of his maned neck, or rears his chest and lifts his face. But who would not marvel that the death of huge bodies comes from a scorpion's sting so small that you would think it had no body at all?

Nor let anyone find fault with the Creator for mixing serpents and other venomous kinds of animals or plants in among his creatures. For these were made for our correction, not for our ruin. Things which usually cause offence and terror to the lazy, the weak or the wicked are useful to others, as tutors are to little children. Tutors seem harsh, severe and tiresome, frightening with the rod; they deny the freedom to run wild and require the necessity of discipline; they restrain childish spirits by fear, so that they do not slide into self-indulgence. And so, through their strictness, children turn out frugal, sober and self-controlled, more devoted to praise than to play. Do you see what good those fearful rods do? In the same way serpents are rods for those whose spirit is still at a weak age and whose mind has only a sort of childish strength; but they cannot harm the stronger. Indeed, to the one who trusts in the Lord it was said: "You will walk on the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon." A viper bit Paul, and people thought that, as a sinner barely saved from shipwreck, he would die of the venom. But after he remained unharmed, having shaken the viper off into the fire, he won greater reverence among those who watched. And the Lord himself said to all: "Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned." And he said that these would be the signs of those who believe: they would stroke serpents with their hand, and poisons and every deadly thing, even if they drank them, could not harm them. So, O man, it is your own unbelief that you should fear more than the venom of serpents. Fear those creatures, then, so that at least while you dread them they may stir you to faith. And if you do not fear God, at least dread the venom that punishes faithlessness.

Now, since you see that elephants are under you and lions are subject to you, know yourself [?], O man. This saying is not, as people claim, from Pythian Apollo, but from holy Solomon, who says: "Unless you know yourself, O fairest among women." Yet long before, Moses wrote in Deuteronomy: "Attend to yourself." O man, attend to yourself, says the Law; and the prophet says: "Unless you know yourself." To whom does he say this? "O fairest among women," he says. Who is beautiful among women, if not the soul, which in both sexes possesses the excellence of beauty? And rightly is she fair, for she desires not earthly but heavenly things, not perishable but imperishable things, in which beauty does not usually fade; whereas all bodily things wither with advancing age or the unevenness of illness. Attend to her, says Moses, the soul in which you wholly are, in which the better part of you lies. In fact the Lord explained who you are when he said: "Beware of false prophets"; for they weaken the soul and undermine the mind. You, then, are not flesh. For what is flesh without the soul to steer it and the mind to give it vigour? Flesh is taken up today and laid aside tomorrow. Flesh is temporary; the soul is lasting. The flesh is the soul's cloak, which the soul puts on as a kind of bodily garment. So you are not the garment, but the one who wears the garment. That is why it is said to you [?] that you should strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who is renewed not in bodily condition but in the spirit of the mind [?] and in knowledge. You, I say, are not flesh; for it is not said to the flesh: "For the temple of God is holy, which you are," and elsewhere: "You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit of God dwells in you." Rather, it is said to those who are renewed and faithful, in whom the Spirit of God remains. But in the carnal he does not remain, for it is written: "My Spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh."

But let us consider the order of our own creation. "Let us make man," he says, "in our image and likeness." Who says this? Is it not God, who made you? What is God? Flesh or spirit? Not flesh, certainly, but spirit, whom flesh cannot resemble, because he is incorporeal and [?], whereas flesh is both grasped and seen. To whom does he say it? Not to himself, certainly, since he does not say "Let me make" [?] but "Let us make". Not to the angels, since they are ministers, and servants cannot share the work with their master, nor works with their maker. No, he says it to the Son, however much the Jews may not like it, however much the Arians may resist. But let the Jews fall silent, and the Arians with their forebears be [?] too; for while they exclude one person from sharing in the divine work, they bring in many, and the prerogative they deny the Son they bestow on lowly servants.

But suppose, as you think, that God needed the help of servants to do the work: if the work is shared between God and the angels, is the image also shared between God and the angels? Would he say to angels, "Let us make man in our image and likeness"? But hear who the image of God is from the one who says: "He has rescued us from the power of darkness and brought us over into the kingdom of the Son of his glory, in whom we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation." He is the image of the Father, he who always is and was in the beginning. Indeed, he is the image who says: "Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father too. How can you, when you see the living image of the living Father, say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?" The image of God is power, not weakness; the image of God is wisdom; the image of God is righteousness. But wisdom is divine, and righteousness is everlasting. He alone is the image of God who said, "I and the Father are one," having such likeness to the Father that he has unity of divinity and of fullness with him. When he says "Let us make", how can there be inequality? When he goes on to say "in our likeness", where is unlikeness? So too in the Gospel: when he says "I and the Father", it is certainly not one person; but when he says "are one", there is no difference of divinity or of work. So in the two there is not one person, but one substance. And he did well to add "are", because always to be is divine, so that you may believe him to be coeternal whom you [?] to be unlike. For he is eternal of whom Moses says: "He who is has sent me." He also did well to put "I" first [?]. For if he had put the Father first, you would judge the Son to be lesser. But he put the Son first, whom it is not proper to believe greater than the Father, and then added the Father, so that you may notice that God the Father and his Son are not bound by any prejudice of order.

"Attend," it says, "to yourself alone." For we ourselves are one thing, what is ours is another, and the things around us are another again. We ourselves are the soul and the mind; what is ours is the body's limbs and its senses; around us are money, servants and the trappings of this life. Attend, then, to yourself; know yourself. That does not mean knowing what sort of arms you have, how much bodily strength, how many possessions or how much power. It means knowing what sort of soul and mind you have, from which all your counsels proceed and to which the fruit of your works returns. For the soul is full of wisdom, full of devotion and justice, since all virtue is from God. To it God says: "Behold, Jerusalem, I have painted your walls." That soul is painted by God which has within it the shining grace of the virtues and the splendour of devotion. That soul is well painted in which the likeness of God's work shines out; that soul is well painted in which there is the brightness of glory and the image of the Father's substance. Painted after this image, which shines out, the picture is precious. Adam was made after this image before sin, but when he fell, he laid aside the image of the heavenly and took on the likeness of the earthly. Let us flee this image, which cannot enter the city of God, for it is written: "Lord, in your city you will bring their image to nothing." An unworthy image does not enter, and any that has entered is driven out, for, it says, "nothing common shall enter it, nor anyone who works abomination and falsehood"; but he shall enter it on whose forehead the name of the Lamb [?] is written.

Our soul, then, is made in the image of God. In it you are wholly yourself, O man, since without it you are nothing; you are earth, and you will be dissolved into earth. And so, that you may know that the flesh without the soul is nothing, he says: "Do not fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul." Why then do you put your confidence in the flesh, when you lose nothing if you lose the flesh? Fear this instead: that you may be cheated of the help of your soul. For what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? In it lies not some small part of himself, but the substance of his whole human being. It is through the soul that you rule over the other living creatures, wild beasts and birds; the soul is in the image of God, while the body is in the form of the beasts. In the soul is the holy badge of likeness to God; in the body, a base fellowship with wild beasts and brutes.

But let us examine more carefully what it means to be in the image of God. Is the flesh in the image of God? Then there is earth in God, since the flesh is earth; then God is bodily; then he is weak like the flesh and subject to passions? Perhaps the head seems to you to be in God's likeness because it stands highest, or the eyes because they see, or the ears because they hear. If you look at height, do we seem tall beside buildings [?] because the crown of our head rises a little above the ground? Are we not ashamed, then, to be called like God on the grounds that we stand taller than snakes and other creeping things, or than fawns and sheep or wolves? And how much taller than us in that respect are camels and elephants! Sight is indeed a fine thing: it surveys the elements of the world and recognises what no one reports, but what your own gaze discovers. Yet how much is it that we actually see, that we should say on that account that we are in the likeness of God, who sees all things, watches all things, detects hidden feelings and searches the secrets of the heart? Are we not ashamed to say this, when I cannot even see the whole of myself? I see what is before my feet; what is behind me I cannot see. I do not know my own neck, I am unacquainted with the back of my head, I cannot see my own loins. Likewise, how much is it that we hear, when I can neither see nor hear what is a little distance away? If walls [?] stand in the way, sight is blocked and hearing is blocked. Then again, our body is stuck in one place and shut up in a narrow space. All wild beasts are larger than man, and all are swifter too.

So it cannot be the flesh that is in the image of God, but our soul, which is free and roams here and there with its far-ranging thoughts and counsels, and which surveys all things by reflection. See: we are now in Italy, and we think about matters that seem to concern the eastern or the western regions; we seem to converse with those settled in Persia, and we see those who live in Africa, if that land has received any whom we know. We follow those who travel, we cling to their charms, we are united with the absent, we speak with those far away; we even raise the dead to converse with us, embrace them and hold them as though alive, and render to them the duties and the uses of life. That, then, is in the image of God which is valued not by bodily [vigour] but by the vigour of the mind: which sees those who are absent, travels with its sight across the seas, runs over them with its gaze, searches out hidden things, and in a single moment carries its perceptions here and there, through the ends of the whole earth and the secret places of the world; which is joined to God, cleaves to Christ, descends into the underworld and ascends again, and moves freely in heaven. Hear, in short, the one who says: "But our citizenship is in heaven." Is that not, then, in the image of God in which God always dwells? But hear that it is in the image of God. For the Apostle says: "And so all of us, beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord."

Since, then, we have learned that the soul is in the image of God, let us now consider whether the privilege of "Let us make man" could have been said [?] of the soul. Hear this too: the soul is called by the name of man. For it is written in Genesis: "And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were nine souls. All the souls, then, who entered Egypt with Jacob were seventy-five." And it is far more fitting for the soul to be called homo [?] in Latin or ἄνθρωπος in Greek, the one taking its name from humanity, the other from the liveliness of looking, which no doubt belongs to the soul more than to the body. With this the saying in the Lamentations of Jeremiah also rightly agrees: "The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul that seeks him." He was speaking of human beings, yet he thought the soul should be added; for the soul seeks better when it is alone, withdrawing itself from the mire of the body and from fleshly desire. It is the soul that, being in the image of God, is conformed to the Lord Jesus; for the saints are conformed to the Son of God. So we read in the words of Paul: "We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those [?] who are called saints according to his purpose, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified." Tell me, please: does justification seem to you to be conferred according to the body or according to the soul? But you cannot be in doubt, since justice, from which justification [?] comes, belongs surely to the mind and not to the body.

You have been painted, then, O man, painted by the Lord your God. You have a good craftsman and painter. Do not erase a good picture, one that shines not with cosmetics but with truth, one drawn not in wax but in grace. You erase the picture, woman, if you smear your face with material [?] whitening, if you flush it with artificial red. That is a picture of vice, not of beauty; a picture of deceit, not of simplicity. That picture is temporary: it is wiped away by rain or by sweat. That picture misleads and deceives, so that you neither please the one you wish to please, for he understands that what pleases him is not yours but borrowed, and you displease your Maker, who sees that his work has been erased. Tell me: if you brought in another artist over some craftsman and he covered the first man's work with new work of his own, would not the one who learned that his work had been adulterated be grieved? Do not take away God's picture and put on the picture of a harlot, for it is written: "Shall I take the members of Christ and make them the members of a harlot? Far from it!" And if anyone adulterates the work of God, he commits a grave [?] offence. For it is a grave crime to think that a human being paints you better than God does. It is a grave thing for God to say of you: "I do not recognise my colours, I do not recognise my image, I do not recognise the face that I myself formed. I reject what is not mine. Go and look for the one who painted you; keep company with him; get your grace from the one you paid." What will you answer?

If it is a grave thing to adulterate the work of God, what shall we say of those who destroy [?] the work of God, who shed human blood, who wrest away the life that God has given, who say: "Let us do away with the just man, for he is of no use to us"? Fittingly, then, it was read today: "Foxes have holes and the birds of the air have nests where they may rest, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head." The fox hides itself in a hole, and the birds protect themselves in a nest; but a man is not hidden in a pit, he is trapped in one. The pit is a man's mouth; a deep pit is a man's heart, where harmful and deceitful counsels and evil thoughts lie. You walk along, and another is preparing a pit [?] for you. You walk in the midst of snares which your enemies have hidden for you on the road. Look carefully all around you, then, so that you may escape like a fawn from the nets and like a bird from the snare. The fawn avoids the nets by the keenness of its sight; the bird escapes snares if it betakes itself to higher places and flies above the things of earth. For no one sets nets in the heights, no one hides a snare there. So the one whose citizenship is above is not usually taken as prey. But why are you surprised that man is deceived by man, when the Son of Man had nowhere to rest? He had indeed made man such that he might lay his head in him. But after our hearts began to hold not a resting place for our neighbour but a pit, after each began to weave snares for the other whom he ought to help, Christ turned his head away from us; yet afterwards he chose to offer that head to death for us. Do not, then, be deceitful, cruel or harsh, so that Christ may lay his head in you.

Finally, when he had made the monsters of the fish, when he had made the kinds of wild animals and beasts, he did not rest; but he rested after he had made man in his own image. Hear in whom he rests: "Or upon whom shall I rest, but upon the one who is humble and quiet and trembles at my words?" Be humble and quiet, then, so that God may rest in your heart. He who did not rest among the beasts rests far less in a beastly heart. For there are beastly minds; there are wild beasts dressed in human form, of whom the Lord says: "Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves." In these God does not rest; he rests in human character, which God made in his own image and likeness when he made man, who ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God. To the soul of this man he says: "Behold, Jerusalem, I have painted your walls." He did not say, "I have painted your belly," he did not say, "I have painted your lower parts," but he says, "I have painted your walls," declaring that he has given man the protection of strong walls, so that if there is a watchful sentry on the walls he may ward off the danger of siege. So he says: "I have not given you pleasures, nor the allurements of desire, nor the incitements of luxury, nor a craving for another's beauty; but I have given you the foundations of walls, I have given you the lofty tops of towers, so that, stationed in them, you need not fear being stormed by the enemy nor dread the assaults of advancing legions, however terrible." Indeed, you have in Isaiah that the soul of the just man, or the Church, says: "I am a fortified city, I am a besieged city": fortified through Christ, besieged by the devil. But one whose helper is Christ need not fear a siege; for he is fortified by spiritual grace even while he is besieged by the dangers of the world. Hence you also have it said in the Song of Songs: "I am a wall, and my breasts are towers." The wall is the Church; her towers are the priests, in whom both teaching on natural things and instruction in morals abound.

Know yourself, then, beautiful soul, for you are the image of God. Know yourself, O man, for you are the glory of God. Hear how you are his glory. The prophet says: "Your knowledge has become wonderful through me"; that is, in my making your majesty is all the more wonderful, in the fashioning [?] of man your wisdom is proclaimed. When I look at myself, whom you discern even in my hidden thoughts and inward feelings, I recognise the mysteries of your knowledge. Know yourself, then, O man, how great you are, and attend to yourself, lest at some time you become entangled in the devil's snares and fall prey to the hunter, lest you run into the jaws of that foul lion who roars and prowls about seeking someone to devour. Attend to yourself, so that you consider what enters you and what comes out of you. I do not mean food, which is swallowed and evacuated; I mean thought, I am speaking of speech. Let no lust for another's bed enter you or creep into your mind; let your eye not snatch at the beauty of a woman passing by, nor your mind shut it in; let your speech not weave contrivances of temptation, nor betray anyone by guile, nor spatter your neighbour with abusive reproach. God has made you a hunter, not a conqueror, for he said: "Behold, I am sending many hunters" — hunters not of crime but of absolution, hunters not of guilt, surely, but of grace. You are Christ's fisherman, to whom it is said: "From now on you will be giving life to men." So cast your nets, so cast your eyes, so cast your words, that you crush no one but lift up the one who is foundering. "Attend," it says, "to yourself." Stand so that you do not fall; run so that you reach the prize; fight so that you often prevail, for the crown is owed to the lawful contest. You are a soldier: scout out the enemy carefully, so that he does not creep up on you by night. You are an athlete: keep closer to your opponent with your hands than with your face, so that he does not strike your eye. Let your gaze be free and your step nimble, so that you may throw him down as he rushes at you, seize him as he gives way, avoid a wound with a watchful eye, and drive him back with a strong attack. And if you are wounded, attend to yourself: run to the physician, seek the remedy of repentance. Attend to yourself, for you have flesh, which quickly slips. Let the divine word, the good physician of souls, come to you; let it sprinkle you with the oracles of the Lord as with healing medicines. Attend to yourself, lest a hidden wicked word arise in your heart; for it creeps like poison and spreads deadly infection. Attend to yourself, lest you forget God who made you, and lest you take his name in vain.

"Attend to yourself," says the Law, "lest, when you have eaten and are full, and have built houses and begun to live in them, and are filled with your flocks, and abound in gold and silver and in all things that you have in plenty, you exalt yourself in your heart and forget the Lord your God." For what do you have, O man, that you did not receive? Do not all these things pass away like a shadow? Is not this house of yours dust and ruin? Are not all these things false? Is not the treasure of this world vanity? Are you not yourself ashes? Look at the tombs of men and see what will remain of you but ashes and bones — of your body, that is. Look, I say, and tell me: which there is the rich man and which the poor? Tell apart the needy and the powerful. We are all born naked, and naked we die. There is no difference among the corpses of the dead, unless perhaps that the bodies of the rich, bloated with luxury, stink the more [?]. Whom have you heard of, a poor man, dying of indigestion? His want does him good: it exercises the body rather than burdening [?] it. Nor yet have we heard of [the just man?] forsaken, or his seed begging bread, since he who works well in his own land has food in plenty. Attend to yourself, then, rich man, for you too carry flesh, just as the poor man does.

Attend to yourself, poor man [?], [for] your soul is [precious?]. Though the flesh is mortal, the soul endures; though you lack money, you do not lack grace; though you have no spacious house and no far-reaching estate, the sky lies open to you and the earth is free. The elements have been given to all in common; the beauties of the world lie open equally to rich and poor. Are the gilded ceilings of the costliest houses more beautiful than the face of heaven adorned with shining stars? Are the estates of the rich wider than the expanses of the earth? Hence it was said to those who join house to house and farm to farm: "Will you alone dwell upon the earth?" You, poor man, have a greater house, in which you cry out and are heard. "O Israel," says the prophet, "how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of his possession! It is great and has no end, lofty and immeasurable." The house of God is common to rich and poor; yet it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. But perhaps you are sad that no light of gilded lamps shines for you: yet the moon shines for you with a far brighter light. Perhaps you complain about winter, because no heated rooms [?] are warmed with fires for you: but you have the heat of the sun, which tempers the whole world for you and protects you from the winter cold. Or do you think those happy who are surrounded by crowds of servants following them? But those who need other people's feet do not know how to use their own; in short, they are preceded by a few and carried by many. Unless perhaps what you admire is that they abound in gold, silver and money. You see how much they abound in; you do not see how much they lack. You think it a precious thing to recline on ivory couches, and you do not consider that the earth is more precious, which spreads beds of grass for the poor man, on which rest is sweet and sleep is pleasant — the sleep that the other, laid out on his golden couch, seeks all night long while lying awake, and does not find. Oh, how much happier than himself he, lying awake, [must think?] you as you rest! Besides this, there is something far more excellent: the just man who has been in want here will have plenty there [?], and whoever has toiled here will have consolation there, but whoever has received good things here cannot hope for their reward there. For poverty stores up its reward, while wealth uses it up.

Attend to yourself, then, poor man; attend, rich man, for there are temptations both in poverty and in riches. That is why the wise man says: "Give me neither riches nor poverty." And he explains why he asked this: it is enough for a man to have what suffices him; excessive [?] riches swell the mind with cares and anxieties just as feasts swell the belly. So he asks to be granted what is needful and sufficient, "lest," he says, "being filled, I become a liar and say, 'Who sees me?' or, being made poor, I steal and swear by the name of the Lord." The temptations of the world, then, are to be fled or [avoided?], so that the poor man does not despair and the wealthy man does not grow insolent. For it is written: "When you have driven out the nations and begun to enjoy their lands, do not say, 'My strength and [the might of my hand?]' [?]." Such is the one who ascribes his wealth to his own merit, and so, as though he were approved, does not recognise his own error, but draws out his sin as with a long rope. For if he believed that the increase of his money came either from chance events or from shameful cunning, there would be no room for insolence about things in which there is either no praise and only empty toil, or a shameless greed that knows not how to set a limit to its pleasure.

But now something must be said about the human body itself. Who would deny that it surpasses all others in comeliness and grace? For although all earthly bodies seem to be of one and the same substance, and some beasts have greater strength and size, yet the form of the human body is [more excellent?] [?]: its stance is upright and lofty, so that it has neither an enormous height nor a mean and abject smallness. Then the very build of the body is pleasant and agreeable, so that it is neither repellent with a brute's bulk nor with slender thinness nor [?].

And first of all let us recognise that the structure of the human body is like that of the world. For as the sky rises above the air, the land and the sea, which are, as it were, the members of the world, so too we see the head rise above the other limbs of our body and stand out as the most excellent of all, like the sky among the elements, like the citadel among the rest of a city's walls. In this citadel dwells a kind of royal wisdom, according to the prophet's saying, "The eyes of the wise man are in his head"; it is safer than the rest, and from it vigour and foresight [flow?] to all the members. For what use is the strength and power of the arms, what use the swiftness of the feet, unless they are supported by the commanding authority of the head as their ruler? On it everything either fails or is upheld. What can courage do unless it has the eye to guide it into battle? What use is flight if sight is lacking? The whole body is a prison in gloomy squalor unless it is lit by the sight of the eyes. What the sun and moon are in the sky, then, the eyes are in man. The sun and moon are the two lights of the world; the eyes are like stars in the head, shining from above and lighting up the lower parts with a clear light, and they do not let us be wrapped in the darkness of night. They are like sentries keeping watch day and night. For they are roused from sleep sooner than the other members, and when awake they look around at everything; for they are nearer to the brain, from which all use of sight flows. Let no one think that I have come down to this point too hastily, praising the eyes and leaving the crown of the head behind; for it is not out of place to praise the whole in one of its parts, and the eyes are certainly a part of the head. So the head explores everything with the eyes. With the ears it searches out what is hidden, learns what is concealed, and hears what is being done in other lands.

And the crown of the head itself: how pleasant and pleasing it is!
