How handsome the head of hair, how venerable in the old, how [?], how [?], how comely in the young, how neatly dressed in women, how soft in boys! Long hair is unbecoming to one sex, a shorn head unbecoming to the other. From trees we may judge what grace belongs to the human head. All the fruit of a tree is in its head; there is all its beauty; its foliage either shelters us from the rain or shields us from the sun. Take away a tree's foliage and the whole tree is unlovely. How great an ornament, then, is the human head, which with the hair of the head protects and clothes our brain, that is, the seat and source of our senses, so that it is troubled neither by cold nor by heat! For there is the fountain of all things, and so where injury does harm, there grace stands out most.

What is a man without a head, when the whole man is in the head? When you see the head, you recognize the man; if the head is missing, no recognition is possible: the trunk lies there undistinguished, without honour, without a name. Only the heads of princes cast in bronze, and faces modelled in bronze or marble, are venerated by men. Not without reason, then, do the other members serve the head as their counsellor, carrying it about with a servant's bearing like a deity and conveying it set on high. From there, with a censor's authority, it directs the services of its little slaves wherever it wishes and decrees the orders each must carry out. You can see each member serving its commander without pay. Some carry, some feed, some defend or perform their own service; they obey it as a prince and wait on it as a master. From it issues something like a watchword: what region the feet must go to, what military duties the hands must carry out in accomplishing their tasks, what rule of fasting or eating the belly must keep under the discipline imposed on it.

The head has a free brow, open with bare temples, which by its appearance betrays the state of the mind: now cheerful, now sadder, now drawn up to severity, now relaxed to gentleness; by outward signs it expresses the inward will. A kind of image of the soul speaks in the face, the foundation of faith, on which the name of the Lord is written and kept every day. Next to the brow come the twin hedges of the eyebrows, which hold up a defence before the eyes and add grace, so that the charm of beauty may smile and careful protection may stand by. For if anything dirty falls from the head, whether sandy dust or the dew of mist or the sweat of a damp crown, it is caught by the eyebrow, so that it does not strike the keen sight and disturb the delicate vision of the tender eyes.

The eyes cling, as it were, to the brows of mountains, so that they are safer under the protecting summit of the mountain and, set as though on high, may look out over everything from a kind of upper stage. For it was not right for them to be low, like the ears or the mouth or the inner hollows of the nostrils themselves. A lookout is always placed on a height, so that the approach of oncoming hostile bands may be detected, lest they unexpectedly seize either the people of a city or the army of a commander while at ease. So too they break up the raids of robbers if scouts are posted on walls or towers or on the brow of a high mountain, so that from above they may survey the level stretches of country, where the ambushes of robbers cannot lie hidden. At sea, too, if someone guesses that he is approaching land, he climbs as a scout of his hopes to the very top of the mast and the high ends of the yards, and from afar greets the land while it is still invisible to the others on board.

And perhaps you will say: if a higher lookout was needed, why were the eyes not set on the very top of the head, as they are on top in crabs or beetles, which, though no head appears, still have necks and backs higher than the rest of their bodies? But they have a strong shell, not a membrane as thin as ours, which can easily be hurt and torn by brambles and other thorns. Other animals too have a form such that they can tuck their eyes either against the neck, like horses or oxen and nearly all wild beasts, or under their wings, like birds, so as to enjoy safe rest. But for us the eyes had to be placed in the highest part of the body, as in a citadel, and also to be defended from every injury, however slight, and these two seemed to conflict. For if they were low down for safety, their function would be hindered; if on the crown, they would lie open to injury. So, that nothing should be taken from the exercise of their function and that nothing [?] for warding off injury, he placed the eyes in a spot where the eyebrows above impart no small protection, the cheeks rising a little below add no slight defence, the nose fences in the inner side, and on the outer side the bulging prominences of the forehead and cheekbones, joined by the framework of the bones, seem to wall round their evened borders. Between these lie the orbs of the eyes, safe for keeping guard, free for looking, and lovely to behold, shining like crystal. In their middle are the pupils, which perform the work of seeing. So that these may not be harmed by any injury that befalls them, they are fortified all round by lashes set close on either side, as by a rampart. Hence the prophet, asking safe help for himself, says: "Keep me, Lord, as the pupil of the eye," so that divine protection might provide for him a guard as careful and safe as that with which God deigned to fortify the pupil of the eye with nature's safest rampart; and also because innocence and integrity are violated when spattered with even slight dirt and lose the gift of their grace, and so care must be taken that no dust gathering on it smears it and no mote of sin troubles it, for it is written: "First cast the beam out of your own eye, and then you will see to cast the mote out of your brother's eye."

So those skilled in medicine say that the human brain was placed in the head for the sake of the eyes, and that the other senses of our body were given a neighbouring dwelling for the sake of the brain. For the brain is the origin of the nerves and of all the senses of voluntary movement, and from it flows the whole cause of the things we have mentioned. Most think, however, that the heart is the origin of the arteries and of the innate heat by which the vital organs are quickened and warmed. The nerves are, as it were, the instrument of the senses; they [?] flow out and are channelled through the parts of the body to each of their particular functions. And so the brain is softer than the rest, because it receives all sensations. From it come also the nerves, which report everything the eye has seen, or the ear has heard, or the smell has breathed in, or the tongue has sounded, or the mouth has received of taste. For what is soft is better suited to feeling with things, while what is hard, from a certain stiffness of the nerves, is more effective for action.

The function of hearing is also most excellent, and nearly equal in grace to sight. That is why the ears stand out further: so that they may display the beauty of an ornament and catch whatever dirt or moisture runs down from the crown, and at the same time so that the voice, echoing in their hollows, may enter the inner windings without causing harm. For if it were not so, who would not be stunned by every louder sound of a voice, since even with these safeguards we often feel ourselves struck by sudden shouting? Then you can see them held out like bulwarks against the harshness of cold and the blaze of heat, so that cold does not penetrate the open passages nor excessive heat scorch them. The winding of the inner ears also provides a certain rhythm and order for modulating sound, since through the windings of the ears a certain [?] is produced, and the sound of the voice, once it has entered, is rendered in certain measures. Experience itself teaches us, moreover, that the very windings of the ears hold fast the speech they receive, since in the [?] of mountains or in the recesses of cliffs [?] in the bend of rivers a voice is heard more sweetly, and the echo rebounds giving back pleasant answers. Even the wax of the ears is not useless, for it binds the voice, so that both our memory of it and its charm remain more firmly within us.

And what shall I say of the nostrils, which with their double and long opening provide a kind of cave for receiving scents, so that a scent does not [?] pass by but lingers longer in the nostrils and through their passage feeds the brain and the senses? So a scent once received is fragrant longer than speech resounds or a sight appears. Often what you have smelled for a brief moment breathes in your nostrils all day. Through them too the waste of the head runs down and is drained away without any harm or injury to the body.
There is also no small sense in touch, and in it a most pleasing delight [?]; for often we test by touch what we cannot test with our eyes.

Last comes the function of the mouth or tongue, which nevertheless supplies strength to all the rest. For the eyes would not have vigour [?] unless they received the strength of bodily substance, which is brought by food and drink, nor would the ears have the power to hear, or the nostrils to smell, or the hands to touch, unless the whole body were strengthened by nourishment. For we fail in strength unless we restore it by the steady taking of suitable food. Indeed, those worn out by hunger take pleasure in none of the delights of the senses, but, as though deprived of them, do not feel their charms.

Why should I describe the rampart of the teeth, by which food is chewed and the voice is given full expression? What nourishment would give pleasure without teeth? Indeed, we often see those advanced in age grow old more quickly for this very reason, that having lost their teeth they cannot take in the strength of more solid food. That is why infancy is mute: it does not yet have the instrument of the voice.

The tongue too has a most precious function, not only in speaking but also in eating. For it is like the plectrum of one who speaks and a kind of hand for one who eats, since it pushes the food that slips away towards the teeth and serves it to them. The voice, too, is carried by a sort of rowing of the air and borne through empty space, and by its force it strikes the air; now it stirs, now it soothes the feelings of the hearer; it calms the angry, raises up the broken, consoles the grieving. Let song, then, be something we share with the birds; but knowing before whom and with what tone of voice one should use it, which belongs to reason, cannot be shared with all the irrational animals. For the senses themselves are common to us and the other animals, yet the other animals do not use them with the same skill. The heifer too raises her eyes to the sky, but does not know what she is looking at; wild beasts raise theirs, birds raise theirs; all have free sight, but only in man is there a mind that interprets what it sees. With his eyes he watches the rising and setting of the constellations, he sees the adornment of the sky, he marvels at the orbits of the stars; he also understands the different brightness of each, when the evening star rises, when the morning star, why the one shines in the evening and the other in the morning, what movements Orion has, what eclipses the moon, how the sun knows its settings and keeps the circuits of its course with regularity. The other animals also hear, but who besides man understands by hearing? Of all the kinds of creatures on earth, man alone gathers the secrets of wisdom by hearing, meditation and prudence, he who can say: "I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me." This is most precious: that man becomes the instrument of the divine voice and expresses a heavenly oracle with bodily lips, as in this: "Cry out. What shall I cry? All flesh is grass." He received what to say, and he cried out. Let those who measure out the spaces of the sky and of the earth with a rod keep their prudence; let them keep their understanding, of which the Lord says: "And the understanding of [?] I will reject." Nor shall I place here the rhythms of oratory [?] and the measures of music as wisdom. Rather I define as wisdom that of which the prophet says: "You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom."

And what shall I say of the kiss of the mouth, which is a sign of affection and love? Doves too kiss each other, but what is that compared with the loveliness of a human kiss, in which the mark of friendship and humanity shines forth, in which the faithful feeling of full love is expressed? Hence the Lord, condemning it in the traitor as a kind of monstrosity, says: "Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" That is: do you turn the mark of love into a sign of betrayal and of faithlessness, and use this pledge, the token of peace, as a workshop of cruelty? So by the oracle of the divine voice he convicts the man who, by a beastly service of the mouth, was bringing death rather than offering the bonds of love. This too is outstanding: that men alone express with the mouth what they feel in the heart, and so we mark the silent thoughts of the mind by the speech of the mouth. What, then, is the mouth of man but a kind of sanctuary of speech, a fountain of discourse, a hall of words, a storehouse of the will? [?] We have finished, as it were, the royal palace of the human body, in which, though it be a portion of some small size, yet in beauty it [?] the rest.

Next comes the throat, through which life-giving exchange and the passage of this breath are poured into the whole body. Then follow the arms and the strong muscles of the upper arms, and hands strong for working and, with their longer fingers, handy for holding. From them comes the readier practice of work, from them the elegance of writing and that pen of a swiftly writing scribe by which the oracles of the divine voice are set down. It is the hand that serves food to the mouth; it is the hand that stands out in glorious deeds; the hand, as winner of divine grace, is laid upon the holy altars; through it we offer and receive the heavenly sacraments; it is the hand that both performs and dispenses the divine mysteries; by its name the [?] of God did not disdain to designate himself, as David says: "The right hand of the Lord has done mighty things; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me." It is the hand that made all things, as almighty God said: "Has not my hand made all these things?" The hand is the bulwark of the whole body, the defender of the head. Though lower in position, it dresses the whole head and graces it with seemly adornment.

Who could worthily describe the framework of the chest and the softness of the belly? For otherwise the softer organs could not be sheltered, and the folds of the intestines would no doubt be injured by hard bones. What is more salutary than that the lungs should be joined to the heart on a neighbouring boundary, so that when the heart blazes with anger and indignation it may quickly be tempered by the blood and moisture of the lungs? That is why the lungs are soft too, because they are always moist, so that they may also soften the harshness of indignation. We run through these things briefly, so that we may seem to touch lightly on what lies at hand, as untrained men, rather than to examine more fully, as physicians, and pursue what is hidden in nature's hiding places.

The spleen too has a fruitful neighbourliness with the liver: while it takes in what it feeds on itself, it wipes away whatever impurity it finds, so that the fine and delicate remnants of food can pass through the smaller fibres of the liver, to be turned into blood and serve our strength, and not be expelled with the filth of dung. And the coiling circles of the intestines, bound to one another though without any knot, what else do they show but the divine foresight of the Creator, so that food should not pass through quickly and run straight down from the stomach? If that happened, constant hunger and an unceasing lust for devouring would arise in men. For with the bowels emptied and drained, being voided in a momentary outflow, an insatiable and unquenchable craving for food and drink would necessarily be produced, which an early death would no doubt follow. So by providence food is first digested in the upper belly, then cooked in the liver, and, digested by its heat, its juice is poured into the remaining parts of the body; and by this substance the human limbs are nourished, which [?] receive for growth and the old for endurance. The rest, as superfluous, is led down through the intestines and drained off through that door in the side.

Indeed, in Genesis too Noah's ark is ordered after the pattern of the human body, of which God said: "Make yourself an ark of squared timber. And you shall make nests in it, and you shall pitch it inside and out with pitch. And so you shall make the ark," and: "you shall make the door in the side, and you shall make the lower parts of the ark with two and three storeys." By this, then, the Lord indicates that there is a door at the rear, through which the superfluous parts of food are expelled. For our Creator, guided by decency, turned the passage of waste away from a man's face, so that we should not defile our sight when we bend down. Consider this too: the parts that are full of shame have been placed where, covered by clothes, they cannot be unseemly.

The pulse of the veins is the messenger either of sickness or of health. Yet although they are spread throughout the whole body, they are neither bare nor uncovered, and they are covered with flesh so light that there is ready opportunity to examine them and speed in feeling them, since there is no thickness of flesh that could mask the pulse. All the bones too are covered with thin flesh and bound fast by sinews; but those of the head in particular are covered with light skin and clothed with thicker hair, so that they may have some protection against rain and cold. What shall I say of the genital organs, which, through veins drawn down from the region of the neck through the kidneys and loins, receive the generative seed for the task and grace of procreation?

What of the service of the feet, which carry the whole body without any harm from the burden? Then the bending knee, by which above all else the Lord's displeasure is softened, his anger appeased, his favour won. For this is the gift of the Father most high to the Son: that at the name of the Lord every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father. For there are two things that above all others appease God: humility and faith. So the foot expresses the disposition of humility and the obedience of diligent service, while faith makes the Son equal to the Father and confesses the same glory of both. And rightly man has not more feet but two; for wild beasts and brutes have four feet, birds two; and so man is, as it were, one of the flying creatures, who seeks the heights with his gaze and flies, as though rowing, by the keenness of his lofty senses. And so it is said of him: "Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's," because he is nearer to heavenly things and loftier than eagles, he who can say: "But our citizenship is in heaven."

But now let there be an end to our discourse, since the sixth day is completed and the sum of the world's making is concluded, now that man has been made perfect, in whom lies the sovereignty over all living creatures, and a kind of summary of the universe, and the grace of all the world's creation. Let us indeed offer silence, since God rested from all the works of the world. And he rested in the inner depths of man; he rested in his mind and purpose; for he had made man capable of reason, an imitator of himself, an emulator of virtues, eager for heavenly graces. In these God rests, who says: "Or on whom shall I rest, if not on the humble and quiet man, who trembles at my words?"

I give thanks to the Lord our God, who made such a work in which he might rest. He made the heavens; I do not read that he rested. He made the earth; I do not read that he rested. He made the sun and the moon and the stars; there too I do not read that he rested. But I do read that he made man and then rested, having someone whose sins he might forgive. Or perhaps even then the mystery of the Lord's future passion was foreshadowed, by which it was revealed that Christ would rest in man, he who was destining for himself a rest in the body for the redemption of man, as he himself said: "I slept and took my rest, and I rose again, because the Lord sustained me." For he who made rested. To him be honour, glory and everlasting duration from the ages, both now and always and for all the ages of ages. Amen.
